NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Visual Field D:
What & why
Visual field defects = loss of part of the visual field, produced by lesions anywhere along the visual pathway — from the retina to the occipital cortex.
The core concept: the pathway is arranged so the site of the lesion produces a characteristic, predictable field defect — so the defect localises the lesion. The single organising principle is the optic chiasm: lesions BEFORE the chiasm affect one eye (monocular); AT the chiasm affect both temporal fields (bitemporal); AFTER the chiasm affect the same side of both eyes (homonymous). One of the highest-yield clinical applications of neuroanatomy.
The visual pathway
📷 Image placeholder — The visual pathway — retina → optic nerve → chiasm → tract → LGN → optic radiation (Meyer’s loop vs parietal) → occipital cortex, with the field defect produced at each level on paired-eye field charts
  • Retina → optic nerve (one eye) → OPTIC CHIASM → optic tract → lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) → optic radiations (temporal = Meyer's loop; parietal) → occipital (visual) cortex.
  • The crossing rule: at the optic chiasm, fibres from the NASAL retina (which see the TEMPORAL field) CROSS to the other side; the temporal retinal fibres stay uncrossed → so after the chiasm each optic tract carries the same half of the visual field from BOTH eyes → a post-chiasmal lesion gives a homonymous defect.
The before / at / after framework: before chiasm (optic nerve) → monocular loss; at chiasm → bitemporal loss (crossing nasal fibres); after chiasm → homonymous loss (contralateral field of both eyes).
The decisive fork: where along the pathway?
Lesion siteField defectCause
Optic nerve / retina (before chiasm)MONOCULAR field loss — a central scotoma (optic neuritis), an altitudinal defect (ischaemic optic neuropathy), an arcuate defect, or complete loss of that eyeoptic neuritis (multiple sclerosis), ischaemic optic neuropathy, giant cell arteritis, retinal artery/vein occlusion; glaucoma too, though that is usually bilateral and asymmetric rather than one whole eye
Optic CHIASMBITEMPORAL hemianopiapituitary tumour, craniopharyngioma
Optic TRACThomonymous hemianopia (contralateral) — "left homonymous hemianopia = RIGHT optic tract lesion"stroke, tumour
Optic radiation — TEMPORAL (Meyer's loop)contralateral SUPERIOR homonymous quadrantanopiatemporal lobe lesion (stroke, tumour)
Optic radiation — PARIETALcontralateral INFERIOR homonymous quadrantanopiaparietal lobe lesion

The PITS rule for quadrantanopias
📷 Image placeholder — PITS memory aid — Parietal radiation = Inferior quadrantanopia; Temporal (Meyer’s loop) = Superior quadrantanopia (“pie in the sky”)
Homonymous quadrantanopia = contralateral PITS: Parietal = Inferior defect; Temporal (Meyer's loop) = Superior defect.
  • The logic: the temporal fibres (Meyer's loop) loop down and forward through the temporal lobe and carry the superior field → temporal lesion → superior quadrantanopia; the parietal fibres carry the inferior field → parietal lesion → inferior quadrantanopia.
The mnemonic: PITS — Parietal Inferior, Temporal Superior. Think: "Temporal lesion = can't see the Sky (Superior); Parietal lesion = can't see the ground (Inferior)."
Bitemporal hemianopia: chiasmal compression
📷 Image placeholder — Sagittal view of the chiasm above the pituitary — a tumour growing UP compresses inferior fibres → upper quadrants lost first (pituitary, adults); a craniopharyngioma pressing DOWN → lower quadrants first (children)

Bitemporal hemianopia = an optic CHIASM defect — loss of both temporal (outer) fields (the crossing nasal fibres are compressed). The direction of compression tells you the cause:

Quadrants worseCompressionCausePopulation
Upper quadrant worseINFERIOR compression (from below)pituitary tumourmore common in adults
Lower quadrant worseSUPERIOR compression (from above)craniopharyngiomaclassically in children, though there is a second adult peak
The logic: the chiasm sits above the pituitary; a pituitary tumour grows UP → compresses the lower chiasmal fibres first → the SUPERIOR field goes first (upper quadrant worse); a craniopharyngioma presses DOWN → the INFERIOR field goes first (lower quadrant worse). The rule: bitemporal hemianopia → image the pituitary/chiasm (pituitary tumour until proven otherwise).
The key localising principles
  • "How many eyes?" — one eye → lesion anterior to the chiasm (optic nerve/retina); both eyes → lesion at or behind the chiasm.
  • "Same side or opposite?" (binocular) — bitemporal (outer fields both eyes) → chiasm; homonymous (same side both eyes) → behind the chiasm (tract/radiation/cortex).
  • "Hemianopia or quadrantanopia?" (homonymous) — complete hemianopia → optic tract (incongruous), a complete optic radiation lesion, or occipital cortex (congruous, macular sparing); quadrantanopia → optic radiation (PITS).
  • Macular sparing → occipital cortex (thought to be due to the large cortical representation of the macula, and possibly a dual blood supply → spared in PCA stroke).
  • Congruency: optic TRACT lesions are characteristically INCONGRUOUS (the two eyes' defects do not match); defects become more congruent (identical in both eyes) the further back the lesion, with the occipital cortex the most congruent of all — which is how you separate a tract lesion from an occipital one.
Causes by pattern
  • Monocular loss → optic nerve OR retina: optic neuritis (multiple sclerosis), ischaemic optic neuropathy, glaucoma, retinal artery/vein occlusion. Amaurosis fugax = transient monocular loss from a retinal TIA (an embolus to the central retinal/ophthalmic artery, usually carotid in origin) — not an optic nerve lesion: give aspirin 300 mg immediately and refer for specialist assessment within 24 hours (NICE), and the patient must not drive for 1 month. Giant cell arteritis — sudden monocular loss over 50 with headache, jaw claudication or scalp tenderness — needs high-dose steroids started immediately and same-day referral, to save the other eye.
  • Bitemporal hemianopia → chiasm: pituitary tumour, craniopharyngioma.
  • Homonymous hemianopia/quadrantanopia → tract/radiation/cortex: stroke (commonest), tumour, abscess — the field defect helps localise the lobe.
Assessment / investigations
  • Confrontation visual field testing (bedside) → then formal perimetry (maps the defect precisely).
  • Fundoscopy (papilloedema, optic atrophy), pupils (RAPD in optic nerve lesions).
  • Neuroimaging (MRI/CT): pituitary MRI for bitemporal defects (urgent neurosurgical/endocrine referral — and sudden onset with headache and ophthalmoplegia is pituitary apoplexy, an emergency needing hydrocortisone); brain imaging for homonymous defects. A SUDDEN homonymous hemianopia is an acute stroke until proven otherwise → emergency stroke pathway and immediate CT head. Note that isolated visual field loss is often FAST-negative posterior-circulation stroke, and is a classic missed diagnosis.
Exam pearls
Organising rule
The field defect localises the lesion; the chiasm: before → monocular; at → bitemporal; after → homonymous.
Driving (DVLA)
A homonymous hemianopia or quadrantanopia normally bars Group 1 driving — the patient must stop driving and notify the DVLA, and the licence is revoked (rare exceptional-case relicensing only). Monocular vision: still notify the DVLA; Group 1 is possible if the other eye meets the standard, but Group 2 is barred.
The urgent ones
Sudden homonymous hemianopia = stroke until proven otherwise (often FAST-negative). Amaurosis fugax = retinal TIA → aspirin 300 mg + assessment within 24 hours. Sudden monocular loss over 50 with headache = GCA → immediate steroids.
Monocular loss
Optic nerve or retina (before the chiasm) — optic neuritis (central scotoma), ischaemic optic neuropathy (altitudinal), giant cell arteritis, retinal vascular occlusion; glaucoma is usually bilateral and asymmetric.
Bitemporal hemianopia
Optic chiasm → upper quadrant worse = inferior compression = pituitary tumour (adults); lower quadrant worse = superior compression = craniopharyngioma (children).
Homonymous hemianopia
Contralateral optic tract ("left homonymous hemianopia = right optic tract lesion").
Quadrantanopia = PITS
Parietal = Inferior, Temporal (Meyer's loop) = Superior.
Occipital cortex
Homonymous hemianopia with MACULAR SPARING (PCA stroke).
Localise the cause
Bitemporal → image the pituitary; homonymous → think stroke/tumour (localise the lobe).
Amaurosis fugax
Transient monocular loss → carotid/embolic (TIA).
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Thoracic Outle:
What & why
Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) = compression of the neurovascular bundle (brachial plexus, subclavian artery, and/or subclavian vein) as it passes through the thoracic outlet at the root of the neck.
The core concept: three structures pass through the same narrow region, but by slightly different routes — the brachial plexus and subclavian artery go through the scalene triangle (behind anterior scalene), while the subclavian vein runs in front of anterior scalene, in the costoclavicular space (which is why venous TOS is a costoclavicular problem) — so TOS splits into three syndromes depending on which is compressed: neurogenic, venous, or arterial. Identifying which is the whole diagnostic task (presentations and urgency differ). The commonest is neurogenic; the vascular forms are rarer but potentially limb-threatening.
  • Often occurs with an anatomical predisposition (e.g. a cervical rib), precipitated by neck trauma or repetitive overhead activity.
The decisive fork: which structure is compressed?
📷 Image placeholder — Three subtypes — neurogenic (pain/paraesthesia/wasting, commonest), venous (swollen cyanotic arm + distended veins, Paget-Schroetter), arterial (pale/cold/claudicating, rarest and most serious)
TypeStructureFeaturesFrequency
Neurogenic TOSbrachial plexus (nerve)arm/hand pain, paraesthesia, weakness, wasting (esp. C8/T1 — ulnar distribution)commonest (~95%)
Venous TOSsubclavian veinpainful, diffuse arm swelling + distended (dilated) veins; cyanotic armrarer
Arterial TOSsubclavian arterypainful arm claudication, pallor, cold, weak pulserarest, most serious
The rule (high-yield): neurogenic = pain/paraesthesia/weakness (commonest); venous = swollen, cyanotic arm + distended veins; arterial = pale, cold, claudicating arm.
Anatomy & causes
📷 Image placeholder — Thoracic-outlet anatomy — the scalene triangle, costoclavicular space and pectoralis-minor space, with a cervical rib narrowing the outlet
  • The thoracic outlet — three potential compression points: the scalene triangle (between anterior + middle scalene), the costoclavicular space (between clavicle + first rib), and the subcoracoid / pectoralis minor space.
  • Predisposing/causative factors: cervical rib (an extra rib from C7 — the classic bony anomaly, though most cervical ribs are asymptomatic incidental findings, so one on X-ray supports but does not make the diagnosis), neck trauma (often the precipitant), anatomical variations (fibrous bands, abnormal first rib, scalene hypertrophy), repetitive overhead activity (athletes, manual workers), poor posture.
The cervical rib point (high-yield): a cervical rib is the classic anatomical predisposition → it narrows the outlet and compresses the bundle.
Clinical features (by subtype)

Neurogenic TOS (commonest):

  • arm/hand pain, paraesthesia, numbness — often in the ulnar (C8/T1) distribution (medial arm, ring + little fingers)
  • hand weakness + wasting of the intrinsic muscles in chronic cases. The lesion sits at the lower trunk (C8/T1), proximal to the median/ulnar division, so both median- and ulnar-supplied intrinsics waste — characteristically with disproportionate thenar wasting (the "Gilliatt-Sumner hand"), even though the sensory loss stays in the ulnar/medial forearm territory. Symptoms are worse with overhead arm positions/activity.

Venous TOS (subclavian vein):

  • painful, diffuse arm swelling + distended (prominent) veins — the arm looks swollen and cyanotic
  • risk of subclavian vein thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter syndrome / "effort thrombosis") — often after vigorous arm use in young, active people

Arterial TOS (subclavian artery):

  • Chronic compression — almost always with a cervical rib or anomalous first rib — damages the subclavian artery → stenosis with a post-stenotic aneurysm → mural thrombus that embolises distally.
  • Painful arm claudication (pain/fatigue on use), pallor, coldness, weak/absent pulse — but note it often presents embolically instead: unilateral digital ischaemia, blue painful fingers or splinter-like digital infarcts, sometimes with a palpable radial pulse. Unilateral digital ischaemia should raise it.
  • The rarest (~1%) but most serious — limb-threatening; acute ischaemia needs emergency vascular referral and CT angiography.
Examination / provocation
📷 Image placeholder — Provocation manoeuvres — Adson’s test (extension, head turn, breath-hold) and Roos/EAST (arms abducted 90°, externally rotated, repeated hand clenching)
  • Provocation tests (reproduce symptoms / diminish the pulse by positioning): Adson's test (neck extension + head turn + deep breath → radial pulse diminishes); Roos test (EAST) (arms abducted 90°, externally rotated, repeated hand clenching for 3 minutes → reproduces symptoms). Both have high false-positive rates — loss of the pulse alone means little, and the test only counts if it reproduces the patient's symptoms.
  • Examine: radial pulses (both arms), arm colour/temperature/swelling, neurological exam (C8/T1 — sensory, wasting), palpate for a cervical rib.
Investigations
  • Chest + cervical spine plain radiographs — identify a cervical rib or bony abnormality, and to exclude an apical lung (Pancoast) tumour.
  • Duplex ultrasound FIRST if venous TOS is suspected (same day) — then venography / CT angiography to demonstrate compression or thrombosis (± provocative positioning).
  • Nerve conduction studies / EMG — usually NORMAL in neurogenic TOS, so a normal study does not exclude it; their real job is to exclude ulnar neuropathy at the elbow and C8/T1 radiculopathy. Abnormal studies point to the rarer "true" neurogenic TOS.
  • MRI/CT — assess soft-tissue causes (fibrous bands, scalene anatomy).
The differential
ConditionDiscriminator
TOSpositional (worse with the arms overhead), neurovascular, ± cervical rib. Provocation tests have poor specificity — often positive in normal people and in carpal tunnel syndrome, so they support but never establish the diagnosis
Cervical radiculopathy (C8/T1)dermatomal, neck pain, root tension signs
Apical lung (Pancoast) tumourRED FLAG — progressive C8/T1 wasting with Horner's syndrome, weight loss, smoking history, supraclavicular mass; exclude on chest X-ray/CT before blaming TOS
Ulnar / cubital tunnel syndromelocalised to the elbow, ulnar territory
Carpal tunnelmedian distribution
Raynaud's / vascular diseasefor the vascular presentations
Management
The principle: conservative first; surgical decompression if conservative fails or for significant vascular compromise.
  • Conservative (first-line): physiotherapy (posture correction, scalene/pectoral stretching, strengthening), activity modification (avoid provoking positions), analgesia — most neurogenic TOS responds.
  • Surgical decompression (if conservative fails): first rib resection ± cervical rib removal, scalenectomy, release of fibrous bands — for failed conservative treatment, significant neurological deficit, or vascular TOS.
  • Vascular TOS: venous TOS with thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter) → this is an urgent presentation: same-day duplex ultrasound, and if axillo-subclavian thrombosis is confirmed, anticoagulate (apixaban or rivaroxaban, at least 3 months) and discuss with vascular surgery — catheter-directed thrombolysis works best within about 2 weeks of symptom onset — then decompression. Remember upper-limb DVT can cause pulmonary embolism, and that most upper-limb DVT is secondary (central line, pacemaker lead, malignancy) rather than effort thrombosis; arterial TOS → surgical repair/decompression (limb-threatening).
Exam pearls
What it is
Compression of the neurovascular bundle (brachial plexus + subclavian artery/vein) at the thoracic outlet.
Three subtypes
Neurogenic (commonest — pain/paraesthesia/weakness, C8/T1), venous (swollen cyanotic arm + distended veins), arterial (claudication, pale/cold arm — rarest, most serious).
Predisposition
Cervical rib (classic), neck trauma, repetitive overhead activity, anatomical bands.
Paget-Schroetter
Venous TOS + subclavian vein thrombosis = "effort thrombosis".
Examination
Provocation tests (Adson's, Roos/EAST) — poorly specific, and only meaningful if they reproduce the symptoms; pulses, C8/T1 signs, palpate for cervical rib.
Investigations
CXR + cervical spine X-ray (cervical rib — and exclude a Pancoast tumour); suspected venous TOS → urgent duplex ultrasound first, then venography/CT angiography; NCS/EMG usually normal in neurogenic TOS (used to exclude ulnar neuropathy and C8/T1 radiculopathy).
Differential
C8/T1 radiculopathy, ulnar neuropathy, carpal tunnel — and a Pancoast tumour, the red flag.
Management
Conservative first (physiotherapy, posture); surgical decompression (first rib / cervical rib resection) if conservative fails or there is vascular compromise. Venous thrombosis → urgent duplex, anticoagulate (apixaban/rivaroxaban, at least 3 months), thrombolysis within ~2 weeks, then decompression. Arterial → emergency vascular referral.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Stroke / TIA:
What & why
Stroke = a sudden neurological deficit due to a vascular cause, lasting >24 hours (or leading to death) — either ischaemic (~85%, blocked artery) or haemorrhagic (~15%, ruptured vessel). TIA = the same process but transient — focal ischaemia WITHOUT infarction (tissue-based: symptoms resolve, usually <1 hour, no infarct on imaging).
The core concept: management pivots on one question answered by an urgent CT — is it ischaemic or haemorrhagic? — because the treatments are opposite (ischaemic → thrombolyse/antiplatelets; haemorrhagic → reverse anticoagulation, never thrombolyse). And "time is brain" — stroke is a time-critical emergency: rapid recognition (FAST), immediate CT, reperfusion within tight windows.
  • A leading cause of death + disability; the deficit localises to the vascular territory.
The decisive fork: ischaemic vs haemorrhagic

The first and most important branch — you cannot treat until you know which (an urgent CT decides):

Ischaemic (~85%)Haemorrhagic (~15%)
Mechanismblocked artery (thrombosis/embolism)ruptured vessel → bleed into brain
Causesatherosclerosis, AF (cardioembolic), small-vessel disease, carotid stenosishypertension (commonest), aneurysm, AVM, anticoagulation, amyloid angiopathy
CTmay be normal early; later low densityhyperdense (bright) blood immediately
Treatmentthrombolysis/thrombectomy + antiplateletsreverse anticoagulation, BP control, neurosurgery; NO thrombolysis/antiplatelets
The rule (high-yield): URGENT non-contrast CT head first — it reliably shows blood and rules it out before any thrombolytic/antiplatelet. Never thrombolyse or give aspirin until haemorrhage is excluded.
Recognition: FAST + the deficit
  • FAST (public/first-responder screen): Face (droop), Arm (weakness/drift), Speech (slurred/aphasic), Time (call 999).
  • ROSIER score — the in-hospital stroke recognition tool (excludes hypoglycaemia; scores face/arm/leg/speech/visual).
Always check glucose (high-yield): hypoglycaemia is a classic stroke mimic → check + correct immediately. Other mimics: seizure (Todd's paresis), migraine with aura, tumour, functional, Bell's palsy.
The Oxford (Bamford) classification

Classifies ischaemic stroke by which territory + how much, using 3 features: (1) unilateral weakness/sensory deficit, (2) homonymous hemianopia, (3) higher cortical dysfunction (dysphasia, neglect):

TypeCriteriaTerritory
TACS (total anterior)all 3large MCA + ACA
PACS (partial anterior)2 of 3 (or higher cortical dysfunction alone)branch of MCA/ACA
LACS (lacunar)pure motor / pure sensory / sensorimotor / ataxic hemiparesis — NO higher cortical/visual signssmall perforators (internal capsule, pons, basal ganglia)
POCS (posterior)cerebellar/brainstem signs, isolated hemianopia, CN palsiesvertebrobasilar
Key discriminators: TACS = all 3 (worst prognosis); LACS = no cortical signs (pure motor/sensory — small-vessel); POCS = brainstem/cerebellar/visual.
Territory syndromes
📷 Image placeholder — the cerebral arterial territories (ACA, MCA, PCA) mapped onto the motor/sensory homunculus — explaining leg>arm (ACA), face+arm>leg (MCA) and isolated homonymous hemianopia (PCA)
ArteryDeficit
Middle cerebral (MCA) — commonestcontralateral hemiparesis + hemisensory loss (face + arm > leg), homonymous hemianopia, aphasia (dominant hemisphere), neglect (non-dominant)
Anterior cerebral (ACA)contralateral leg > arm weakness, behavioural change
Posterior cerebral (PCA)homonymous hemianopia (macular sparing), visual agnosia

The MCA point (high-yield): the commonest territory — face + arm > leg (vs ACA's leg > arm) + aphasia if dominant (the language areas are MCA-supplied).
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — non-contrast CT head — a hyperdense acute haemorrhage vs a hypodense/loss-of-grey-white-differentiation ischaemic infarct (and the hyperdense-MCA sign)
  • Immediate non-contrast CT head — excludes haemorrhage (and mimics); may be normal early in ischaemia → still allows thrombolysis if within window and no bleed.
  • CT/MR angiography — identify a large-vessel occlusion (for thrombectomy); CT/MR perfusion — identify salvageable penumbra (extends the window).
  • Bloods: glucose (mimic), FBC, coagulation, U&E, lipids; ECG (AF); echocardiogram + carotid Doppler (source — cardioembolic vs carotid stenosis).
  • MRI (DWI) — most sensitive for early ischaemia/infarct (also defines TIA as tissue-based).
Acute management of ISCHAEMIC stroke
The principle: exclude haemorrhage → reperfuse (thrombolysis ± thrombectomy) fast → then antiplatelet + supportive care. "Time is brain."
  • Thrombolysis: within 4.5 hours of known onset with alteplase or tenecteplase (tenecteplase now endorsed alongside alteplase) — after excluding haemorrhage + no contraindications (largely bleeding-risk). Extended window: 4.5–9 hours (or wake-up stroke) may be thrombolysed if perfusion imaging shows salvageable tissue (mismatch).
  • Mechanical thrombectomy: for proximal large-vessel occlusion. Anterior circulation — up to 6 hours (with thrombolysis if eligible), and up to 24 hours in selected patients with salvageable tissue on perfusion imaging. Posterior circulation (basilar or posterior cerebral artery) — also considered up to 24 hours with salvageable tissue; a basilar occlusion has the highest mortality of all, so a fluctuating brainstem syndrome warrants urgent CT angiography (NICE).
  • Aspirin: 300 mg as soon as possible (and certainly within 24 hours) once haemorrhage is excluded — orally, or rectally / by enteral tube if there is dysphagia, so the swallow assessment does not delay it; delayed until 24h after thrombolysis (repeat CT first) → continue 300 mg until 2 weeks after onset (or discharge, whichever is sooner), then long-term antiplatelet (§10).
  • Supportive ("stroke unit care"): admit to a stroke unit; maintain glucose/oxygenation/hydration; swallow assessment (aspiration risk — NBM until assessed); permissive hypertension (don't lower BP acutely — the brain needs perfusion; the exception is a thrombolysis candidate, who must be brought below 185/110 mmHg first — uncontrolled BP is a reversible barrier to thrombolysis, not a permanent one); VTE prophylaxis (intermittent pneumatic compression, not early heparin).
Acute management of HAEMORRHAGIC stroke
  • Stop + reverse anticoagulation (warfarin → vitamin K + prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC); dabigatran → idarucizumab; apixaban/rivaroxaban → PCC).
  • Blood pressure control — lower BP more aggressively than in ischaemic stroke: if presenting within 6 hours with systolic 150–220 mmHg, aim for a systolic of 130–140 mmHg within 1 hour and maintain it for at least 7 days. Not offered where the bleed has an underlying structural cause (tumour, AVM, aneurysm).
  • Neurosurgical referral — evacuation of selected haematomas, or management of hydrocephalus/raised ICP.
  • NO thrombolysis, NO antiplatelets/anticoagulants. (Subarachnoid haemorrhage has its own pathway.)
TIA management
TIA = transient (resolves), no infarct — but a warning sign of impending stroke → urgent action.
  • Give aspirin 300 mg immediately (unless contraindicated). This is the one place aspirin precedes imaging — the symptoms have resolved, so a haemorrhage is very unlikely, and the early stroke risk is high. In an acute stroke the rule still holds: CT first.
  • Specialist assessment within 24 hours (ABCD² is not used to decide referral urgency — all suspected TIAs are seen urgently).
  • Carotid imaging (stenosis → endarterectomy if significant) and ECG (AF). Imaging of the brain: do not routinely CT a suspected TIA (NICE) unless an alternative diagnosis that CT would show is suspected — after specialist assessment, MRI is the imaging of choice, on the same day.
  • Driving (DVLA): after a stroke or a single TIA, no driving for 1 month (car/motorcycle); the DVLA need only be told if a deficit persists at 1 month. Multiple TIAs in a short period → 3 months off driving and the DVLA must be told. Bus/lorry (Group 2) licences: must tell the DVLA, and 1 year off. Start secondary prevention (§10).
The rule: a TIA is a medical urgency (high early stroke risk) → aspirin + urgent specialist review within 24h.
Secondary prevention (after ischaemic stroke/TIA)
  • Antiplatelet: after a high-risk TIA or minor ischaemic stroke (non-cardioembolic, haemorrhage excluded, confirmed by a stroke specialist), give clopidogrel plus aspirin for 21 days, then clopidogrel alone. Otherwise, clopidogrel 75 mg daily is first-line long-term; aspirin + dipyridamole if clopidogrel is unsuitable.
  • If AF (cardioembolic): anticoagulation (a DOAC) instead of an antiplatelet. Timing balances recurrence against haemorrhagic transformation: after a TIA, start immediately once imaging has excluded a bleed; after a mild stroke, within about 5 days; after a moderate-to-severe stroke, from about 5–14 days.
  • High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg) — start after ~48h.
  • BP control (the biggest modifiable risk factor), diabetes control, smoking cessation, lifestyle.
  • Carotid endarterectomy — for symptomatic stenosis of 50–99% on the relevant side, in someone with a TIA or non-disabling stroke whose symptoms have stabilised. Refer urgently: the benefit falls away with delay, so surgery is aimed for within 14 days of the event, alongside best medical treatment.
  • Address the cause: AF, carotid disease, patent foramen ovale (in the young), etc.
Exam pearls
Definitions
Stroke = sudden vascular neurological deficit >24h; TIA = transient, no infarct (tissue-based); ischaemic ~85% vs haemorrhagic ~15%.
The decisive step
Urgent non-contrast CT to exclude haemorrhage — treatments are opposite; never thrombolyse/give aspirin until bleed excluded; always check glucose (mimic).
Recognition
FAST (Face/Arm/Speech/Time); ROSIER in hospital.
Bamford
TACS (all 3), PACS (2/3), LACS (pure motor/sensory, no cortical signs), POCS (brainstem/cerebellar/visual).
Territories
MCA (commonest): contralateral face + arm > leg, hemianopia, aphasia (dominant); ACA = leg > arm; PCA = hemianopia.
Ischaemic acute
Thrombolysis (alteplase OR tenecteplase) within 4.5h — BP must be <185/110 first (extended to 9h/wake-up with perfusion mismatch); thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion up to 6h, or up to 24h perfusion-selected (anterior OR posterior circulation); aspirin 300mg as soon as a bleed is excluded, after 24h if thrombolysed, until 2 weeks; stroke unit + swallow assessment + permissive hypertension.
Haemorrhagic
Reverse anticoagulation (warfarin → vit K + PCC; dabigatran → idarucizumab; apixaban/rivaroxaban → PCC), lower systolic to 130–140 within 1 hour, neurosurgery; NO thrombolysis/antiplatelet.
TIA
Aspirin 300mg + specialist review within 24h (urgent — high stroke risk); do not routinely CT a TIA; no driving for 1 month.
Secondary prevention
Clopidogrel + aspirin for 21 days after a high-risk TIA/minor stroke, then clopidogrel alone (or anticoagulation if AF — immediately after a TIA, ~5 days after a mild stroke, 5–14 days if moderate-severe); high-dose statin; BP control; carotid endarterectomy for symptomatic 50–99% stenosis, aiming within 14 days.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Restless Legs:
What & why
Restless legs syndrome (RLS), also called Willis-Ekbom disease, = a sensorimotor disorder characterised by an uncontrollable urge to move the legs, usually with unpleasant sensations, worse at rest and in the evening/night, and relieved by movement.
The core concept: RLS is defined by a specific, reproducible clinical pattern — urge to move the legs + worse at rest + worse in the evening + relieved by movement — a four-part pattern that is essentially diagnostic. The two clinical priorities: check ferritin (iron deficiency is a common, treatable cause that drives the dopamine dysfunction), and treat with dopaminergic/gabapentinoid agents. It links to iron + dopamine in the CNS.
  • A common cause of insomnia; can be primary (idiopathic/familial) or secondary (esp. iron deficiency, pregnancy, chronic kidney disease).
The decisive fork: primary vs secondary RLS

The first clinical question is whether there's an underlying/treatable cause (because treating it can cure the RLS):

Primary RLSSecondary RLS
Causeidiopathic, often familial (positive family history)an underlying condition
Onsetoften youngeroften later / with the cause
Key secondary causes—iron deficiency (± anaemia), pregnancy, chronic kidney disease/uraemia, diabetes/peripheral neuropathy, drugs
The rule (high-yield): always check ferritin (iron deficiency is the key reversible cause) and consider pregnancy, chronic kidney disease, and neuropathy. Drugs that worsen RLS include antidepressants (SSRIs/TCAs/mirtazapine), antipsychotics, antihistamines, and dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide).
Pathophysiology (the iron/dopamine link)
📷 Image placeholder — Iron is a cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase → low brain iron impairs dopamine synthesis — explaining both why iron deficiency causes RLS and why dopamine agonists help
Central dopaminergic dysfunction, and crucially iron is a cofactor for dopamine synthesis (tyrosine hydroxylase) → low brain iron → impaired dopamine function. This explains both why iron deficiency causes RLS and why dopamine agonists treat it. Genetic predisposition in primary/familial cases.
Clinical features

A sensorimotor syndrome: an urge to move the legs, usually with unpleasant paraesthesia, relieved by voluntary movement. (The involuntary movements, PLMS, happen in sleep and are periodic, not continuous.)

FeatureDetail
Urge to move the legsan uncontrollable urge to move; usually at night and worse at rest
Paraesthesiacrawling or throbbing sensations in the legs
Periodic limb movements of sleep (PLMS)repetitive leg jerks in sleep, often noted by the partner
The diagnostic criteria — the "URGE" pattern (high-yield): (1) Urge to move the legs, usually with uncomfortable sensations; (2) worse at Rest; (3) relieved by movement (Getting up/walking); (4) worse in the Evening/night. The relief-by-movement feature is defining — distinguishing it from other leg complaints.
  • Consequences: sleep disturbance/insomnia (difficulty falling asleep), daytime fatigue.
The differential
📷 Image placeholder — Relieved by movement / worse at rest = RLS — the exact opposite of vascular claudication (worse on exertion, relieved by rest)
ConditionDiscriminator
RLSurge to move + worse at rest/evening + relieved by movement
Akathisia (drug-induced)generalised inner restlessness, not confined to the legs; follows starting or increasing an antipsychotic, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine or an SSRI; crucially there is no evening/night pattern — akathisia is also worse sitting still and eased by moving, so "relief by movement" does not separate them
Peripheral neuropathysensory loss/burning, not relieved by movement
Nocturnal leg crampspainful muscle contraction, not an urge
Peripheral vascular diseaseclaudication on exertion (relieved by rest — the opposite)
The key discriminator: RLS is relieved by movement and worse at rest — the opposite of vascular claudication (worse on movement).
Investigations
  • Clinical diagnosis — based on the characteristic pattern (the four URGE criteria).
  • Ferritin — the key investigation, and NOT simply to "exclude iron deficiency". The RLS action threshold sits well above the threshold for diagnosing iron deficiency: offer iron replacement if ferritin is ≤75 micrograms/L or transferrin saturation is <20%, even when the full blood count is normal. (Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant, so it can be falsely normal in inflammation.) Then work out WHY the iron is low — a low ferritin in a man or a postmenopausal woman warrants GI investigation.
  • Consider: U&E (chronic kidney disease), glucose/HbA1c (diabetes), pregnancy test, and review the drug chart.
  • Polysomnography only if diagnostic doubt or to assess PLMS.
Management
📷 Image placeholder — Augmentation (earlier-onset, more intense, spreading symptoms) is the classic dopamine-agonist complication — modern practice favours gabapentinoids first-line; also warn about impulse-control disorders
The overarching principle: treat any underlying iron deficiency + address triggers; then an alpha-2-delta ligand (gabapentin or pregabalin) if drug treatment is needed.
  • Treat the underlying cause: treat iron deficiency — oral iron (ferrous sulfate or fumarate) if the ferritin is low; this alone can resolve the RLS (IV iron is a specialist option). Manage chronic kidney disease, and review and stop the aggravating drug (antidepressants, antipsychotics, antihistamines, metoclopramide) — often curative on its own. In pregnancy RLS is usually third-trimester, linked to iron and folate deficiency, and settles within days of delivery — manage with non-drug measures plus iron, and avoid dopamine agonists and pregabalin.
  • Lifestyle: sleep hygiene, avoid caffeine/alcohol/nicotine in the evening, moderate exercise, leg massage/stretching.
  • Pharmacological (troublesome, persistent symptoms) — FIRST-LINE is an alpha-2-delta ligand: gabapentin or pregabalin (NICE), especially if there is pain or neuropathy. Both are off-label for RLS and are Schedule 3 controlled drugs, so CD prescribing rules apply. Reduce the dose in renal impairment — relevant here, since CKD is a leading cause. The MHRA warns of severe respiratory depression, especially with opioids, in respiratory disease and in the elderly; and pregabalin should be avoided in pregnancy unless clearly necessary (small increased risk of major malformations), which matters because pregnancy is itself a common cause of RLS.
  • Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine patch) are NO LONGER first-line (NICE) — because of augmentation and impulse-control disorders. Warn the patient and their family about impulse-control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating) before starting and ask at every review, since patients rarely volunteer it; also warn about excessive daytime sleepiness and sudden onset of sleep — do not drive if affected.
The augmentation caveat (high-yield): long-term dopamine agonists can cause "augmentation" (symptoms become earlier, more intense, and spread — a paradoxical worsening) → which is why NICE now recommends gabapentin or pregabalin first-line and says dopamine agonists should not be used first-line. If augmentation happens, do NOT increase the dose (escalation drives it) — reduce and withdraw the dopamine agonist slowly with specialist advice and switch to an alpha-2-delta ligand. Also watch dopamine agonists for impulse-control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating) and for sudden onset of sleep. Iron replacement where indicated remains a cornerstone.
Exam pearls
What it is
RLS (Willis-Ekbom disease) = urge to move the legs + worse at Rest + Relieved by movement + worse in the Evening/night ("URGE") ± paraesthesia (crawling/throbbing); often with periodic limb movements of sleep (PLMS).
Primary vs secondary
Primary (familial) vs secondary — key secondary causes: iron deficiency, pregnancy, chronic kidney disease, neuropathy; worsened by antidepressants, antipsychotics, antihistamines, metoclopramide.
Mechanism
CNS dopamine dysfunction; iron is a cofactor for dopamine → low iron → RLS (and why dopamine agonists work).
Investigations
Clinical diagnosis + ferritin — replace iron if ≤75 micrograms/L or transferrin saturation <20%, even with a normal FBC, and then find out why the iron is low.
Management
Treat iron deficiency + lifestyle; then an alpha-2-delta ligand (gabapentin/pregabalin) FIRST-LINE. Dopamine agonists are no longer first-line (augmentation, impulse-control disorders) — and if augmentation occurs, do NOT increase the dose.
Discriminator
Relieved by movement / worse at rest — the opposite of vascular claudication.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Raised Intracr:
What & why
Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) = an increase in the pressure inside the skull above normal (normal ICP = 5–15 mmHg) — a neurological emergency because the brain is enclosed in a rigid box.
The core concept: the whole topic flows from the Monro-Kellie doctrine — the skull is a fixed rigid container holding three things (brain ~1400 mL + CSF ~150 mL + blood ~150 mL), so any increase in one must be offset by a decrease in another, or ICP rises. Once the compensatory reserve is exhausted, ICP rises steeply → reduced cerebral perfusion → ischaemia → herniation → death. Priorities: recognise the syndrome early (headache, vomiting, papilloedema), spot the late/emergency signs (Cushing's triad, herniation), and lower ICP fast.
  • Causes span mass lesions, oedema, CSF obstruction, and venous problems (§3).
The Monro-Kellie doctrine
📷 Image placeholder — Intracranial pressure–volume compliance curve — ICP stays flat while CSF/venous blood are displaced, then rises steeply once the reserve is exhausted (decompensation)
  • The rigid skull holds three components in dynamic equilibrium: brain tissue (~1400 mL) + CSF (~150 mL) + blood (~150 mL) = ~1700 mL total.
  • The principle: because the skull is rigid, CSF and venous blood are displaced first as the primary compensation — if something new appears (tumour, bleed, oedema), CSF is pushed into the spinal theca and venous blood is squeezed out to keep ICP normal at first.
The compliance curve (high-yield): compensation works up to a point — once CSF/venous reserve is exhausted, small further volume increases cause large ICP rises (flat, then steep) → decompensation.
Cerebral perfusion (high-yield): CPP (cerebral perfusion pressure) = MAP − ICP. As ICP rises, CPP falls → cerebral ischaemia → this drives the Cushing's response (§5). CSF is produced at ~500 mL/day in a normal production–absorption equilibrium; disrupting it → hydrocephalus + raised ICP.
The decisive fork: what's raising the ICP?
MechanismCauses
Mass lesion (extra volume)tumour (primary/mets), haematoma (extradural/subdural/intracerebral), abscess
Cerebral oedematraumatic brain injury, ischaemic stroke, hypoxic injury, hepatic encephalopathy
↑CSF (hydrocephalus)obstruction to CSF flow or impaired absorption
↑venous volumecerebral venous sinus thrombosis, venous obstruction
Idiopathicidiopathic intracranial hypertension (§7)
Clinical features

Early features:

FeatureDetail
Headacheworse in the morning, and worse on coughing, exertion, or moving the head — the classic raised-ICP headache
Vomitingeffortless or projectile, and it may occur without preceding nausea — but the presence of nausea does not exclude raised ICP
Lethargy + altered mental statusdrowsiness, ↓consciousness
On examinationpapilloedema and a CN VI palsy (a false localising sign). Note a unilateral dilated pupil is NOT an early sign — it means uncal herniation and is a pre-terminal emergency (see below)
The morning/positional headache (high-yield): worse on waking, lying down, bending over, coughing/straining/Valsalva — because lying flat + raised intrathoracic pressure further raise ICP.
Papilloedema (the key sign): swelling of the optic disc from raised ICP — the optic nerve sheath is continuous with the subarachnoid space, so raised CSF pressure is transmitted along the sheath → the disc bulges forward. Fundoscopy: blurred disc margins and an elevated disc. Important caveat: papilloedema takes hours to days to develop, so a normal fundus does not exclude acutely raised ICP — for example after a head injury. CN VI (abducens) palsy is a false localising sign — its long intracranial course makes it vulnerable to stretch (failure of abduction/diplopia).
  • Late features: persistent vomiting, Cushing's reflex/triad, reduced GCS, herniation (§5, §6).
Cushing's reflex (the emergency response)
📷 Image placeholder — Cushing’s triad — hypertension with a widened pulse pressure + bradycardia + irregular breathing — a pre-terminal sign of critically raised ICP
  • Cushing's reflex = the physiological response to dangerously raised ICP → hypertension + bradycardia.
  • The logic: if ICP is high, MAP must also rise to maintain CPP (CPP = MAP − ICP) → the body drives up blood pressure (hypertension) to perfuse the brain → the hypertension triggers a reflex bradycardia (baroreceptor response).
Cushing's TRIAD (high-yield): (1) hypertension (widened pulse pressure), (2) bradycardia, (3) irregular breathing — the breathing abnormality because the respiratory centre is in the brainstem, and rising ICP compresses it. The rule: Cushing's triad = a pre-terminal sign of critically raised ICP → herniation imminent → emergency.
Brain herniation ("coning")
📷 Image placeholder — Herniation syndromes — subfalcine, uncal (CN III → fixed dilated “down-and-out” pupil) and tonsillar (foramen magnum → brainstem compression/respiratory arrest)

If ICP keeps rising, the brain is forced out of its compartment through the dural openings → herniation:

HerniationFeature
Uncal (transtentorial)the uncus compresses CN III → a fixed, dilated pupil + "down-and-out" eye on the affected side; ± contralateral hemiparesis
Tonsillar ("coning")cerebellar tonsils herniate through the foramen magnum → brainstem (respiratory centre) compression → respiratory arrest + death
Subfalcinecingulate gyrus under the falx
The critical rule (high-yield): a unilateral fixed dilated pupil in a deteriorating patient = uncal herniation compressing CN III → emergency. This is why lumbar puncture is CONTRAINDICATED where ICP is raised — removing CSF from below can precipitate tonsillar herniation (coning). Image first — but note the trap: a normal CT does NOT make an LP safe. If the clinical signs of raised ICP are there (a falling GCS, new focal neurology, seizures, papilloedema, abnormal posturing, bradycardia with hypertension), the LP is still contraindicated whatever the scan shows.
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) — a specific cause
IIH = raised ICP without a mass lesion or hydrocephalus (a diagnosis of exclusion). Classic patient: a young, obese female; risk factors include pregnancy, corticosteroid withdrawal, tetracyclines, retinoids (vitamin A) and lithium.
  • Features: headache, blurred vision, papilloedema, enlarged blind spot, CN VI palsy; the key risk is progressive visual loss.
  • Investigations: neuroimaging (normal / exclude other cause) → then LP shows raised opening pressure with normal CSF constituents (LP is safe here — no mass lesion).
  • Management: weight loss + acetazolamide (↓CSF production); topiramate is an alternative, but note it is contraindicated in pregnancy and in women and girls able to have children unless a pregnancy prevention programme is in place (MHRA) — which matters here, because the typical patient is a young woman; vision-threatening → optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunting.
See the dedicated Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension note for the full workup.
Investigations
  • Urgent CT head — identify the cause (mass, bleed, hydrocephalus, oedema) and guide emergency management; MRI for further characterisation.
  • Fundoscopy — papilloedema.
  • AVOID lumbar puncture if a space-occupying lesion / raised ICP with mass effect (herniation risk) — image first.
  • ICP monitoring (invasive, in ITU/neurosurgical settings — e.g. after severe TBI).
Management (lower the ICP)
The overarching principle: treat the cause + emergency measures to lower ICP + protect cerebral perfusion — a neurosurgical emergency.
  • Treat the underlying cause — evacuate a haematoma, resect/debulk a tumour, shunt hydrocephalus, anticoagulate CVST.
  • Positioning: head up ~30°, neutral neck (aids venous drainage).
  • Osmotic therapy: IV mannitol or hypertonic saline (draws fluid out of the brain). Hypertonic saline is often preferred where the patient is hypovolaemic or hypotensive, because mannitol's osmotic diuresis can drop the MAP and therefore the CPP. Monitor sodium and osmolality. Remember this is temporising — it buys time; it is not the treatment.
  • Controlled ventilation: intubate and keep the PaCO₂ at 4.5–5.0 kPa — the low end of normal, not lower. Hyperventilating below that constricts cerebral vessels and drops ICP, but it does so by reducing cerebral blood flow, and sustained hypocapnia causes ischaemia and worsens outcome. Deeper hyperventilation is a short-term rescue only, for impending herniation, while definitive treatment is arranged.
  • Sedation + analgesia, treat fever/seizures (reduce metabolic demand); CSF drainage (external ventricular drain) if hydrocephalus.
  • Corticosteroids (dexamethasone) — for vasogenic oedema around tumours/abscess (NOT for trauma/stroke oedema).
  • Decompressive craniectomy — surgical last resort for refractory raised ICP.
  • Escalate early. Everything above buys time; the definitive treatment is usually surgical. Discuss immediately with neurosurgery if the GCS is 8 or less after resuscitation, if the GCS deteriorates at any point, if there is unexplained confusion beyond four hours, or if imaging shows a surgically significant lesion. Resuscitate, stabilise and establish full monitoring before any transfer.
  • Fluids: never use hypotonic fluids — 5% dextrose and 0.45% saline both worsen cerebral oedema — and avoid hyponatraemia.
  • Maintain CPP: aim for a CPP of 60–70 mmHg, treating a sustained ICP above 20–22 mmHg. Support the MAP and avoid hypotension and hypoxia, which worsen the ischaemia.
Exam pearls
Foundations
Normal ICP 5–15 mmHg; Monro-Kellie: rigid skull = brain + CSF + blood; new volume → CSF/blood displaced first, then ICP rises steeply; CPP = MAP − ICP.
Early features
Morning headache (worse on coughing/bending/lying/Valsalva), vomiting without nausea, papilloedema, ↓consciousness, CN VI palsy (false localising).
Papilloedema
Raised CSF pressure transmitted along the optic nerve sheath → disc swelling (blurred margins, elevated disc).
Cushing's triad (LATE)
Hypertension + bradycardia + irregular breathing (brainstem compression) → impending herniation.
Herniation
Uncal → CN III palsy (fixed dilated pupil, down-and-out eye); tonsillar ("coning") → foramen magnum → respiratory arrest.
Do NOT LP
If raised ICP with a mass lesion (→ coning) — CT first.
IIH
Young obese woman; RFs (pregnancy, corticosteroid withdrawal, tetracyclines, retinoids); papilloedema + CN VI palsy + visual loss; LP = raised opening pressure; weight loss + acetazolamide.
Management
Treat the cause + head up 30°, mannitol/hypertonic saline (temporising), ventilation to a PaCO₂ of 4.5–5.0 kPa (deeper hyperventilation causes ischaemia), CPP 60–70 mmHg and ICP under 20–22, dexamethasone for TUMOUR oedema only, decompressive craniectomy. Escalate to neurosurgery early.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Radiculopathie:
What & why
Radiculopathy = dysfunction of a spinal nerve ROOT (as it exits the spine) → pain, sensory disturbance, weakness, and reflex loss in that root's dermatome/myotome.
The core concept: a radiculopathy is a root-level (dermatomal) problem — the deficit follows a single nerve root's dermatome and myotome, distinguishing it from a peripheral nerve palsy (nerve territory) and a cord/central lesion (UMN signs). The commonest cause is a prolapsed intervertebral disc compressing the root. The clinical skill is mapping the deficit to the root level using dermatomes, myotomes and reflexes — and recognising the red flags (cauda equina, myelopathy) that need emergency action.
  • Very common (especially lumbar → sciatica); usually a compressive LMN-type root problem.
The decisive fork: radiculopathy vs peripheral nerve palsy vs myelopathy

Three levels produce weakness — distinguishing them is the core localisation skill:

Radiculopathy (root)Peripheral nerve palsyMyelopathy (cord)
Patterndermatome + myotome (single root)peripheral nerve territorybelow the level (long tracts)
SignsLMN (↓reflex, ↓power, dermatomal sensory)LMN (nerve territory)UMN (↑tone, ↑reflexes, upgoing plantars) + sensory level
Painradicular (shooting down the dermatome)local ± nerve territoryoften painless
ExampleS1 radiculopathy → sciatica, ↓ankle jerkcommon peroneal → foot dropcervical myelopathy, cord compression
The rule (high-yield): radiculopathy follows a dermatome/myotome (root), a peripheral nerve palsy follows a nerve, and myelopathy gives UMN signs below the lesion.
Causes
  • Prolapsed (herniated) intervertebral disc — the commonest (nucleus pulposus herniates → compresses the exiting root).
  • Degenerative — spondylosis, osteophytes, foraminal stenosis (commoner in older patients).
  • Other: trauma, tumour (spinal mets), infection (abscess, herpes zoster → dermatomal), spondylolisthesis.
Clinical features

Prolapsed disc usually causes dermatomal leg pain with neurological deficits:

  • leg pain usually worse than the back pain; pain often worse on sitting; the pain is radicular — shooting/electric, radiating down the dermatome.

The deficit follows the root:

  • dermatomal sensory disturbance (numbness/paraesthesia in the root's dermatome)
  • myotomal weakness (weakness of the muscles that root supplies)
  • reduced/absent reflex (if the root subserves a reflex)
Nerve root tension signs: straight leg raise (SLR) reproduces radicular pain in lower lumbar (L5/S1) radiculopathy; the femoral stretch test is used for upper lumbar (L3/L4).

The high-yield trio: L5 = big toe, weak dorsiflexion (mimics foot drop); S1 = little toe/sole, weak plantarflexion, ↓ankle jerk; L3/L4 = medial knee, weak knee extension, ↓knee jerk. "Sciatica" = radicular pain down the back of the leg (usually L5 or S1).
RED FLAGS: cauda equina syndrome (the emergency)
📷 Image placeholder — Cauda equina red flags — saddle anaesthesia, bilateral sciatica, early bladder symptoms (loss of the urge to void) → emergency lumbosacral MRI + surgical decompression
Cauda equina syndrome (CES) = compression of the cauda equina nerve roots (below L1/L2) — a surgical emergency that can cause permanent paralysis + incontinence.

RED FLAG features:

  • Bladder — and the EARLY changes are the ones that matter: loss of the sensation of bladder filling, loss of the urge to void, loss of awareness of urinary flow, a poor stream or having to strain. Painless retention with overflow incontinence is a LATE sign with a far worse prognosis — waiting for it is the classic error.
  • Faecal incontinence or loss of the sensation of needing to open the bowels
  • Sexual dysfunction — loss of genital sensation, new inability to achieve an erection or to ejaculate (often the first thing volunteered)
  • Bilateral sciatica; bilateral or severe leg weakness
  • Saddle anaesthesia (perineal sensory loss) — test this
  • Do NOT rely on a digital rectal examination: normal anal tone does not exclude cauda equina and must never delay the MRI.
Action: immediate hospital admission → emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine, within 4 hours of request and at the presenting hospital (before transfer) → immediate spinal surgical referral with the images. The rule (high-yield): any radiculopathy with bladder/bowel dysfunction or saddle anaesthesia = cauda equina until proven otherwise → emergency MRI. New bilateral sciatica WITHOUT those features = urgent (2-week) spinal/MSK referral with cauda equina safety-netting — and emergency referral the moment any of the above appears.
  • Other back-pain red flags (sinister cause): age <20 or >50 with new-onset pain, trauma, cancer history, fever/weight loss, immunosuppression, IV drug use or recent bacterial infection (spinal infection), long-term corticosteroids/osteoporosis (fracture), night pain, thoracic pain, progressive neurology. No single red flag is diagnostic — it is the pattern that counts.
  • Suspected cervical MYELOPATHY (UMN signs below a level, deteriorating gait or hand function): urgent same-day referral for whole-spine MRI and a spinal surgical opinion — not the lumbosacral-only pathway.
Investigations
  • Diagnosis is clinical — history + the dermatome/myotome/reflex exam localises the root; SLR / femoral stretch for tension signs.
  • MRI spine — do NOT routinely image in a non-specialist setting (NICE). MRI belongs in a specialist setting where the result would change management (considering injection or surgery), or where there are red flags or a severe/progressive deficit; emergency MRI if cauda equina is suspected.
  • Most simple radiculopathies don't need immediate imaging — treat conservatively first.
Management
The overarching principle: most improve with conservative management; escalate for red flags or persistent/severe deficit; emergency surgery for cauda equina.
  • Conservative (first-line for most): stay active / avoid bed rest, analgesia (NICE: NSAIDs at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time are the usual first-line, with codeine ± paracetamol short-term only if NSAIDs are unsuitable — and no opioids for chronic sciatica. Do not offer gabapentinoids, other anticonvulsants, oral corticosteroids or benzodiazepines for sciatica; the amitriptyline/duloxetine/gabapentin/pregabalin ladder is the general neuropathic-pain approach of NICE, not NICE sciatica), physiotherapy — most disc-related radiculopathies resolve over weeks.
  • Epidural injection of local anaesthetic and steroid — considered in acute and severe sciatica (NICE); it is not an escalation step for chronic pain, and spinal injections are not offered for low back pain alone.
  • Safety-net EVERY patient with sciatica: give cauda equina warning information and tell them to attend the emergency department immediately if bladder, bowel, saddle or sexual symptoms develop, or if the leg symptoms become bilateral.
  • Surgery (discectomy / decompression): for severe/progressive neurological deficit, or symptoms refractory to conservative treatment.
  • EMERGENCY surgical decompression: cauda equina syndrome — time-critical.
  • Treat the cause: e.g. spinal mets, infection.
Exam pearls
What it is
Spinal nerve ROOT dysfunction → dermatomal sensory loss + myotomal weakness + ↓reflex + radicular pain; commonest cause = prolapsed disc.
Localisation
Radiculopathy (root/dermatome, LMN) vs peripheral nerve palsy (nerve territory) vs myelopathy (UMN below lesion).
Reflexes
Ankle = S1–2, knee = L3–4, biceps = C5–6, triceps = C7–8.
Dermatomes
C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L1 inguinal, L4 knee, L5 big toe, S1 little toe/sole.
Common lumbar roots
L4 (medial knee, ↓knee jerk), L5 (big toe, weak dorsiflexion), S1 (little toe/sole, weak plantarflexion, ↓ankle jerk); sciatica = L5/S1.
Tension sign
SLR reproduces L5/S1 radicular pain; femoral stretch for L3/L4.
RED FLAG — cauda equina
Saddle anaesthesia, bilateral sciatica, and EARLY bladder change (loss of the urge to void, loss of awareness of flow) — painless retention with overflow is a LATE sign; sexual dysfunction counts too. A normal anal tone does not exclude it. → Emergency lumbosacral MRI within 4 hours + immediate spinal surgical referral.
Management
Mostly conservative (stay active, NSAIDs at the lowest effective dose, physio) — NICE says do NOT offer gabapentinoids, other anticonvulsants, oral corticosteroids or benzodiazepines for sciatica, and no opioids for chronic sciatica. Safety-net everyone about cauda equina. Surgery for progressive deficit or refractory pain; emergency decompression for cauda equina.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Peripheral Ner:
What & why
Peripheral nerve injuries = damage to individual peripheral nerves (or the brachial plexus) → a lower motor neurone (LMN) pattern of weakness + sensory loss in that nerve's territory.
The core concept: each peripheral nerve has a predictable motor + sensory territory and a characteristic mechanism of injury (usually a specific fracture or compression point). The whole clinical skill is pattern recognition — the deficit localises the lesion: "wrist drop → radial nerve → humeral shaft fracture", "claw hand → ulnar nerve", "foot drop → common peroneal nerve". These are LMN lesions (wasting, hyporeflexia).
  • High-yield because the nerve–muscle–fracture associations are constantly tested; most are compression- or fracture-related.
The decisive fork: which nerve, from the deficit + mechanism?

Median nerve & carpal tunnel syndrome
📷 Image placeholder — Median-nerve territory (palmar lateral 3½ digits) with Tinel’s and Phalen’s tests and thenar wasting — the carpal-tunnel exam picture
Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) = compression of the median nerve as it passes under the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) at the wrist.
  • Features: pain + tingling/numbness of the palmar surface of the lateral 3½ fingers, worse at night, relieved by shaking the hand; thenar wasting + weakness of thumb abduction/opposition (LOAF) in chronic cases.
  • The localising point (high-yield): the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves the nerve a few centimetres above the wrist and passes over the flexor retinaculum, not through the tunnel. So sensation over the thenar eminence and the palm is SPARED in carpal tunnel syndrome. Numbness that includes the palm points to a lesion proximal to the tunnel — or to a C6 root problem — and not to carpal tunnel syndrome.
  • Signs: Tinel's sign (tapping over the nerve → tingling), Phalen's test (wrist flexion → symptoms).
  • Causes/associations: idiopathic (commonest), pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly, obesity.
Management: for mild or intermittent symptoms — a night wrist splint in the neutral position, activity modification, and a corticosteroid injection if that is not enough. Refer for decompression (flexor retinaculum release) if symptoms are severe or constant, if there is a progressive or established motor or sensory deficit — thenar wasting or weakness, or if there is no improvement after about 3 months of conservative treatment. Do not put a patient with thenar wasting into a splint and wait: that is axonal loss, and thenar bulk recovers poorly after late decompression.
Ulnar nerve & cubital tunnel syndrome
Cubital tunnel syndrome = compression of the ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel (elbow, behind the medial epicondyle).
  • Features: tingling + numbness of the 4th + 5th fingers (medial 1½), worse on elbow flexion; wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles → claw hand (hyperextended MCPs, flexed IPs of the 4th/5th fingers).
The ulnar paradox (high-yield): a more proximal (elbow) ulnar lesion produces a LESS obvious claw than a distal (wrist) lesion — because the proximal lesion also knocks out the ulnar-supplied flexor digitorum profundus to the ring/little finger (so they don't flex as much). The corollary is that a striking claw points to a wrist lesion, not an elbow one.
Froment's sign is the bedside test of ulnar motor function: ask the patient to grip a sheet of paper between thumb and index finger. Adductor pollicis is ulnar-supplied, so if it is weak they cheat by flexing the thumb at the interphalangeal joint, using flexor pollicis longus (median/anterior interosseous) instead — a visible bend in the thumb as they pinch is a positive test.
  • Management: elbow splinting / avoiding pressure; decompression surgery if severe.
The brachial plexus palsies
📷 Image placeholder — Erb’s palsy “waiter’s tip” (C5–6, upper trunk) vs Klumpke’s claw hand ± Horner’s (C8–T1, lower trunk)
PalsyLesionMechanismPicture
Erb's palsyupper trunk (C5, C6)shoulder dystocia at birth, or traction"waiter's tip" — arm adducted + internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated; C5–6 sensory loss
Klumpke's palsylower trunk (C8, T1)traction on an ABDUCTED arm — classically breech delivery with the arm above the head, or an adult grabbing something to break a fall. Note this is not the shoulder dystocia mechanism, which produces Erb'sclaw hand (intrinsic muscle paralysis); ± Horner's syndrome (T1 → sympathetic)
Erb's vs Klumpke's (high-yield): Erb's = upper (C5–6) = waiter's tip; Klumpke's = lower (C8–T1) = claw hand ± Horner's. Both may follow shoulder dystocia during birth.
The lower limb: common peroneal nerve
📷 Image placeholder — Foot drop from common peroneal (fibular) nerve injury at the fibular neck — high-stepping gait and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot/lateral shin
  • Common peroneal (fibular) nerve — winds around the neck of the fibula (superficial, vulnerable) → injured by fibular neck fracture, tight plaster casts, prolonged leg crossing/squatting, or compression.
  • Features: foot drop (weak dorsiflexion + eversion) → high-stepping gait to compensate; sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot + lateral shin.
  • Also: sciatic nerve (hip dislocation, misplaced IM injection), tibial nerve (tarsal tunnel), femoral nerve (weak knee extension, absent knee jerk).
The foot-drop differential (high-yield) — and how to tell them apart at the bedside, using two movements:
• Inversion (tibialis posterior — a tibial-nerve muscle, but an L5 myotome): preserved in a common peroneal palsy; weak in an L5 radiculopathy or a sciatic lesion.
• Ankle jerk (S1): preserved in both common peroneal palsy and L5 radiculopathy; lost in a sciatic nerve lesion.
So: foot drop with normal inversion and a normal ankle jerk = common peroneal. Weak inversion with a normal ankle jerk = L5 root (look for back pain, and ask about saddle sensation and bladder — a foot drop can be the first sign of a spinal problem). Weak inversion with an absent ankle jerk = sciatic.
Seddon classification of nerve injury
GradeInjuryRecovery
Neurapraxiatemporary conduction block (myelin), axon intactfull recovery (days–weeks) — best prognosis
Axonotmesisaxon severed, connective tissue sheath intactrecovery by axonal regrowth (~1 mm/day)
Neurotmesiscomplete nerve transectionpoor — needs surgical repair
The point: neurapraxia (e.g. "Saturday night palsy" — radial nerve compression while asleep) recovers fully; neurotmesis (a cut nerve) needs surgery.
Assessment & management
  • Assessment: characterise the motor + sensory deficit → localise the nerve; identify the mechanism (fracture, compression, laceration); examine for the classic sign (wrist drop, claw hand, winged scapula, foot drop).
  • Investigations: nerve conduction studies / EMG (confirm + localise + grade), imaging for the underlying fracture.
  • Conservative (compression/neurapraxia): remove the cause, splinting, physiotherapy, treat the underlying cause — many recover; corticosteroid injection (e.g. carpal tunnel).
  • Surgery: decompression (carpal/cubital tunnel), or nerve repair/grafting for transection (neurotmesis).
  • Foot drop / wrist drop: splints/orthoses (AFO for foot drop) + physiotherapy while awaiting recovery.
Exam pearls
Principle
Peripheral nerve palsies = LMN pattern; the deficit + mechanism localise the nerve.
Axillary
Shoulder dislocation → flattened deltoid, regimental-badge sensory loss.
Radial
Spiral groove (midshaft humerus) → wrist drop with TRICEPS SPARED; an axillary lesion also knocks out triceps.
Median
Carpal tunnel → thenar wasting, LOAF, lateral 3½ fingers — but the palm itself is spared.
Ulnar
Medial epicondyle → claw hand, medial 1½ fingers.
Long thoracic
→ winged scapula. Median = LOAF muscles; ulnar = all other intrinsics.
Carpal tunnel
Median compression at the flexor retinaculum, with the palm SPARED (the palmar cutaneous branch passes over the retinaculum); Tinel's + Phalen's; associations (pregnancy, hypothyroid, diabetes, rheumatoid, acromegaly). Splint ± steroid injection for mild/intermittent symptoms — but refer for decompression if symptoms are severe or constant, if there is thenar wasting or weakness, or if there is no improvement after ~3 months.
Brachial plexus
Erb's (C5–6, upper) = waiter's tip, from downward traction/shoulder dystocia; Klumpke's (C8–T1, lower) = claw hand ± Horner's, from traction on an ABDUCTED arm (breech). Horner's in a neonate means a T1 root avulsion — the worst prognostic group, needing early specialist referral.
Common peroneal
Fibular neck → foot drop + high-stepping gait, with inversion and the ankle jerk PRESERVED (weak inversion = L5 root or sciatic; a lost ankle jerk too = sciatic).
Seddon
Neurapraxia (full recovery) → axonotmesis (regrows ~1mm/day) → neurotmesis (needs surgery).
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Essential Trem:
Definition & The Core Concept

Essential tremor = the commonest movement disorder — a chronic, slowly progressive, bilateral POSTURAL + ACTION (kinetic) tremor, usually of the hands/arms, worse with sustained posture and voluntary (kinetic) movement — but without the target-worsening of a cerebellar intention tremor, often improved by ALCOHOL, with a strong family history.

The core concept — distinguishing it from PARKINSON'S disease (the two most-confused tremors, with opposite characteristics): essential tremor is an ACTION tremor — it appears when the hands are DOING something (holding a posture, reaching, writing, holding a cup) and is absent or much reduced at rest. Parkinson's is a REST tremor — worst when still, improving with movement. The single most useful question: “when is the tremor worst — using the hands, or resting them?”
Three more hallmarks clinch it: typically SYMMETRICAL, family-history-positive (autosomal dominant), and RELIEVED BY ALCOHOL, with NO other Parkinsonian features (no bradykinesia, rigidity or gait disturbance). Not a dangerous condition, but frequently functionally and socially disabling (the old label "benign essential tremor" is no longer used for that reason). First-line = propranolol or primidone. Bimodal presentation (young adults + elderly); prevalence rises with age.
The Decisive Fork — Essential Tremor vs Parkinson's Disease
📷 Image placeholder — Side-by-side hands — a symmetrical ACTION/postural tremor (arms outstretched, worse on movement, alcohol-responsive) vs the asymmetrical pill-rolling REST tremor of Parkinson’s
FeatureEssential tremorParkinson's disease
Tremor typePOSTURAL + ACTION — worse with movement/postureREST tremor — worse at rest, improves with movement
At resttremor improves/absenttremor present/worst
Symmetrysymmetrical (bilateral)ASYMMETRICAL (starts one side)
Frequencyfaster (~4–12 Hz, typically 6–12), fine — but overlaps with Parkinson's in older patientsslower (~4–6 Hz), “pill-rolling”
AlcoholIMPROVES the tremorno effect

Other signsNONE (isolated tremor)bradykinesia, RIGIDITY, gait/postural change
Head/voice tremorcommon (titubation, vocal tremor)uncommon
The rule: essential tremor = ACTION/postural, SYMMETRICAL, better with ALCOHOL, positive family history, NO other neurology; Parkinson's = REST tremor, ASYMMETRICAL, + bradykinesia/rigidity/gait. The single best discriminator: essential tremor is worse on ACTION; Parkinson's is worse at REST.
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Archimedes-spiral drawing and outstretched-arm/holding-a-cup manoeuvres to bring out a postural/action tremor (± “yes-yes” head titubation)
✋ The tremor
  • Bilateral, symmetrical, POSTURAL + ACTION tremor of the hands/arms — brought out by holding the arms outstretched, holding a cup, writing, pouring, spoon-to-mouth
  • Absent/reduced at rest; worse with anxiety, caffeine, fatigue + precise tasks
  • IMPROVED by ALCOHOL in about half to two-thirds — a supportive feature, but its absence does not exclude essential tremor, and alcohol also relieves dystonic tremor
🗣️ Other sites + signs
  • HEAD tremor (titubation — “yes-yes”/“no-no”), VOICE tremor (quavering); less often jaw/tongue/legs
  • NO bradykinesia, rigidity or gait disturbance (their presence points away from essential tremor)
  • Family history often autosomal dominant — ask about affected relatives
The rule: symmetrical postural/action hand tremor (± head/voice tremor), worse on action + with anxiety, better with alcohol, family history, no other neurology = essential tremor.
Investigations
A CLINICAL diagnosis (characteristic action tremor + no other signs + family history). Investigations are to EXCLUDE mimics, not to confirm it.
🩸 Exclude reversible causes
  • Thyroid function (hyperthyroidism) — a key reversible cause
  • Review drugs/substances: caffeine, salbutamol/β-agonists, levothyroxine, lithium, valproate, SSRIs, stimulants
🧠 Consider
  • Wilson's disease in the young (copper studies)
  • Alcohol/withdrawal; Parkinson's (if rest tremor/other features → ± DaT scan)
The rule: clinical diagnosis; check TFTs + review drugs/caffeine; consider Wilson's in the young; DaT scan only if Parkinson's is in question.
The Wider Tremor Differential
TremorFeature
Essential (postural/action)worse on action, symmetrical, alcohol-responsive, family history
Rest (Parkinsonian)worse at rest, asymmetrical, + bradykinesia/rigidity
Intention (cerebellar)worsens as the hand approaches a target (past-pointing, + ataxia/nystagmus/dysdiadochokinesis)
Physiological / enhancedfine, fast; worse with anxiety, caffeine, thyrotoxicosis, β-agonists
Dystonicwith abnormal posturing
The rule: action/postural = essential; rest = Parkinson's; intention (target-worsening) = cerebellar; fine/fast + trigger = enhanced physiological (thyroid/caffeine/drugs).
Management
📷 Image placeholder — Treatment ladder — treat only if impairing → propranolol OR primidone (first-line; primidone if asthma) → topiramate/gabapentin → DBS or MR-guided focused-ultrasound thalamotomy
The principle: only treat if it's bothering the patient (functional/social impact); first-line = PROPRANOLOL or PRIMIDONE; escalate to second-line drugs, then DBS / focused ultrasound for refractory disease.
General: treat only if the tremor causes functional/psychosocial impairment (many need only reassurance); reduce caffeine + review aggravating drugs; avoid relying on alcohol (transiently helps, not a treatment).
Drug (first-line)Notes
PROPRANOLOL (beta-blocker)first-line; effective in ~50–70%; start 40 mg two to three times daily, usual maintenance 80–160 mg daily; regular or situational (before social events); avoid in asthma, bradycardia, heart block, uncontrolled heart failure
PRIMIDONE (barbiturate anticonvulsant)first-line alternative (esp. if propranolol contraindicated — e.g. asthma); start LOW + titrate SLOWLY (sedation, acute first-dose reaction — which is exactly why you start 62.5 mg at NIGHT and increase slowly over 4–6 weeks to a usual effective 250–750 mg daily in divided doses); teratogenic
⬆️ Second-line
  • Topiramate — contraindicated in pregnancy and in women and girls able to have children unless a pregnancy prevention programme is in place (MHRA), which matters because essential tremor also presents in young adults; gabapentin; benzodiazepines (e.g. clonazepam — dependence risk)
  • Botulinum toxin for head/voice tremor
🔧 Refractory / severe
  • Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS — thalamic/VIM)
  • MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy
The rule: treat if impairing → PROPRANOLOL (1st-line; avoid in asthma) or PRIMIDONE (1st-line alternative, esp. asthma; start 62.5 mg at night and titrate slowly; the two can be combined) → topiramate/gabapentin/benzodiazepines → DBS / focused ultrasound for refractory. DVLA: the patient must notify the DVLA if the tremor affects safe vehicle control — and warn that primidone, benzodiazepines, topiramate and gabapentin are all sedating.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Commonest movement disorder; bilateral, SYMMETRICAL POSTURAL + ACTION tremor of the hands (± HEAD/VOICE tremor); worse on ACTION, better with ALCOHOL, positive FAMILY HISTORY (autosomal dominant), NO other neurology.
vs Parkinson's
Essential tremor = ACTION tremor, symmetrical, alcohol-responsive, no other signs; Parkinson's = REST tremor, asymmetrical, + bradykinesia/rigidity/gait.
Best discriminator
Essential tremor worse on ACTION; Parkinson's worse at REST.
Investigations
CLINICAL diagnosis; check TFTs + review drugs/caffeine (exclude thyroid/drug tremor); consider Wilson's if young.
Management
Treat only if impairing → PROPRANOLOL 40 mg two to three times daily (1st-line; avoid asthma) or PRIMIDONE starting 62.5 mg at night (1st-line alternative, esp. asthma; slow titration) → topiramate (MHRA pregnancy prevention programme)/gabapentin/benzodiazepines → DBS / focused ultrasound (refractory). Notify the DVLA if it affects safe driving.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Parkinson's Di:
What & why
Parkinson's disease = a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by loss of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra (pars compacta) → dopamine deficiency in the basal ganglia → a movement disorder.
The core concept: Parkinson's is fundamentally a dopamine-deficiency state in the nigrostriatal pathway. Losing that dopamine tips the basal ganglia toward excess inhibition of movement → the classic motor triad of bradykinesia + rigidity + resting tremor. Because it's a dopamine-deficiency disease, almost all treatment aims to restore dopaminergic signalling — and, symmetrically, blocking dopamine (antipsychotics) or withdrawing dopaminergic drugs worsens it or causes NMS. Priorities: the clinical diagnosis (asymmetric, resting tremor, bradykinesia), excluding mimics, and staged dopaminergic therapy.
  • Common in the elderly (~60s+); the second commonest neurodegenerative disease; a clinical diagnosis.
The decisive fork: Parkinson's disease vs the mimics (parkinsonism)

"Parkinsonism" = the syndrome (bradykinesia + rigidity + tremor); Parkinson's disease is the commonest cause, but you must exclude the mimics:

Parkinson's diseaseMimics (atypical/secondary)
SymmetryASYMMETRIC onsetoften symmetric
Tremorresting tremor prominentmay be absent/atypical
Levodopa responsegoodoften poor
Key mimics—drug-induced (antipsychotics, metoclopramide), vascular, Lewy body dementia, PSP, MSA, Wilson's (young). Note essential tremor is a differential for the tremor, not a cause of parkinsonism — there is no bradykinesia or rigidity

The high-yield discriminators:

  • Essential tremor = action/postural tremor, symmetric, improves with alcohol, no bradykinesia (vs Parkinson's's resting tremor + bradykinesia).
  • Drug-induced parkinsonism = symmetric, temporally related to a dopamine antagonist (antipsychotic/metoclopramide) → always review the drug chart.
  • "Parkinson's plus" red flags (atypical syndrome, poor levodopa response): early falls (PSP), early autonomic failure (MSA), early dementia/visual hallucinations (Lewy body), vertical gaze palsy (PSP), symmetry.
The rule (high-yield): asymmetric onset + resting tremor + good levodopa response = idiopathic Parkinson's; symmetry, early falls/dementia/autonomic failure, or poor levodopa response → think a mimic.
The dopamine / basal ganglia mechanism
  • Loss of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra pars compacta → ↓dopamine to the striatum:
    • dopamine normally facilitates movement (excites the direct pathway via D1, inhibits the indirect pathway via D2)
    • ↓dopamine → the movement-suppressing indirect pathway dominates → excess inhibition of the thalamus/cortex → reduced movement (bradykinesia, rigidity)
  • Pathology: Lewy bodies (intracellular α-synuclein aggregates) in surviving neurones — the pathological hallmark (shared with Lewy body dementia).
The therapeutic corollary (high-yield): restore dopamine → improve symptoms (levodopa etc.); block dopamine (antipsychotics) → worsen Parkinson's/parkinsonism; suddenly withdraw dopaminergic drugs → NMS / parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia.
Clinical features: the motor triad
📷 Image placeholder — Parkinsonian posture and gait — stooped flexed posture, reduced arm swing, shuffling/festinant gait, hypomimic (mask-like) face and a “pill-rolling” resting tremor

The classic triad (TRAP):

FeatureDetail
Tremorresting tremor, ~4–6 Hz, "pill-rolling", asymmetric, worse at rest / with distraction, improves with movement
Rigidity"cogwheel" (tremor superimposed on lead-pipe) rigidity — increased tone throughout the range
Akinesia / Bradykinesiaslowness + poverty of movement — the core diagnostic feature; micrographia, reduced arm swing, shuffling festinant gait, difficulty initiating movement, hypomimia (mask-like face)
Postural instabilityimpaired balance (later feature) → falls
High-yield: bradykinesia is essential for the diagnosis — a resting tremor alone isn't Parkinson's. Parkinson's is characteristically asymmetric (starts on one side) — a key discriminator from mimics. Gait: stooped posture, reduced arm swing, shuffling/festinating gait, freezing, difficulty turning.
Non-motor features (often precede motor symptoms)
  • Anosmia (loss of smell — early), REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams — an early marker), constipation, depression/anxiety.
  • Autonomic: postural hypotension, urinary symptoms, erectile dysfunction.
  • Cognitive: dementia (late — Parkinson's dementia; if dementia is early/prominent → Lewy body dementia), hallucinations.
The prodrome (high-yield): anosmia + REM sleep behaviour disorder + constipation + depression can predate the motor diagnosis by years and drive quality of life.
Diagnosis / investigations
📷 Image placeholder — DaTSCAN (dopamine transporter SPECT) — reduced, asymmetric putaminal uptake supporting nigrostriatal degeneration
  • Diagnosis is CLINICAL — based on the UK Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank criteria (bradykinesia + at least one of rigidity / resting tremor / postural instability, with supportive features and no red flags for a mimic).
  • Do NOT routinely image. A DaTSCAN is used for one question only: is this parkinsonism or essential tremor? (reduced uptake in Parkinson's, normal in essential tremor). It does NOT separate Parkinson's from a Parkinson-plus syndrome — uptake is reduced in PSP, MSA and Lewy body dementia too.
  • Do not use a levodopa or apomorphine challenge test to make the diagnosis (NICE). Suspected Parkinson's is referred to a specialist quickly and untreated. A sustained response to levodopa is a supporting feature seen over time, not a test you order.
  • Review the drug chart (exclude drug-induced); consider Wilson's in young patients (copper studies).
  • Driving: Parkinson's disease is a notifiable condition — the patient must inform the DVLA. Anyone with excessive daytime sleepiness or sudden onset of sleep must stop driving until it is controlled.
Management (NICE)
The overarching principle: dopaminergic therapy titrated to symptoms + MDT; the first-line choice depends on whether motor symptoms affect quality of life; never stop Parkinson's drugs abruptly.

First-line pharmacotherapy (the key NICE split — high-yield):
