  • If motor symptoms DO affect quality of life → offer LEVODOPA (most effective for motor symptoms + activities of daily living — but more motor complications long-term).
  • If motor symptoms DON'T yet affect quality of life → a choice of levodopa, a (non-ergot) dopamine agonist, or a MAO-B inhibitor (less motor improvement, but fewer motor complications).

The main drug classes:

ClassExamplesNotes
Levodopa (+ decarboxylase inhibitor)co-careldopa, co-beneldopamost effective; carbidopa/benserazide prevents peripheral conversion (↓nausea); long-term → motor complications
Dopamine agonists (non-ergot)ropinirole, pramipexole, rotigotinefewer motor complications, but the highest risk of impulse-control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating, compulsive shopping) — though these can occur with any dopaminergic drug, so warn everyone, involve the family, and ask at every review. Also hallucinations, and excessive daytime sleepiness with sudden onset of sleep — such patients must not drive and must tell the DVLA
MAO-B inhibitorsrasagiline, selegilineblock dopamine breakdown; mild benefit; useful early/adjunct
COMT inhibitorsentacaponeadjunct to levodopa — prolong its action (reduce "wearing off")
Amantadine—for dyskinesia
Anticholinergicsprocyclidineno longer used for idiopathic Parkinson's; its role is drug-induced parkinsonism and acute dystonic reactions. Do not use where there is dyskinesia or motor fluctuation; avoid in the elderly (confusion)
Levodopa long-term motor complications (high-yield): "wearing off" (benefit fades before the next dose), "on-off" fluctuations, dyskinesias (involuntary movements at peak dose) → managed by adjuncts (dopamine agonists / MAO-B / COMT inhibitors), fractionating doses, or advanced therapies.
  • Advanced / other: deep brain stimulation (DBS) — for motor fluctuations/dyskinesia refractory to medication; apomorphine (subcutaneous), intrajejunal levodopa gel for advanced disease.
Critical safety points (high-yield): NEVER stop Parkinson's medication abruptly, and never let doses be missed → acute akinesia and parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome (an NMS-like emergency).
In hospital, Parkinson's drugs are time-critical: give levodopa within 30 minutes of the patient's own prescribed times (record their home timings on admission; let them self-administer where appropriate). If they cannot swallow or are nil by mouth, do not simply omit the doses — convert to dispersible co-beneldopa down an NG tube, or to a transdermal rotigotine patch using an established conversion, with specialist input.
Avoid dopamine-blocking drugs: metoclopramide, prochlorperazine and cinnarizine (all commonly given for nausea or dizziness in older people, and leading causes of drug-induced parkinsonism), plus typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol and chlorpromazine, and risperidone. For nausea use cyclizine or ondansetron, or domperidone — but domperidone prolongs the QT interval, so use the lowest dose for the shortest time and avoid it with cardiac conduction problems (MHRA). If an antipsychotic is genuinely needed, first reduce the dopaminergic drug most likely responsible, then consider quetiapine; clozapine if that fails (needs registration with a monitoring service); never olanzapine.
MDT care: Parkinson's nurse specialist, physiotherapy, OT, SALT, dietitian; treat non-motor symptoms.
Exam pearls
What it is
Loss of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra → dopamine deficiency in the basal ganglia; Lewy bodies (α-synuclein).
Motor triad (TRAP)
Resting "pill-rolling" tremor (4–6 Hz), cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia (essential), postural instability — ASYMMETRIC onset.
Bradykinesia is essential
Micrographia, shuffling festinant gait, hypomimia, reduced arm swing.
Non-motor (often precede)
Anosmia, REM sleep behaviour disorder, constipation, depression.
Diagnosis is CLINICAL
UK Brain Bank criteria; DaTSCAN only to distinguish from essential tremor (action tremor, symmetric, alcohol-responsive, no bradykinesia).
Mimics
Drug-induced (antipsychotics/metoclopramide — symmetric), vascular, Lewy body dementia (early dementia/hallucinations), PSP (falls, vertical gaze palsy), MSA (autonomic failure).
Management (NICE)
Motor symptoms affect QoL → levodopa; don't → choice of levodopa / dopamine agonist / MAO-B inhibitor.
Drug caveats
Levodopa = most effective but → wearing-off, on-off, dyskinesias; impulse-control disorders can occur with any dopaminergic drug and are commonest with dopamine agonists, which also cause sudden onset of sleep (no driving).
Safety
NEVER stop Parkinson's drugs abruptly or miss doses (→ acute akinesia/parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia); in hospital give levodopa within 30 minutes of the patient's own times, and convert to NG dispersible co-beneldopa or a rotigotine patch if nil by mouth. Avoid metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, cinnarizine and typical antipsychotics; use cyclizine/ondansetron for nausea and quetiapine if an antipsychotic is needed. DBS for refractory motor complications.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Neuroleptic Ma:
What & why
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) = a rare but life-threatening reaction to dopamine-blocking drugs (antipsychotics) — or to sudden withdrawal of dopaminergic drugs (e.g. levodopa) — characterised by fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, and altered mental state.
The core concept: NMS is fundamentally a state of acute dopamine deficiency/blockade in the CNS → and the whole tetrad follows from that. Its danger lies in hyperthermia + rhabdomyolysis (from the rigidity), which can cause AKI and death. The clinical priorities are recognising it early, stopping the offending drug, and aggressive supportive cooling/hydration — and distinguishing it from its main mimic, serotonin syndrome.
  • A drug emergency; commoner with typical than atypical antipsychotics, but every atypical causes it too (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, clozapine) — and atypical-associated NMS may have milder rigidity and less fever, so do not exclude it on that basis. Any dopamine antagonist can cause it, including the antiemetics metoclopramide and prochlorperazine (a phenothiazine, very widely prescribed).
The decisive fork — NMS vs serotonin syndrome vs the mimics
📷 Image placeholder — NMS (lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, slow onset over days, dantrolene/bromocriptine) vs serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, rapid onset over hours, cyproheptadine)

The critical differential — because management differs and they're easily confused:

NMSSerotonin syndrome
Triggerdopamine antagonist (antipsychotic) / levodopa withdrawalserotonergic drug (SSRI, MAOI, triptan, tramadol)
Onsetslow (days)rapid (hours)
Neuromuscular"lead-pipe" rigidity, HYPOreflexiaclonus, HYPERreflexia, myoclonus
Pupilsnormaldilated (mydriasis)
GI—diarrhoea common
Key drugdantrolene / bromocriptine (severe cases only — the evidence is weak and supportive care remains the mainstay)cyproheptadine
The rule (high-yield): NMS = rigidity + hyporeflexia, slow onset (antipsychotic); serotonin syndrome = clonus + hyperreflexia + mydriasis, rapid onset (serotonergic drug).
  • Other mimics to exclude: malignant hyperthermia (anaesthetic-triggered — succinylcholine/volatiles), sepsis/CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis), anticholinergic toxicity, thyroid storm.
The mechanism — why it happens
  • Dopamine blockade: antipsychotics block D2 dopamine receptors → central dopamine deficiency:
    • in the hypothalamus → impaired thermoregulation → hyperthermia
    • in the basal ganglia/nigrostriatal pathway → muscle rigidity (and the rigidity itself generates heat → worsens hyperthermia)
  • There is also a direct effect on skeletal muscle (increased sarcoplasmic calcium release) adding to the rigidity and heat — this is why dantrolene, a muscle-level drug, works.
  • Levodopa withdrawal: suddenly stopping levodopa (or a dopamine agonist) in a Parkinson's patient causes the same acute dopamine-deficient state → NMS-like syndrome ("parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia").
The rigidity → rhabdomyolysis cascade (high-yield): sustained muscle rigidity → muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) → ↑↑CK → myoglobin → AKI.
Clinical features — the tetrad
📷 Image placeholder — The NMS tetrad — hyperthermia, generalised “lead-pipe” rigidity, autonomic instability and altered mental state
  • Most cases occur within about 2 weeks of starting, increasing or switching an antipsychotic — but NMS can happen at any point, including after months or years on a stable dose, so do not exclude it because the drug is not new. Once it starts, the syndrome evolves over 1–3 days (contrast serotonin syndrome, which builds over hours).
FeatureDetail
Fever (hyperthermia)>38°C on at least two occasions; often >40°C in severe cases
Muscle rigiditygeneralised "lead-pipe" rigidity
Autonomic labilityhypertension, tachycardia, tachypnoea, labile BP, sweating
Altered mental stateagitated delirium with confusion, fluctuating consciousness
The mnemonic — "FEVER": Fever, Encephalopathy (altered mental state), Vitals unstable (autonomic), Elevated CK/enzymes, Rigidity.
Investigations
  • Raised CK — the key supporting test; typically at least 4× the upper limit of normal and often in the thousands. It can lag behind the rigidity, so a normal early CK does not exclude NMS.
  • Leucocytosis — raised white cell count.
  • AKI secondary to rhabdomyolysis — myoglobinuria → acute kidney injury; check U&E and creatinine. (A urine dipstick positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy suggests myoglobinuria — serum myoglobin is not a routine UK test.)
  • Check the potassium urgently and do an ECG: rhabdomyolysis causes hyperkalaemia (with hypocalcaemia and metabolic acidosis) — this, not the AKI, is what kills first. Also ↑LFTs.
  • Sepsis is commoner than NMS in a febrile confused patient and cannot be excluded quickly — take cultures (consider LP/CT for CNS infection) and treat empirically for sepsis alongside NMS management until it is ruled out.
Diagnosis is clinical — recent dopamine antagonist + the tetrad + supportive labs.
Management — a medical emergency
📷 Image placeholder — Emergency ladder — stop the antipsychotic (or restart levodopa if withdrawal-precipitated) → IV fluids + active cooling + ICU → dantrolene + bromocriptine in severe cases
The overarching principle: STOP the offending drug + aggressive supportive care (cooling + hydration) + specific pharmacotherapy in severe cases.
  • 1. Stop the antipsychotic — the immediate, essential step. Stop every other dopamine antagonist too, antiemetics included (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine). Do NOT treat the agitation or delirium with an antipsychotic — use a benzodiazepine such as lorazepam. If due to levodopa withdrawal → restart the dopaminergic drug. Note that a depot antipsychotic cannot be stopped: recovery takes days after an oral drug but can take weeks from the last injection, so supportive care must continue for longer.
  • 2. Supportive care (the mainstay):
    • IV fluids — generous crystalloid to prevent renal failure (protect kidneys from myoglobin), titrated to a urine output of about 1–2 mL/kg/hour, watching for fluid overload
    • Active cooling for hyperthermia
    • Benzodiazepines (e.g. lorazepam) — first-line for the agitation, and for mild/early cases
    • manage in a high-dependency/ICU setting; monitor + support airway/breathing/circulation; correct electrolytes; VTE prophylaxis (immobile, high-risk)
  • 3. Specific pharmacotherapy (severe cases):
    • Dantrolene — a muscle relaxant (reduces rigidity + heat generation), given intravenously in critical care, not on the ward
    • Bromocriptine (a dopamine agonist) — restores dopaminergic tone (counters the block)
  • 4. After recovery: mortality is now around 5–10% (historically far higher — the fall is down to early recognition and supportive care). Rechallenge only cautiously: wait at least 2 weeks after complete resolution (longer after a depot), choose an agent structurally unrelated to the culprit, start at a very low dose, titrate slowly, and monitor temperature, pulse, BP and CK. Recurrence risk on rechallenge is roughly 30%.
Exam pearls
What it is
Life-threatening reaction to dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics) or sudden levodopa withdrawal; dopamine blockade → the syndrome.
Onset & tetrad
Onset over days (slow); tetrad = FEVER + "lead-pipe" RIGIDITY + AUTONOMIC instability + ALTERED mental state.
Investigations
↑↑CK (rhabdomyolysis), leucocytosis, AKI (myoglobinuria); exclude infection.
NMS vs serotonin syndrome
NMS = rigidity + HYPOreflexia, slow onset (antipsychotic); serotonin syndrome = clonus + HYPERreflexia + mydriasis, rapid onset (serotonergic) → cyproheptadine.
Also exclude
Malignant hyperthermia — triggered by volatile anaesthetics/suxamethonium, onset within minutes of induction, masseter spasm and a rising end-tidal CO₂ (also treated with dantrolene); plus sepsis and thyroid storm.
Management
STOP the antipsychotic and all other dopamine antagonists including antiemetics (or restart levodopa if withdrawal) + IV fluids (prevent AKI; watch the potassium) + active cooling + a benzodiazepine for agitation — never another antipsychotic; ICU. Dantrolene/bromocriptine in severe cases only (weak evidence).
Key danger
Rhabdomyolysis → AKI; any dopamine antagonist (incl. metoclopramide) can cause it.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Muscular Dystr:
What & why
The muscular dystrophies = a group of inherited disorders causing progressive muscle weakness and wasting, due to genetic defects in muscle structural proteins (most importantly dystrophin).
The core concept: these are primary muscle (myopathic) diseases — the defect is in the muscle fibre itself, not the nerve. The prototype is Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), caused by absent dystrophin → a young boy with progressive proximal weakness, calf pseudohypertrophy, Gower's sign, and a very high CK. The key skills: recognise the myopathic pattern (proximal weakness), know the X-linked inheritance, and anticipate the cardiac + respiratory complications that determine prognosis.
  • Duchenne is the commonest childhood muscular dystrophy and the most severe; Becker is the milder allelic form; myotonic dystrophy is the commonest adult-onset dystrophy.
The decisive fork — which dystrophy?
Duchenne (DMD)Becker (BMD)Myotonic dystrophy
Gene/proteindystrophin — ABSENT (frameshift)dystrophin — reduced/abnormal (in-frame)DMPK gene (CTG trinucleotide repeat)
InheritanceX-linked recessiveX-linked recessiveautosomal dominant
Onsetsymptoms 2–3 yrs; diagnosed ~4–5 yrslater (teens–adult)adulthood (variable)
Severitysevere — loss of ambulation around 10 yrs untreated but typically 13–15 yrs on daily corticosteroids; median survival mid-to-late 20s, extending into the 30s with nocturnal ventilation and cardioprotectionmilder, slowermultisystem
HallmarkGower's, calf pseudohypertrophy, ↑↑CKas DMD but mildermyotonia (delayed relaxation) + distal weakness + systemic
Duchenne vs Becker: same gene (dystrophin), different mutation — DMD = frameshift → no dystrophin → severe, early; BMD = in-frame → some functional dystrophin → milder, later. Myotonic dystrophy is different: autosomal dominant, a trinucleotide-repeat disorder, with myotonia + a multisystem picture.
Duchenne muscular dystrophy — the prototype
📷 Image placeholder — Gower’s sign — the child “walks” the hands up the thighs to stand, indicating proximal/pelvic-girdle weakness; with calf pseudohypertrophy (muscle replaced by fat/fibrous tissue)
  • Genetics: X-linked recessive defect in the dystrophin gene — dystrophin anchors the muscle-fibre cytoskeleton to the membrane; without it, fibres are damaged by contraction and degenerate → affects boys. About two-thirds inherit it from a carrier mother and about one-third are new (de novo) mutations, so a negative family history does not exclude Duchenne. Some female carriers are symptomatic ("manifesting carriers").
  • Symptoms usually start at 2–3 years — delayed walking, toe-walking, frequent falls, difficulty running and climbing stairs, waddling gait, and often speech/language delay. Diagnosis is commonly delayed to ~4–5 years, so check a CK in any boy with delayed motor milestones.
  • Calf pseudohypertrophy — calves look bulky but are replaced by fat/fibrous tissue, not true muscle.
  • Gower's sign — the child "walks up" their own legs with their hands to stand from the floor (proximal/pelvic girdle weakness) — the classic sign.
  • About a third have learning difficulties — and speech and language delay is common, often the earliest clue of all.
The key complication: dilated cardiomyopathy — the commonest association; cardiac + respiratory (diaphragm) muscle involvement determines prognosis.
  • Investigations: raised CK (very high — leaked from damaged muscle); definitive = genetic testing (dystrophin gene); muscle biopsy (immunohistochemistry for dystrophin) is now rarely needed — only if genetic testing is non-diagnostic.
  • Management: supportive — no cure; corticosteroids slow progression (prednisolone or deflazacort; vamorolone is a NICE-approved alternative) — but they cause weight gain, growth suppression, vertebral fractures and adrenal suppression, so every boy needs a steroid emergency card, sick-day rules and stress dosing, and must never stop abruptly. Plus MDT — physiotherapy, respiratory support (NIV), cardiac surveillance/treatment, orthopaedic care.
  • ANAESTHETIC ALERT: in dystrophinopathies suxamethonium is contraindicated — it can cause rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest — and volatile agents can trigger rhabdomyolysis; use total intravenous anaesthesia. Flag any boy with an unexplained high CK or an undiagnosed myopathy before surgery.
The myopathic pattern — dystrophy vs neuropathy vs NMJ
Muscle (dystrophy)Nerve (neuropathy/MND)NMJ (myasthenia)
Weakness patternproximal (shoulder/pelvic girdle)often distal (or mixed in MND)fatigable, ocular/bulbar
Wastingpresent (± pseudohypertrophy)present, with fasciculations (LMN)minimal
Sensationnormaloften abnormal (neuropathy)normal
CKvery high (10–100× normal) in Duchenne/Becker — but normal or only mildly raised in myotonic dystrophynormal or mildly raised (up to a few hundred in about half of MND) — the discriminator is the magnitudenormal
The rule: proximal weakness + very high CK + normal sensation = a myopathy/dystrophy (contrast MND = fasciculations + mixed UMN/LMN; myasthenia = fatigable + eye involvement).
Becker muscular dystrophy — the milder allelic form
  • Same gene as Duchenne (dystrophin), same X-linked recessive inheritance — but the mutation is in-frame, so some partially-functional dystrophin is produced → a milder, later-onset, slower course.
  • Features: like DMD but presents later (teens/adulthood), slower progression, often ambulant into adulthood, longer life expectancy.
  • Cardiac involvement (dilated cardiomyopathy) still occurs and can be significant even when skeletal weakness is mild. Raised CK; genetic testing.
Myotonic dystrophy — the commonest adult dystrophy
📷 Image placeholder — Myotonic facies — bilateral ptosis, temporalis/masseter wasting (“hatchet face”) and frontal balding, with grip myotonia (delayed hand release)
  • Autosomal dominant, a CTG trinucleotide-repeat expansion (DMPK gene) → shows anticipation (worsens/earlier onset down generations).
  • The hallmark = myotonia: delayed muscle relaxation — e.g. can't release a handshake/grip, or slow eye opening after forced closure.
Distinctive multisystem picture — unlike DMD, weakness is often distal + facial: facial weakness, ptosis, wasting of temporalis/masseter ("hatchet face"), frontal balding; distal muscle weakness + myotonia; cataracts, cardiac conduction defects/arrhythmias (need ECG monitoring), endocrine (diabetes, hypogonadism/testicular atrophy), cognitive changes, daytime somnolence.
  • Management: supportive; treat/monitor the cardiac conduction defects (pacemaker risk), cataract surgery, manage the systemic features. Anaesthetic alert: marked sensitivity to opioids, sedatives and anaesthetic agents with delayed postoperative apnoea — and avoid suxamethonium (masseter spasm). Even mildly affected patients are high risk.
General management principles
📷 Image placeholder — X-linked recessive pedigree — a carrier mother, 50% of sons affected — underpinning genetic counselling in Duchenne/Becker
The overarching principle: no cure → multidisciplinary supportive care; anticipate + treat cardiac and respiratory complications; genetic counselling.
  • No cure — management is supportive via an MDT; corticosteroids slow progression in Duchenne.
  • Cardiac (a leading cause of death): in DMD/BMD — dilated cardiomyopathy; ECG and echo (or cardiac MRI) at diagnosis and at least annually, and start an ACE inhibitor (± beta-blocker) by around age 10 regardless of ejection fraction — do not wait for heart failure to appear, because fibrosis precedes any fall in EF. In myotonic dystrophy the problem is conduction disease — that is where the pacemaker belongs.
  • Respiratory support: as respiratory muscles weaken → monitor FVC and watch for nocturnal hypoventilation (morning headache, daytime sleepiness, disturbed sleep) prompting a sleep study; a weak cough risks retained secretions. Non-invasive ventilation (the other leading cause of death, and what has most extended survival).
  • Physiotherapy/OT (maintain function, prevent contractures), orthopaedic care (scoliosis, contractures), mobility aids.
  • Genetic counselling (X-linked in DMD/BMD — carrier mothers, 50% of sons affected, but about a third of cases are de novo; autosomal dominant + anticipation in myotonic). Carriers are not just transmitters: around 1 in 10 develop a dilated cardiomyopathy themselves, so offer them cardiac surveillance (ECG/echo every 3–5 years from early adulthood).
  • Disease-modifying drugs (UK): beyond corticosteroids, ataluren (for nonsense-mutation Duchenne), vamorolone and givinostat are available. Exon-skipping and gene therapies remain investigational in the UK.
Exam pearls
What they are
Inherited progressive muscle weakness from defects in muscle structural proteins (dystrophin).
Duchenne (DMD)
X-linked recessive, dystrophin ABSENT; boys, proximal weakness from 2–3 yrs (often diagnosed ~5), calf pseudohypertrophy, Gower's sign, ↑↑CK; 30% intellectual impairment; dilated cardiomyopathy; genetic testing = definitive; supportive + steroids.
Becker (BMD)
Same gene, in-frame mutation → milder, later onset; cardiac involvement still occurs.
DMD vs BMD
Frameshift (no dystrophin, severe) vs in-frame (reduced dystrophin, mild).
Myotonic dystrophy
Autosomal dominant, CTG trinucleotide repeat (anticipation); myotonia (can't release grip) + distal/facial weakness, cataracts, cardiac conduction defects, diabetes, frontal balding.
Myopathic pattern
Proximal weakness + very high CK + normal sensation (vs MND, neuropathy, myasthenia).
Management
No cure → MDT supportive; cardiac + respiratory surveillance (leading causes of death); genetic counselling; steroids (DMD).
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Multiple Scler:
What & why
Multiple sclerosis (MS) = a chronic, autoimmune, inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system (brain + spinal cord + optic nerves) — immune-mediated destruction of CNS myelin (oligodendrocytes), driven by both T cells and B cells — which is why the most effective drugs are B-cell depleting.
The core concept: MS is fundamentally a disease of "lesions disseminated in space AND time" — ≥2 different CNS sites affected on ≥2 different occasions. The demyelinating plaques are scattered across the CNS (space) and occur as separate episodes over time. Because myelin can be affected anywhere, MS can present with almost any neurological symptom — but sensory disturbance, optic neuritis, and limb weakness are classic.
  • CNS only (oligodendrocytes) — spares peripheral nerves (contrast Guillain-Barré/CMT); typically a young woman (20–40) — women are affected about three times as often as men. Risk rises with distance from the equator (the latitude/low vitamin D link), and the strongest associations are with previous Epstein-Barr virus infection and smoking.
The decisive fork — which disease course?
CoursePattern
Relapsing-remitting (RRMS)the commonest (~85%) — discrete relapses followed by remission (partial/full recovery); no progression between relapses
Secondary progressive (SPMS)begins as RRMS, then evolves into steady progression ± superimposed relapses (many RRMS patients eventually convert)
Primary progressive (PPMS)progressive from the outset (no distinct relapses/remissions) — ~10–15%; older, more equal sex ratio
The rule: RRMS is the commonest pattern; a relapse = new neurological symptoms lasting >24h, in the absence of infection/fever, developing over days and recovering over weeks.
Clinical features — demyelination anywhere in the CNS
📷 Image placeholder — Optic neuritis with a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD); and internuclear ophthalmoplegia (failure of adduction + contralateral nystagmus) from a medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion
SiteFeature
Optic nerveoptic neuritis — the most characteristic first presentation: subacute unilateral visual loss + painful eye movements + red desaturation. Needs urgent ophthalmology/neurology assessment. Steroids speed recovery but do not change the final visual acuity, so they are used selectively — and standard-dose oral prednisolone must NOT be used, as it does not help and increases the recurrence rate. Bilateral, very severe or non-recovering optic neuritis is a reason to test for aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies, because those are different diseases treated differently
Spinal cordsensory disturbance, limb weakness (UMN), bladder dysfunction, Lhermitte's sign (electric-shock down the spine on neck flexion), transverse myelitis
Brainstemdiplopia, internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO), vertigo, facial sensory loss
Cerebellumataxia, intention tremor, dysarthria
Cerebrum / generalcognitive impairment, fatigue (very common), paraesthesia, numbness, trigeminal neuralgia
Classic high-yield signs:
• Optic neuritis — often the first presentation (painful visual loss, ↓colour vision, RAPD).
• Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) — lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) → impaired adduction of one eye + nystagmus in the other (bilateral INO in a young person is very suggestive of MS).
• Lhermitte's sign — neck flexion → electric-shock down the spine (dorsal column).
• Uhthoff's phenomenon — symptoms worsen with heat (hot bath, exercise, fever).
The diagnostic principle — dissemination in space + time

Diagnosis (McDonald criteria) requires lesions disseminated in:

  • SPACE — ≥2 separate CNS locations (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord).
  • TIME — ≥2 separate episodes (clinically, or MRI showing lesions of different ages — simultaneous enhancing + non-enhancing — or CSF oligoclonal bands as a substitute for dissemination in time).
The rule: MS = dissemination in space AND time — one attack in one place isn't enough (that's a clinically isolated syndrome (CIS), which may progress to MS).
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — MRI brain in MS — “Dawson's fingers”: ovoid periventricular white-matter plaques oriented perpendicular to the lateral ventricles (dissemination in space)
  • MRI brain + spinal cord (with contrast) — the key investigation: T2/FLAIR hyperintense demyelinating plaques in characteristic locations (periventricular — "Dawson's fingers", juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord); gadolinium enhancement = active/new lesions (helps establish dissemination in time).
  • Lumbar puncture / CSF: oligoclonal bands (IgG) in CSF but NOT in serum → evidence of intrathecal (CNS) inflammation (can substitute for dissemination in time).
  • Visual evoked potentials (VEPs): delayed responses → evidence of previous optic nerve demyelination.
  • Bloods: to exclude mimics (B12, TFT, ESR/CRP, autoantibodies, aquaporin-4 for NMO, HIV).
The differential — exclude MS mimics
  • Other demyelinating: neuromyelitis optica (NMO/Devic's — aquaporin-4 antibodies), ADEM.
  • Other: B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration), SLE/vasculitis, sarcoidosis, Lyme, HIV, CNS lymphoma, functional.
The rule: MS is a diagnosis requiring exclusion of mimics + the space/time criteria.
Management
The overarching principle: treat acute relapses with steroids; reduce relapses/progression with disease-modifying therapy; manage symptoms; MDT care.

Acute relapse:

  • First, check it really is a relapse. Rule out infection — a UTI or chest infection can unmask old deficits (a pseudorelapse), and steroids on top of an untreated infection do harm. Distinguish a true relapse from a fluctuation or from steady progression. Not every relapse needs treating — discuss with an MS specialist.
  • Then, if steroids are indicated: offer oral methylprednisolone 0.5 g daily for 5 days (NICE). IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3–5 days is the alternative, considered where oral steroids have failed or were not tolerated, or where the person needs admission for a severe relapse or for monitoring. Do not use a lower dose than 0.5 g for 5 days, and do not give patients a supply of steroids to keep at home for future relapses.
  • Steroids shorten the relapse but do NOT change long-term disability or the disease course.
  • Plasma exchange for severe steroid-refractory relapses. Steroids treat the relapse, not the disease.

Disease-modifying therapy (DMT) — reduces relapse frequency + progression:

  • The principle matters more than the roster: DMTs reduce relapse frequency and slow disability, are started and monitored by a neurology specialist, are for active relapsing disease, and do not treat an acute relapse. Treatment escalates from moderate-efficacy agents (injectables such as interferon-beta and glatiramer, and orals) to high-efficacy monoclonals such as ocrelizumab and natalizumab, and early effective treatment reduces long-term disability.
  • Progressive disease: ocrelizumab for early primary progressive MS with imaging evidence of inflammatory activity; siponimod for active secondary progressive MS.
  • Two safety points: natalizumab carries a risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, stratified by JC virus serostatus; and several DMTs — teriflunomide and fingolimod in particular — are contraindicated in pregnancy and need effective contraception, which matters in a disease of young women.

Symptomatic management:

  • Spasticity → baclofen first-line, gabapentin second-line if baclofen is not tolerated or is not enough (avoid using the two together — risk of severe respiratory depression), alongside physiotherapy; fatigue → exercise, amantadine, energy management; bladder → assess residual volume, anticholinergics or catheterisation.
  • Neuropathic pain → a choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin (switch between them if one fails); trigeminal neuralgia in MS comes from a plaque at the trigeminal root entry zone in the pons and is treated with carbamazepine; depression (common) → treat; mobility → physio/OT; MDT (neurology, MS nurse, physio, OT, continence, psychology). Note that NICE says do not offer vitamin D solely to treat MS — it does not affect relapses or progression, and is given only for the ordinary reasons anyone else would need it.
Exam pearls
What it is
Autoimmune demyelination of the CNS (oligodendrocytes; brain/cord/optic nerve); young women 20–40, latitude/vitamin D link.
Diagnosis
Lesions disseminated in SPACE and TIME (McDonald criteria).
Courses
Relapsing-remitting (commonest ~85%), secondary progressive, primary progressive (~10–15%).
Classic features
Optic neuritis (painful visual loss — the classic first presentation), internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF), Lhermitte's sign (neck flexion → shock), Uhthoff's (heat worsens), sensory/spinal/bladder involvement, fatigue.
Investigations
MRI (periventricular plaques/"Dawson's fingers", gadolinium enhancement), CSF oligoclonal bands (in CSF not serum), delayed VEPs.
Mimics
NMO (aquaporin-4), B12 deficiency, sarcoid, SLE, Lyme.
Relapse
Methylprednisolone (shortens relapse, no effect on progression); plasma exchange if refractory.
DMT + symptomatic
Escalate injectables → orals → high-efficacy monoclonals (ocrelizumab/natalizumab); specialist-started, for active relapsing disease, not for acute relapses. Baclofen first-line for spasticity, amantadine for fatigue; MDT. Do NOT give vitamin D as MS treatment.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Motor Neurone:
What & why
Motor neurone disease (MND) = a group of progressive neurodegenerative disorders selectively affecting motor neurones — upper (UMN) and/or lower (LMN) — with NO sensory involvement.
The core concept: the defining signature is combined UMN + LMN signs, WITHOUT sensory loss and WITHOUT eye-movement involvement. That combination — a patient with both wasting/fasciculations (LMN) and spasticity/brisk reflexes (UMN) but normal sensation and normal eye movements — is almost unique to MND, and is the whole diagnostic key. It is relentlessly progressive and incurable — management is disease-slowing + supportive + palliative.
  • Typically late-middle-aged, ± family history; can start focally (a limb, or speech) before spreading.
The decisive fork — which MND subtype?
Subtype% / featuresSigns
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)the commonestBOTH UMN + LMN signs (the classic mix)
Progressive bulbar palsy2nd commonest; worst prognosisaffects muscles of talking + swallowing (bulbar — CN IX–XII)
Progressive muscular atrophybetter prognosisLMN signs only; anterior horn cells
Primary lateral sclerosisslowestUMN signs only
The rule: ALS = commonest, mixed UMN + LMN; progressive bulbar palsy = speech/swallowing, worst prognosis; the others are pure LMN (muscular atrophy) or pure UMN (primary lateral sclerosis).
The core diagnostic signature — mixed UMN + LMN, no sensory, eyes spared
📷 Image placeholder — Diagram: the MND signature — simultaneous LMN signs (wasting, fasciculations, reduced tone) and UMN signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars) in the same limb, with NO sensory loss and preserved eye movements

PRESENT — mixed UMN + LMN signs:

LMN signsUMN signs
Muscle wastingincreased tone / spasticity
Reduced tonebrisk (hyper) reflexes
Reduced reflexesupgoing plantar (Babinski)
Fasciculations (muscle twitches)—
The UMN/LMN mechanism: UMNs normally regulate (inhibit) LMNs → UMN damage → LMNs become inappropriately overactive → hyper signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia); LMN damage → the muscle loses its supply → wasting, fasciculations, hypotonia. In ALS both coexist → e.g. a wasted, fasciculating limb (LMN) with brisk reflexes (UMN) — a hallmark combination.
ABSENT — the crucial negatives: NO sensory symptoms/signs (distinguishes from neuropathy, radiculopathy, MS); extraocular (eye) muscles NOT affected (distinguishes from myasthenia gravis); no sphincter (bladder/bowel) involvement (spared until late); cognition is often affected, contrary to the old teaching — around 10–15% have frank frontotemporal dementia, and up to about half have milder cognitive or behavioural change. This matters practically, because it affects capacity for the gastrostomy, ventilation and advance-care decisions that this disease demands.
Clinical features & presentation
📷 Image placeholder — Clinical image: wasting and fasciculations of the intrinsic hand muscles (“split hand”) and a wasted, fasciculating tongue in bulbar-onset disease
  • Typical patient: late middle age, ± positive family history.
  • Insidious, progressive muscular weakness spreading through the body — limbs, trunk, face, speech.
  • Early complaints: clumsiness, dropping things, tripping, fatigue on exercise, slurring of speech.
  • Bulbar features (progressive bulbar palsy): dysarthria, dysphagia, nasal speech, tongue wasting + fasciculations, aspiration risk.
  • Respiratory: progressive respiratory muscle weakness → breathlessness, orthopnoea, type 2 respiratory failure (the usual cause of death).
The pattern: progressive, painless weakness with mixed UMN/LMN signs, no sensory loss, sparing eye movements → MND.
The decisive fork — MND vs its mimics

MND is a positive clinical diagnosis — the characteristic progressive mixed UMN and LMN picture — but you must still rule out the treatable mimics:

MimicDiscriminator
Myasthenia gravisfatigable weakness + EYE involvement (ptosis/diplopia); MND spares eyes
Cervical myelopathy / cord compressionsensory level + sphincter signs; MND has no sensory loss → MRI to exclude
Multiple sclerosissensory symptoms, relapsing-remitting, CNS-only
Peripheral neuropathy (CMT, diabetic)sensory involvement; MND is pure motor
Lambert-Eaton / myopathyno UMN signs, no fasciculations
The rule: sensory signs, eye involvement, or sphincter involvement should make you doubt MND and look for a mimic — MND is pure motor, eye-sparing, sphincter-sparing.
Investigations
  • Diagnosis is clinical — the characteristic progressive UMN + LMN pattern, supported by EMG, with mimics excluded.
  • Nerve conduction studies: sensory studies are normal — which is what excludes a neuropathy; motor conduction velocities are normal too, though the response amplitudes fall as axons are lost. Look specifically for conduction block, the signature of multifocal motor neuropathy.
  • EMG: ↓ number of action potentials with ↑ amplitude — reflecting denervation + reinnervation (fewer, larger motor units) → supports LMN involvement.
  • MRI (brain + spinal cord): to exclude cervical cord compression + myelopathy and other structural mimics.
  • Bloods: to exclude mimics (CK mildly raised; exclude metabolic causes).
Management
The overarching principle: no cure → riluzole (modest survival benefit) + multidisciplinary supportive care + NIV + nutrition + early palliative care.
  • No treatment halts or reverses progression.
  • Riluzole (the only disease-modifying drug in UK use): a glutamate release inhibitor (reduces excitotoxicity), 50 mg twice daily, for the ALS form of MND. Be precise about what it does: it extends survival, or time to ventilation, by around 3 months. It does not slow symptomatic progression, improve strength or reverse anything. Monitoring: it is hepatotoxic and can cause severe neutropenia — check LFTs monthly for 3 months, then 3-monthly for the rest of the first year, then annually, and tell the patient to report any febrile illness.
  • Respiratory support — the intervention that changes outcome most. Do not wait to be told: measure oxygen saturation on air plus FVC (or VC), or SNIP/MIP, at diagnosis and every 2–3 months. Refer for NIV when FVC is below 50% predicted, or below 80% with symptoms or signs of respiratory impairment (especially orthopnoea), or when SNIP/MIP falls below 40 cmH2O (or below 65 in men / 55 in women with symptoms). A PaCO2 above 6 kPa needs urgent referral, to be seen within a week. NIV (usually BiPAP) improves survival and quality of life, most clearly in those without severe bulbar involvement.
  • The oxygen trap: respiratory failure in MND is ventilatory, not a problem of oxygenation. Giving oxygen alone worsens CO2 retention — do not give it without specialist advice. The answer to breathlessness here is ventilation, not oxygen.
  • Nutrition: discuss gastrostomy early and revisit it regularly — do not wait for dysphagia to become severe. The reason is timing: once respiratory function has fallen, the procedure itself becomes far more dangerous, so early placement is safer than late. Weigh swallowing, weight loss, respiratory function, the effort of eating and the choking risk. Route depends on respiratory function: PEG while it is preserved, RIG once FVC is below about 50% predicted. Malnutrition worsens prognosis.
  • Multidisciplinary care: MDT (neurology, specialist nurse, physiotherapy, OT, SALT for speech/swallowing, dietitian, respiratory, palliative) improves survival + quality of life.
  • Symptom control (know the specific first choices): muscle cramps → quinine first-line, baclofen second-line; spasticity → an exercise programme plus baclofen (or tizanidine, dantrolene, gabapentin); drooling → an antimuscarinic first-line, glycopyrronium if there is cognitive impairment (it penetrates the brain poorly), with referral for botulinum toxin A only if that fails; thick secretions → carbocisteine; emotional lability (pseudobulbar affect) → amitriptyline or an SSRI; communication aids via SALT.
  • Early palliative care + advance care planning: given the progressive fatal course — discuss ventilation wishes, an advance decision to refuse treatment, DNACPR, preferred place of death and an emergency healthcare plan, while the person still has capacity to make them. Breathlessness at the end of life: consider opioids, and a benzodiazepine where anxiety is driving it; prescribe anticipatory medicines for people using NIV at home.
Prognosis: patients typically die of respiratory failure or pneumonia — usually within 2–4 years of onset.
Exam pearls
What it is
Progressive degeneration of motor neurones, MIXED UMN + LMN signs, NO sensory loss, EYE MOVEMENTS SPARED, sphincters spared.
Subtypes
ALS (commonest — UMN + LMN), progressive bulbar palsy (speech/swallowing, worst prognosis), progressive muscular atrophy (LMN only), primary lateral sclerosis (UMN only).
Signature combination
A wasted, fasciculating limb (LMN) with brisk reflexes + upgoing plantars (UMN) — and normal sensation.
Key negatives
No sensory signs, eyes spared (vs myasthenia = eye involvement), sphincters spared.
Exclude mimics
Cervical cord compression (MRI — sensory level/sphincters), myasthenia gravis, MS, neuropathy.
Investigations
Positive clinical diagnosis supported by EMG (↓ number of APs with ↑ amplitude — denervation + reinnervation); normal SENSORY studies; MRI to exclude cord compression.
Management
Riluzole (glutamate release inhibitor — extends survival by about 3 months in ALS; monitor LFTs); NIV when FVC <50% predicted, or <80% with symptoms — measure FVC every 2–3 months, and never treat the breathlessness with oxygen alone; discuss gastrostomy EARLY (late placement is more dangerous); quinine for cramps, glycopyrronium for drooling; MDT and early palliative care.
Prognosis
Death from respiratory failure/pneumonia, usually within 2–4 years.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Meningitis / E:
What & why
Meningitis = inflammation of the meninges (membranes covering the brain/spinal cord) — usually infective (bacterial or viral). Encephalitis = inflammation of the brain parenchyma itself — usually viral (classically HSV).
The core concept: the crucial distinction is where the inflammation is — meningitis affects the coverings (→ meningism: headache, neck stiffness, photophobia) while encephalitis affects the brain substance (→ altered brain function: confusion, personality/behaviour change, seizures, focal deficits). They overlap (meningoencephalitis), but the split guides the two treatment reflexes: bacterial meningitis → immediate antibiotics and encephalitis → immediate aciclovir. Both are time-critical emergencies.
  • Bacterial meningitis has high mortality; do not delay treatment for investigations.
The decisive fork — meninges vs brain
MeningitisEncephalitis
Sitemeninges (coverings)brain parenchyma
HallmarkMENINGISM — headache, neck stiffness, photophobiaALTERED BRAIN FUNCTION — confusion, ↓consciousness, personality/behaviour change, seizures, focal deficits
Commonest causebacterial or viralviral — HSV-1
Treatment refleximmediate antibiotics (if bacterial)immediate IV aciclovir
The rule: meningism (neck stiffness/photophobia) → meningitis; altered mental state / personality change / seizures / focal deficit → encephalitis. They overlap → meningoencephalitis; if in doubt, cover both (antibiotics + aciclovir).
Bacterial vs viral meningitis
📷 Image placeholder — meningococcal non-blanching purpuric rash (negative glass/tumbler test); and Kernig's / Brudzinski's meningism signs
BacterialViral
Severitysevere, life-threateningusually self-limiting
Onsetrapid (hours)more gradual
CSFturbid; ↑↑neutrophils; ↑↑protein; ↓↓glucoseclear; ↑lymphocytes; normal/↑protein; normal glucose
Commonest causesNeisseria meningitidis, Strep pneumoniaeenteroviruses (commonest), HSV, mumps

Bacterial causes by age:

GroupCommon organisms
Under 3 monthsGroup B Strep (much the commonest), then E. coli and Listeria
Children / young adultsStrep pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis — since the MenB and MenACWY programmes, pneumococcus is now the commoner of the two in the UK. Think Haemophilus influenzae type b in an unimmunised or incompletely immunised child.
Elderly / immunocompromised / pregnant+ Listeria monocytogenes (→ add amoxicillin)
Clinical features
  • The classic triad: fever + neck stiffness + altered mental status (all three in a minority — don't wait for the full triad).
  • Meningism: headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, nausea/vomiting.
  • Meningeal signs: Kernig's sign (pain on knee extension with hip flexed), Brudzinski's sign (neck flexion → involuntary hip/knee flexion).
  • In infants: non-specific — fever, lethargy, poor feeding, irritability, bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry.
  • Raised ICP signs: reduced consciousness, papilloedema, focal signs, seizures.
Meningococcal septicaemia: a non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash (doesn't fade under a glass — "tumbler test") → septicaemia, a life-threatening emergency (can occur with or without meningitis).
Investigations
  • Blood cultures + bloods: FBC, CRP, whole-blood PCR for meningococcal/pneumococcal DNA, glucose (for CSF:blood ratio), U&E, clotting.
  • Lumbar puncture + CSF (the key test): send for cell count/differential, protein, glucose (with paired blood glucose), Gram stain, culture, PCR (viral/bacterial).

CSF interpretation:

BacterialViralTB/fungal
Appearanceturbid/cloudyclearfibrin web
Cells↑↑ neutrophils (polymorphs)↑ lymphocytes↑ lymphocytes
Protein↑↑ highnormal/mildly ↑↑↑ high
Glucose (CSF:blood)↓↓ low (<0.5)normal↓ low
Before the LP — two separate questions. (1) Does this patient need a scan first? Most do not. Image first only if there are signs of raised intracranial pressure, new focal neurology (including seizures or posturing), GCS of 9 or less, a progressive or rapid fall in consciousness, or a risk of a space-occupying lesion (NICE). Note that a normal CT does not make an LP safe if the clinical signs of raised ICP are there. (2) Is the LP safe to do at all right now? Shock, respiratory compromise, coagulopathy or infection over the LP site mean you defer the LP until it is corrected — a CT does not help with any of those. CRITICAL: neither question delays antibiotics — take blood cultures, give the antibiotics, then image or tap.
Management of meningitis (NICE)
The overarching principle: don't delay antibiotics; community benzylpenicillin; hospital ceftriaxone + dexamethasone (but not steroids in meningococcal disease); add amoxicillin for Listeria cover; notify, and give prophylaxis to meningococcal contacts.
  • Community / pre-hospital: strongly suspected meningococcal disease (esp. a non-blanching rash) → IM or IV benzylpenicillin (or ceftriaxone) immediately: under 1 year 300 mg; 1–9 years 600 mg; 10 years and over, including adults, 1.2 g. The overriding rule is that it must not delay transfer — if giving it would hold the ambulance up, go.

Hospital — empirical treatment (start within 1 hour):

  • IV ceftriaxone = first-line empirical antibiotic at any age. Use cefotaxime instead in a neonate who is jaundiced, acidotic or hypoalbuminaemic, who is pre-term, or who is receiving a calcium-containing infusion (MHRA). Every baby under 3 months also gets IV amoxicillin for Listeria — that is automatic, not risk-stratified.
  • ADD IV amoxicillin if there is Listeria risk: babies under 3 months, adults aged 60 and over, pregnancy, and the immunocompromised (including diabetes, chronic liver or kidney disease, and alcohol excess). Cephalosporins do not cover Listeria.
  • IV dexamethasone — 10 mg (children 0.15 mg/kg, max 10 mg) 6-hourly for 4 days, given with or just before the first antibiotic dose, in anyone over 3 months with strongly suspected or confirmed bacterial meningitis. It reduces neurological complications, especially hearing loss, and the benefit is greatest in pneumococcal meningitis. If it is missed, it can still be given up to 12 hours late. Never delay antibiotics to give it.
  • The exception — do NOT routinely give corticosteroids in meningococcal disease (NICE): they do not help and have been associated with higher mortality. The only steroid role there is low-dose replacement in septic shock that is not responding to high-dose vasoactive drugs.
  • Do NOT routinely give aciclovir unless encephalitis is suspected — but if the patient is confused or seizing as well as febrile, cover both (antibiotics AND aciclovir) until you know.
  • Antibiotic duration: tailor it to the organism — about 10 days where the CSF suggests bacterial meningitis but nothing grows, shorter for meningococcal, and 21 days for Listeria.
  • Supportive: ABCDE, fluids/shock management (septicaemia), ICU if severe, treat raised ICP/seizures.
  • Public health: acute meningitis and meningococcal septicaemia are NOTIFIABLE → inform public health at once. Separately, chemoprophylaxis is for close contacts of meningococcal disease (and of Hib) only — a single dose of ciprofloxacin, suitable at any age including pregnancy, ideally within 24 hours; rifampicin is the alternative. Contacts are also offered vaccination where the serogroup is vaccine-preventable. Contacts of pneumococcal, group B streptococcal and viral meningitis need no prophylaxis.
Complications: sensorineural hearing loss (commonest — audiology follow-up), seizures/epilepsy, hydrocephalus, focal deficits, cognitive impairment, death; Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (adrenal haemorrhage in meningococcal septicaemia).
Encephalitis — the "aciclovir" reflex
📷 Image placeholder — HSV encephalitis — MRI showing unilateral medial temporal lobe oedema/hyperintensity
Inflammation of the brain parenchyma — usually viral; the crucial treatable cause is herpes simplex virus (HSV-1).
  • Causes: HSV-1 (the key one — treatable), other herpesviruses (VZV, CMV, EBV), enteroviruses, and autoimmune encephalitis (e.g. anti-NMDA receptor — the key non-infective cause).

Clinical features:

  • Altered mental state / ↓consciousness, confusion, personality + behaviour change; fever, headache, seizures, focal neurology (dysphasia, hemiparesis).
  • HSV encephalitis targets the temporal lobes → memory/behaviour/psychiatric features (can mimic psychiatric illness).

Investigations:

  • LP/CSF: lymphocytic picture (like viral meningitis), ↑protein, normal glucose; HSV PCR (the diagnostic test — but can be negative very early).
  • MRI: temporal lobe changes (oedema/hyperintensity) in HSV encephalitis.
  • EEG: may show temporal lobe abnormalities.
Management — the reflex: suspected encephalitis → start IV aciclovir NOW, 10 mg/kg 8-hourly, empirically — do NOT wait for the PCR. It stays intravenous throughout; the course is 14 days in confirmed HSV encephalitis (21 days if immunocompromised). In a febrile patient who is confused or seizing, give antibiotics as well — you cannot tell meningitis from encephalitis at the bedside, so cover both. Supportive care (ICU, seizures, raised ICP); treat autoimmune encephalitis with immunotherapy (steroids/IVIG) + tumour search. Mirrors "suspected bacterial meningitis → start antibiotics now".
Exam pearls
Meningitis vs encephalitis
Meningitis = meninges (MENINGISM: neck stiffness/photophobia); encephalitis = brain parenchyma (ALTERED BRAIN FUNCTION: confusion, behaviour change, seizures); overlap = meningoencephalitis.
Bacterial causes by age
Under 3 months → GBS (commonest)/E. coli/Listeria; children/adults → pneumococcus and meningococcus (Hib if unimmunised); 60 and over/pregnant/immunocompromised → + Listeria (add amoxicillin).
Signs
Kernig's, Brudzinski's; non-blanching rash → meningococcal septicaemia (tumbler test — emergency).
CSF
Bacterial = neutrophils, ↑↑protein, ↓↓glucose, turbid; viral = lymphocytes, normal glucose, clear; TB = lymphocytes, ↑↑protein, ↓glucose, fibrin web.
LP caution
Most patients need no scan before LP — image first only for raised ICP, new focal signs/seizures, GCS ≤9 or a falling GCS. Shock or coagulopathy means defer the LP, not scan it. NEVER delay antibiotics for either.
Meningitis management
Community → IM benzylpenicillin (under 1y 300 mg, 1–9y 600 mg, 10y+ 1.2 g) but never delay transfer; hospital → IV ceftriaxone + dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly for 4 days (+ amoxicillin if Listeria risk) — but NOT steroids in meningococcal disease; notifiable, with ciprofloxacin prophylaxis for meningococcal contacts only; commonest complication = hearing loss.
Encephalitis
Usually HSV-1 → temporal lobes; CSF lymphocytic + HSV PCR, MRI temporal lobe changes; START IV ACICLOVIR IMMEDIATELY (empirically); consider autoimmune (anti-NMDA).
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ménière's Dise:
What & why
Ménière's disease = a chronic inner-ear disorder — the triad of episodic vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss, and tinnitus, with aural fullness — caused by endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph in the inner ear).
The core concept: the diagnosis is the classic triad + ear fullness, in episodic attacks lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, on a background of fluctuating then progressive sensorineural hearing loss. It sits within the wider peripheral vertigo differential — so the key skill is placing it correctly among the causes of vertigo (BPPV, vestibular neuronitis, labyrinthitis, acoustic neuroma) and distinguishing peripheral from central vertigo (the must-not-miss being a posterior circulation stroke).
  • Typically middle-aged adults; usually unilateral (initially); a relapsing condition that can significantly affect quality of life.
The decisive fork — peripheral vs central vertigo

Before diagnosing Ménière's (a peripheral cause), place the vertigo — peripheral (inner ear) vs central (brainstem/cerebellum); the central causes are the dangerous ones:

FeaturePeripheral (inner ear)Central (brainstem/cerebellum)
Durationvaries with the cause — BPPV seconds, Ménière's 20 min – 12 h, neuronitis/labyrinthitis daysusually continuous once established — but vestibular migraine and TIA are episodic, so duration alone never separates the two
Hearing loss/tinnitusoften present (except BPPV)usually absent — but new hearing loss does NOT exclude a stroke: AICA infarction causes vertigo with sudden deafness
Coordinationintactimpaired (cerebellar signs)
Other neurologynoneataxia, diplopia, CN signs, limb signs
HINTS exam — valid only when the vertigo is continuous and present as you examine; it is uninterpretable between attacks, so it does not apply to a Ménière's patient who is currently well, and a "peripheral" result never overrules other neurological signs or new hearing loss. (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) — distinguishes peripheral from central: head impulse test shows a corrective saccade in peripheral dysfunction (eyes overshoot then refixate) but is normal in central. A reassuringly peripheral picture = abnormal head impulse + unidirectional horizontal nystagmus + no skew.
The rule: peripheral vertigo = sudden, ± hearing loss/tinnitus, intact coordination — duration varies with the cause; central = other neurology, usually continuous (though vestibular migraine and TIA are episodic) → exclude stroke (also tumour, MS, vestibular migraine).
The peripheral vertigo differential — where Ménière's sits
CauseDiscriminator
Ménière's diseasetriad (vertigo + SNHL + tinnitus) + aural fullness, attacks 20 min – 12 h, recurrent
BPPVbrief (seconds) vertigo triggered by head position; no hearing loss; Dix-Hallpike +ve, treated with Epley
Vestibular neuronitisacute prolonged vertigo (days) after viral illness; NO hearing loss
Labyrinthitislike vestibular neuronitis + hearing loss (labyrinth involved)
Acoustic neuromagradual unilateral SNHL + tinnitus + imbalance
The key discriminators: Ménière's = the triad + fullness, attacks lasting 20 min – 12 h — shorter than 20 minutes or longer than 12 hours, think again (under 20 min → BPPV or a posterior-circulation TIA; over 12 h, especially with headache/photophobia → vestibular migraine, the commonest thing mistaken for Ménière's). BPPV = seconds, positional, no hearing loss; vestibular neuronitis = no hearing loss; labyrinthitis = with hearing loss.
Pathophysiology
📷 Image placeholder — Cross-section of the membranous labyrinth showing endolymphatic hydrops — distension of the endolymphatic space causing combined cochlear (hearing loss/tinnitus) and vestibular (vertigo) dysfunction
  • Endolymphatic hydrops: excess endolymph accumulates in the membranous labyrinth (impaired reabsorption/drainage) → distension → episodic dysfunction of the cochlea (hearing loss + tinnitus) and vestibular apparatus (vertigo).
  • This explains the fluctuating early course and the combined cochlear + vestibular symptoms.
Clinical features — the triad + fullness
📷 Image placeholder — The Ménière’s triad — episodic vertigo (20 minutes to 12 hours) + fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss + tinnitus, with a sense of aural fullness in the affected ear
FeatureDetail
Episodic vertigorecurrent attacks lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours (typically 2–3 hours; often with nausea/vomiting); the most disabling feature
Sensorineural hearing lossfluctuating initially (typically low- to mid-frequency), becoming progressive + permanent; usually unilateral
Tinnitusin the affected ear
Aural fullnessa sense of pressure/fullness in the affected ear
The attack pattern: clusters of attacks over weeks, with periods of remission; between attacks the patient may be well (early), but hearing progressively declines over years. Nystagmus during attacks; drop attacks (Tumarkin crises) — sudden falls without warning — occur in later disease.
Assessment / investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Pure-tone audiogram of early Ménière’s — a fluctuating low-frequency (rising) sensorineural hearing loss that later becomes progressive/permanent
  • Diagnosis is clinical — the characteristic triad + recurrent episodes; usually a specialist (ENT) diagnosis. Do not label a single first episode as Ménière's: hearing loss that came on suddenly (over 3 days or less) within the last 30 days needs referral to be seen within 24 hours (NICE).
  • Audiometry: confirms a sensorineural pattern of hearing loss (typically low-frequency, fluctuating early) — the key test.
  • Exclude other causes: MRI to exclude acoustic neuroma (unilateral SNHL) and central causes; the vertigo differential (BPPV → Dix-Hallpike; central → HINTS).
  • Rinne/Weber at the bedside may suggest a sensorineural pattern (Weber lateralises to the better ear) — audiometry is what confirms it.
Management
The overarching principle: acute symptom relief (vestibular sedatives) + long-term prophylaxis (betahistine + lifestyle) + specialist input; inform DVLA.
  • Acute attack: vestibular sedatives / antiemetics — prochlorperazine (fast relief of vertigo/nausea), antihistamines (cyclizine, cinnarizine) — a short course, maximum 7 days: longer use delays central vestibular compensation and makes the chronic imbalance worse. Prochlorperazine is a phenothiazine — warn about extrapyramidal effects (acute dystonia, oculogyric crisis, parkinsonism), especially in the young and the elderly. All are sedating → do not drive. Reassurance, safe environment.
  • Prophylaxis: betahistine (a histamine analogue, licensed for Ménière's; 16 mg three times daily initially) — the usual UK prophylactic, given as a trial to reduce attack frequency, though the trial evidence for benefit is weak. Avoid in phaeochromocytoma; caution in asthma and peptic ulcer. Lifestyle — low-salt diet, reduce caffeine/alcohol, avoid identified triggers (widely advised, though trial evidence is lacking).
  • Refractory (specialist): intratympanic steroids or intratympanic gentamicin (ablates vestibular function — but ototoxic, hearing-loss risk); surgery (endolymphatic sac decompression, labyrinthectomy).
  • Supportive: hearing aids (for progressive SNHL), vestibular rehabilitation, tinnitus support.
DVLA: patients must inform the DVLA and stop driving during active disease (sudden, unpredictable vertigo attacks) until symptoms are controlled.
Exam pearls
What it is
Episodic vertigo + sensorineural hearing loss + tinnitus + aural fullness, from endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph).
Attack pattern
Attacks last 20 minutes to 12 hours, recurrent, usually unilateral; hearing loss fluctuates then becomes progressive/permanent.
Peripheral vs central (HINTS)
Only valid in continuous, ongoing vertigo: abnormal head impulse + unidirectional horizontal nystagmus + no skew = peripheral; normal head impulse, direction-changing/vertical nystagmus or skew = central → stroke. Useless between attacks.
vs other peripheral causes
BPPV (seconds, positional, no hearing loss, Dix-Hallpike/Epley), vestibular neuronitis (no hearing loss), labyrinthitis (+ hearing loss), acoustic neuroma (gradual unilateral SNHL).
Investigations
Audiometry (sensorineural, low-frequency fluctuating); MRI to exclude acoustic neuroma.
Management
Acute → prochlorperazine/antihistamines (vestibular sedatives); prophylaxis → betahistine + low-salt diet; refractory → intratympanic steroids/gentamicin, surgery; hearing aids.
Other
Inform the DVLA (sudden vertigo attacks); usually specialist (ENT) managed.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Idiopathic Int:
What & why
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) = raised intracranial pressure with NO identifiable cause (no mass, no hydrocephalus, no venous thrombosis), causing headache and papilloedema — with a normal CSF composition (formerly "benign intracranial hypertension"; also called "pseudotumour cerebri").
The core concept: raised ICP without a space-occupying lesion — it mimics a brain tumour clinically (headache + papilloedema) but imaging is normal. The classic patient is a young obese woman, and the overriding priority is protecting VISION — the papilloedema can cause permanent visual loss if untreated. It's a diagnosis of exclusion.
  • Increasingly common (rising with obesity); strong female + obesity association; "benign" is a misnomer given the sight-threatening risk.
The decisive fork — idiopathic or secondary raised ICP?

IIH is diagnosed only after excluding secondary causes of raised ICP:

Must excludeHow
Space-occupying lesion (tumour, abscess)normal neuroimaging (MRI)
Hydrocephalusnormal/small ventricles on imaging (not dilated)
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosisMR/CT venography (a key mimic — same young-woman/COCP demographic)
Meningitisnormal CSF (cells/protein/glucose)
The rule: IIH = raised ICP (raised CSF opening pressure) + papilloedema + NORMAL imaging + NORMAL CSF composition, with no other cause (the modified Dandy criteria). The key mimic to exclude: cerebral venous sinus thrombosis — same demographic (young woman, COCP, pregnancy) → always do venography.
Risk factors
  • The classic patient: a young obese female — the single most important association.
  • Other risk factors: pregnancy, corticosteroid withdrawal, tetracyclines, retinoids (isotretinoin), lithium; excess vitamin A. (The COCP is not an established cause of IIH — it is a risk factor for the key mimic, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, which is exactly why venography is mandatory.)
The drug mnemonic: think "the acne/hormone drugs" — tetracyclines (acne antibiotics) and retinoids (isotretinoin) are classic culprits (young women on acne treatment).
Clinical features
📷 Image placeholder — bilateral papilloedema — a swollen optic disc with blurred margins, engorged veins and loss of the optic cup (the cardinal sign of raised ICP in IIH)
FeatureDetail
Headachefeatures of raised ICP — worse in the morning, on coughing/straining/lying down
Papilloedemabilateral optic disc swelling — the key sign; risk to vision
Visual symptomsblurred vision, transient visual obscurations (brief greying with posture change), enlarged blind spot, visual field loss
CN VI (6th nerve) palsyfalse localising sign (horizontal diplopia)
Pulsatile tinnitus"whooshing" in the ears — a characteristic symptom
The vision points: papilloedema → enlarged blind spot → progressive visual field loss → permanent blindness if untreated — the reason IIH needs urgent treatment; CN VI palsy is a false localising sign (not a focal lesion). Apart from a CN VI palsy, there should be no focal neurological deficit — any other focal sign, drowsiness or seizure points away from IIH and towards a mass lesion or venous thrombosis.
Investigations
  • Neuroimaging FIRST (MRI + MR venography): normal (no mass, no hydrocephalus, excludes venous sinus thrombosis) — must be done before LP.
  • Lumbar puncture (diagnostic): raised CSF opening pressure (>25 cmH₂O) — the diagnostic finding; normal CSF composition (distinguishes from meningitis). Removing CSF does transiently lower the pressure, but the effect wears off within hours, so repeated "therapeutic" LPs are not used as ongoing management — only as a holding measure while urgent surgery is arranged.
  • Ophthalmology (essential): fundoscopy (papilloedema), visual fields (perimetry), visual acuity, OCT — to monitor vision (the key outcome measure).
Management
The overarching principle: weight loss + acetazolamide, with the overriding goal of protecting vision; escalate to surgery if sight-threatening.
  • Conservative: weight loss (the key disease-modifying step — a sustained loss of around 10% of body weight can resolve papilloedema and can be curative); stop the causative drug (tetracyclines, retinoids, lithium) and avoid abrupt corticosteroid withdrawal.
  • Acetazolamide (1st-line drug): a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor → reduces CSF production. Typically started at 250–500 mg twice daily and titrated up as tolerated. Warn about the common, often dose-limiting side effects: paraesthesiae (tingling fingers/toes), altered taste (especially fizzy drinks), fatigue, nausea; it can also cause a metabolic acidosis and renal stones. It is unlicensed for this indication in the UK.
  • Topiramate: an alternative; also causes weight loss (a useful dual benefit). But it is contraindicated in pregnancy and in women and girls able to have children unless a pregnancy prevention programme is in place (MHRA) — which matters greatly here, because the typical patient is a young woman. Furosemide is a further option.
  • Therapeutic LP — only as a temporising measure while definitive surgery is arranged, not as ongoing treatment.

Sight-threatening / refractory → surgery (vision deteriorating despite medical treatment):

  • CSF diversion — VP or lumboperitoneal shunt (lowers ICP).
  • Optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF) — a window in the optic nerve sheath to protect the optic nerve/vision (preferred if vision-threatening without severe headache).
  • Venous sinus stenting — for selected cases with transverse sinus stenosis + a pressure gradient.
Emerging: GLP-1 receptor agonists and bariatric surgery for weight management (given obesity's central role). Monitor vision throughout (serial visual fields) — the treatment target. Beware medication-overuse headache.
Exam pearls
What it is
Raised ICP with NO identifiable cause (normal imaging, normal CSF composition, raised CSF opening pressure) — mimics a brain tumour; a diagnosis of exclusion.
Classic patient
Young, obese woman; drugs — tetracyclines, retinoids (isotretinoin), lithium, corticosteroid withdrawal. (COCP is a risk factor for the mimic, venous sinus thrombosis — not for IIH.)
Features
Headache (raised ICP) + bilateral papilloedema + visual symptoms (blurring, transient obscurations, enlarged blind spot) + CN VI palsy (false localising) + pulsatile tinnitus.
Exclude CVST
Same demographic → do venography.
Investigations
MRI + MR venography (normal) → LP (raised opening pressure, normal CSF); monitor visual fields (vision is the key outcome).
Management
Weight loss (~10% body weight) + acetazolamide (± topiramate — MHRA pregnancy prevention programme applies); stop causative drug; LP is diagnostic (therapeutic LP only as a holding measure); sight-threatening → CSF shunt / optic nerve sheath fenestration / venous sinus stenting.
The priority
Protect VISION (untreated papilloedema → permanent visual loss). Rapidly worsening visual loss over days to a few weeks ("fulminant" IIH) is a same-day emergency — admit, discuss urgently with ophthalmology and neurosurgery for surgery, do not just start a tablet and review in clinic.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hydrocephalus:
What & why
Hydrocephalus = an accumulation of CSF within the cerebral ventricles causing ventricular dilatation — from a mismatch between CSF production, flow, and absorption.
The core concept: CSF is continuously produced (choroid plexus), circulates through the ventricles, and is absorbed (arachnoid villi) — a lesion anywhere in that loop causes a backlog → ventricular dilatation → raised ICP → brain injury. The classification hinges on where the problem is: obstruction of flow (obstructive) vs impaired absorption/overproduction (non-obstructive/communicating). Normal pressure hydrocephalus is the important special case.
  • Can be acute (raised ICP emergency) or chronic; a treatable cause of neurological decline.
The CSF circulation
📷 Image placeholder — CSF pathway — choroid plexus → lateral ventricles → foramina of Monro → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → foramina of Luschka/Magendie → subarachnoid space → arachnoid granulations, with the common block sites labelled
  • Produced by the choroid plexus (in the ventricles).
  • Flows: lateral ventricles → (foramina of Monro) → third ventricle → (cerebral aqueduct) → fourth ventricle → (foramina of Luschka/Magendie) → subarachnoid space.
  • Absorbed by the arachnoid granulations/villi into venous blood.
The rule: hydrocephalus results from obstruction of flow, impaired absorption, or (rarely) overproduction — the site of the problem defines the type.
The decisive fork — obstructive vs non-obstructive
Obstructive (non-communicating)Non-obstructive (communicating)
Mechanismblockage of the ventricular drainage system / CSF flowreduced absorption by the arachnoid villi (or rarely ↑ production)
Causesobstructing tumour or cyst, congenital aqueduct stenosis, Dandy-Walker (4th-ventricle outflow-foramina obstruction)infective meningitis, SAH, head injury; NPH is the chronic idiopathic form
Site of problemwithin the ventricular system (flow blocked)outside (absorption at the arachnoid villi)
The rules: obstructive = a block in CSF flow (tumour, cyst, aqueduct stenosis) → CSF can't get out of the ventricles; non-obstructive (communicating) = impaired absorption (after meningitis or SAH the arachnoid villi get "clogged", or NPH). Critical: do NOT do an LP in obstructive hydrocephalus — removing CSF below a block risks coning/herniation.
Clinical features

Features of raised ICP — the typical acute/subacute presentation:

FeatureDetail
Headacheworse in the morning (following prolonged lying supine overnight); worse on coughing/bending
Nausea & vomitingraised ICP
Papilloedemaraised ICP (fundoscopy)
Alsoreduced consciousness, visual disturbance (CN VI palsy — false localising), drowsiness
In infants/children: because the skull sutures are open → head circumference crossing centiles on the growth chart, bulging fontanelle, "sunset eyes" (upward gaze palsy), irritability, poor feeding. While the anterior fontanelle is open, cranial ultrasound through it is the first-line scan (no radiation, at the bedside).
Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) — the special case
📷 Image placeholder — Axial CT of NPH — ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy, with the “wet, wobbly, wacky” triad (incontinence, magnetic gait, dementia) and the LP tap-test
NPH = ventricular dilatation with NORMAL CSF pressure — mostly idiopathic. The characteristic triad — "Wet, Wobbly & Wacky":
• Wet = urinary incontinence
• Wobbly = gait abnormality (magnetic, shuffling, wide-based apraxic gait — often earliest/most responsive)
• Wacky = dementia (cognitive decline)
  • The key point: a potentially reversible cause of dementia + gait disturbance — must be distinguished from Alzheimer's/other dementias, and can improve with CSF shunting, though it is the gait that improves most reliably; cognitive recovery is much less predictable.
  • Imaging: ventriculomegaly WITHOUT sulcal enlargement (big ventricles but not the generalised atrophy of Alzheimer's — the ventricles are disproportionately large).
Investigations
  • 1st-line: CT head — shows ventricular enlargement, loss of the sulcal/gyral pattern, and CSF exudation from the ventricles (periventricular lucency — transependymal CSF flow).
  • NPH on imaging: ventriculomegaly without sulcal enlargement.
  • MRI: better detail — identify the level of obstruction (e.g. aqueduct stenosis) and the cause (tumour).
  • Lumbar puncture: diagnostic + therapeutic (measures pressure; removing CSF can help) — but always image FIRST: you cannot know it is non-obstructive until you have, and DO NOT do an LP in obstructive hydrocephalus (nor in anyone with a possibly blocked shunt) (coning risk). In NPH, a large-volume LP ("tap test") that transiently improves gait predicts a good response to shunting.
Management
📷 Image placeholder — Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt vs endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV), with shunt complications — infection, blockage, over-drainage
The overarching principle: relieve raised ICP (EVD acutely), then definitive CSF diversion (VP shunt) + treat the underlying cause.
  • Acute — 1st-line: external ventricular drain (EVD) — a temporary measure to reduce ICP (drains CSF externally in an emergency).
  • There is no effective medical treatment: drugs that reduce CSF production (acetazolamide, furosemide) do not work and are not recommended — in the randomised trial in infants they increased shunt rates and disability. Do not let them delay CSF diversion.
  • Definitive (depends on the cause): treat the cause (e.g. debulking a resectable obstructing tumour); ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt for long-term CSF drainage (ventricles → peritoneum) — the mainstay for chronic/NPH; endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) — an alternative for obstructive hydrocephalus (creates a new drainage route, bypassing the block).
  • NPH: VP shunt — gait is the most likely symptom to improve.
Shunt complications: blockage → returning raised-ICP symptoms; over-drainage → the opposite picture, a postural headache worse on standing, and a risk of subdural haematoma; infection → fever, malaise, meningism, redness along the shunt tract, or abdominal pain (commonest in the first few months after insertion). A shunted patient with headache, vomiting or drowsiness has a blocked shunt until proven otherwise — this is a neurosurgical emergency: A to E, urgent CT head, and immediate discussion with the on-call neurosurgeon. A normal CT does NOT exclude shunt malfunction (the ventricles may not dilate), and CSF must be sampled by shunt tap, not LP.
Exam pearls
What it is
CSF accumulation in the ventricles → ventricular dilatation → raised ICP; from obstruction, impaired absorption, or (rarely) overproduction.
Obstructive vs communicating
Obstructive (non-communicating) = block in CSF flow (tumour, cyst, aqueduct stenosis); non-obstructive (communicating) = impaired absorption (post-meningitis, post-SAH; NPH is the chronic idiopathic form). Dandy-Walker is obstructive.
No LP if obstructive
Removing CSF below a block risks coning.
Features
Raised ICP — morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema; infants → ↑head circumference, bulging fontanelle, sunset eyes.
NPH = "Wet, Wobbly, Wacky"
Incontinence + gait + dementia, with normal CSF pressure + ventriculomegaly without sulcal atrophy → a potentially reversible dementia → VP shunt (gait improves most reliably).
Investigations
CT 1st-line (ventricular enlargement, loss of sulcal pattern, periventricular CSF exudation); LP diagnostic + therapeutic (NOT if obstructive).
Management
Acute → external ventricular drain (EVD); definitive → VP shunt + treat cause; ETV for obstructive. No effective medical treatment (acetazolamide/furosemide are not recommended).
Shunt complications
Blockage → returning raised ICP; over-drainage → postural headache + subdural haematoma; infection → fever/meningism/tract redness. Headache + vomiting + drowsiness in a shunted patient = blocked shunt until proven otherwise → urgent CT + immediate neurosurgical referral (a normal CT does not exclude it).
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Huntington's D:
What & why
Huntington's disease (HD) = an autosomal dominant, progressive neurodegenerative disorder causing a triad of movement disorder (chorea), cognitive decline, and psychiatric disturbance.
The core concept: the archetypal CAG trinucleotide repeat disorder — an expanded repeat in the HTT gene → toxic huntingtin protein → degeneration of the basal ganglia (especially the striatum/caudate). This basal ganglia loss explains the chorea, and the disease shows anticipation (worsens down generations). The clinical hallmark is a middle-aged adult with personality/mood change + involuntary movements. It is incurable — management is supportive.
  • Poor prognosis: ~15–20 years' life expectancy from symptom onset (range roughly 10–25); death often from aspiration/pneumonia.
The genetics — a CAG trinucleotide repeat disorder
📷 Image placeholder — CAG-repeat expansion in HTT with a pedigree showing anticipation (earlier onset down the generations, paternal expansion bias)
  • Autosomal dominant — a single copy causes disease; 50% risk to offspring.
  • Trinucleotide (CAG) repeat expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4, which codes for the huntingtin protein → an abnormal, toxic huntingtin protein → neurodegeneration.
Anticipation: a feature of trinucleotide repeat disorders where successive generations have MORE repeats → earlier age of onset + increased severity down the generations. The repeat number decides whether disease occurs, and largely sets the age of onset: ≤26 normal; 27–35 intermediate (no disease in the carrier, but unstable and can expand into the pathogenic range); 36–39 reduced penetrance; ≥40 full penetrance. Above the threshold, more repeats → earlier onset — it does not reliably predict severity or rate of progression, and is not used to predict onset age for an individual. Expansion occurs especially through the paternal line — which is why juvenile HD (onset under 20, presenting with rigidity and bradykinesia rather than chorea) is almost always inherited from an affected father.

Cross-ref genetics/inheritance physiology — autosomal dominant + anticipation.

Pathophysiology — basal ganglia degeneration
📷 Image placeholder — Coronal imaging of caudate atrophy producing enlarged, squared-off frontal horns (“boxcar” ventricles)
  • The toxic huntingtin protein causes degeneration of the striatum (caudate + putamen) — especially loss of GABAergic medium spiny neurons of the indirect pathway.
  • Imaging correlate: caudate atrophy → enlarged frontal horns of the lateral ventricles ("boxcar ventricles").
The chorea mechanism (cross-ref basal ganglia): loss of the indirect pathway (which normally suppresses unwanted movement) → disinhibition of the thalamus → excess, unwanted movement = chorea (the opposite of Parkinson's, where the balance shifts toward too little movement).
The decisive fork — Huntington's vs other causes of chorea
