📷 Image placeholder — Causes of chorea and their discriminators — Huntington’s, Sydenham’s (post-strep), drug-induced, Wilson’s, SLE, chorea gravidarum
CauseDiscriminator
Huntington's diseaseautosomal dominant, family history, mid-life onset, chorea + cognitive + psychiatric, CAG repeat
Sydenham's choreapost-streptococcal (rheumatic fever), children
Drug-inducedlevodopa, antipsychotics (tardive dyskinesia), stimulants
Wilson's diseaseyoung + liver disease + Kayser-Fleischer rings
SLE / antiphospholipidautoimmune chorea
Pregnancychorea gravidarum
Other geneticneuroacanthocytosis, HD-like syndromes
The rule: middle-aged adult + family history + chorea + personality/mood change + cognitive decline = Huntington's. But a negative family history does NOT exclude it — around 5–10% have none, through a new expansion from a paternal intermediate allele, non-paternity, early death of the affected parent, or earlier misdiagnosis.
Clinical features
The classic vignette: "middle-aged patient with personality changes + involuntary movements = likely Huntington's disease." Insidious, progressive worsening; typical onset 30–50 years; often begins with cognitive, psychiatric, or mood problems, followed by the movement disorder.
DomainFeatures
Psychiatric/mood (often first)personality change, depression, irritability, anxiety, apathy, psychosis; high suicide risk
Cognitiveprogressive decline → subcortical dementia (slowed thinking, executive dysfunction)
Movement disorderchorea (involuntary, random, irregular movements), dystonia, rigidity, eye movement disorders, dysarthria, dysphagia
Chorea: involuntary, random, irregular, "dance-like" movements — the hallmark hyperkinetic feature; as disease progresses, rigidity/bradykinesia and dystonia can emerge. The dysphagia point: swallowing difficulty → aspiration → pneumonia is the common cause of death.
Assessment / investigations
  • Diagnosis is by genetic testing — confirms the CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene.
  • Genetic counselling (critical): because it's a fatal, autosomal dominant, adult-onset condition, predictive testing in at-risk relatives requires careful pre- and post-test genetic counselling and has firm rules. It is offered only to adults (18 or over) with capacity who ask for it themselves; asymptomatic children are NOT tested, because there is no medical benefit in childhood and it removes the child's right to decide later. (Diagnostic testing of someone who already has symptoms is different, and can be done at any age.) A result is never private to one person — it can reveal a relative's status without their consent, so counselling involves the wider family. Insurance (UK): under the Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance, HD is the only condition for which insurers may ask about a predictive test result, and only for life cover above £500,000 — so applicants are usually advised to arrange cover before testing. Reproductive options include prenatal diagnosis and pre-implantation genetic testing.
  • MRI: may show caudate/striatal atrophy (supportive, not diagnostic).
  • Assess psychiatric state (including suicide risk), swallow, and function.
Management — supportive, no cure
The overarching principle: no cure → multidisciplinary supportive care; treat chorea, mood, and complications; genetic counselling for the family.
  • Chorea: tetrabenazine (a dopamine-depleting agent) for troublesome chorea — but it can cause or worsen depression and suicidal ideation, and is contraindicated in untreated or inadequately treated depression and in anyone actively suicidal. In a disease defined by depression and a high suicide rate, screen for and treat depression first, monitor closely, and warn the patient and family. An antipsychotic (olanzapine, risperidone or sulpiride) is often preferred where depression, psychosis or agitation coexist.
  • Psychiatric: antidepressants for depression; antipsychotics for psychosis/agitation. Ask directly about suicidal thoughts at every review — suicide risk is several times that of the general population and peaks around the time of diagnosis or a positive predictive test result, and again as independence is lost.
  • Driving: the patient must notify the DVLA; fitness to drive needs reassessing as the motor and cognitive impairment progress.
  • Speech and language therapy (SALT) — for dysarthria + swallowing/aspiration risk.
  • End-of-life / palliative care — given the progressive, fatal course.
  • MDT: neurology, physiotherapy, OT, dietitian (nutrition/aspiration), social care, family support.
  • Genetic counselling for the patient and at-risk family members (autosomal dominant inheritance).
Exam pearls
What it is
Autosomal dominant, progressive neurodegeneration → chorea + cognitive decline + psychiatric disturbance.
Genetics
CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in HTT (chromosome 4) → toxic huntingtin protein; anticipation (more repeats → earlier onset + more severe down generations); 50% risk to offspring.
Pathology
Striatal (caudate) degeneration → loss of the indirect pathway → chorea; caudate atrophy on MRI.
Classic
Middle-aged adult + personality/mood change + involuntary movements (chorea); onset 30–50; often psychiatric first, then movement disorder.
Progression
Dystonia, rigidity, dysarthria, dysphagia → aspiration/pneumonia (common cause of death); ~15–20 years from onset; high suicide risk — ask about it directly.
Diagnosis
Genetic testing (CAG repeats: ≤26 normal, 27–35 intermediate, 36–39 reduced penetrance, ≥40 full penetrance); predictive testing is adults-only, never asymptomatic children, with pre- and post-test counselling — and HD is the one condition insurers may ask about, for life cover over £500,000.
Management (no cure — supportive)
Tetrabenazine for chorea, antidepressants, SALT (speech + swallow), palliative care; MDT + family genetic counselling.
Chorea differential
Sydenham's (post-strep), drug-induced, Wilson's, SLE, pregnancy.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Head Injury &:
What & why
Head injury = any trauma to the head, from trivial to life-threatening; the clinical concern is traumatic brain injury, especially intracranial haemorrhage (extradural, subdural, subarachnoid, intracerebral).
The core concept: the whole approach is risk stratification — using the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and a set of red-flag criteria to decide who needs a CT head (and how urgently), who needs admission/observation, and who can be discharged safely. The overriding physiology is the Monro-Kellie doctrine — the skull is a fixed box, so an expanding haematoma/oedema raises ICP → herniation → death. Time-critical detection of a treatable bleed is the goal.
  • Extremely common ED presentation; most are minor — the task is not to miss the dangerous minority.
The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
📷 Image placeholder — GCS scoring grid (Eyes/4, Verbal/5, Motor/6) with decorticate flexion vs decerebrate extension illustrated — extension indicates a deeper/worse lesion

The GCS quantifies consciousness, scored 3 (worst) to 15 (best), across three components:

ComponentScoreResponse
Eyes (E, /4)4 / 3 / 2 / 1spontaneous / to speech / to pain / none
Verbal (V, /5)5 / 4 / 3 / 2 / 1orientated / confused / inappropriate words / incomprehensible sounds / none
Motor (M, /6)6 / 5 / 4 / 3 / 2 / 1obeys commands / localises to pain / withdraws / abnormal flexion (decorticate) / extension (decerebrate) / none
The high-yield thresholds:
• GCS ≤8 = coma → cannot protect the airway → intubate ("GCS 8, intubate").
• Motor is the most prognostically important component.
• Flexion (decorticate) vs extension (decerebrate): extension is worse (deeper/lower brainstem involvement).
  • Best-response rule: record the best response in each category; report as E_V_M_ (e.g. E3V4M5 = 12).
  • Severity: mild = GCS 13–15; moderate = 9–12; severe = ≤8.
The decisive fork — who needs a CT head, and how urgently? (NICE)
📷 Image placeholder — NICE decision flowchart — CT-within-1-hour vs CT-within-8-hour criteria, plus the anticoagulant/antiplatelet branch

The central clinical decision. NICE stratifies into CT within 1 hour vs CT within 8 hours (adults ≥16):

CT head within 1 HOUR — any of:
  • GCS < 13 on initial ED assessment
  • GCS < 15 at 2 hours after injury
  • suspected open or depressed skull fracture
  • any sign of basal skull fracture: haemotympanum, "panda"/raccoon eyes, CSF leak from ear/nose, Battle's sign (mastoid bruising)
  • post-traumatic seizure, focal neurological deficit, or >1 episode of vomiting
CT head within 8 HOURS — some loss of consciousness or amnesia PLUS any of:
  • age ≥ 65
  • any current bleeding or clotting disorder
  • dangerous mechanism (pedestrian/cyclist vs vehicle, ejection, fall >1 m or 5 stairs)
  • >30 minutes retrograde amnesia of events before the injury
Anticoagulant/antiplatelet pathway (NICE): a head injury with NO other CT indication but the patient is on an anticoagulant (warfarin, DOAC, heparin) or antiplatelet (excluding aspirin monotherapy) → consider CT within 8 hours (or within 1 hour if presenting >8 hours after injury).
The intracranial bleeds to detect
📷 Image placeholder — Side-by-side CT heads — biconvex/lens-shaped extradural vs crescent-shaped subdural, with the extradural “lucid interval” timeline

The CT is looking for a treatable bleed — the classic patterns:

BleedClassic feature
Extradural"lucid interval" then rapid deterioration; biconvex (lens-shaped) on CT; middle meningeal artery, temporal trauma
Subduralcrescent-shaped; elderly/alcoholics/anticoagulated; can be acute or chronic
Subarachnoidtraumatic SAH; (spontaneous → thunderclap headache)
Intracerebral / contusionwithin the parenchyma
The lucid interval: a brief recovery of consciousness after the injury, then deterioration → classic for extradural haematoma (arterial bleed expanding) → a neurosurgical emergency.
Signs of raised ICP / deterioration
  • Falling GCS — the most important sign of deterioration.
  • Cushing's reflex (late, ominous): hypertension + bradycardia + irregular breathing → impending herniation.
  • Pupillary changes: a fixed dilated pupil (CN III compression from uncal herniation — "blown pupil").
  • Vomiting, worsening headache, focal deficits, seizures.
The physiology: fixed skull (Monro-Kellie) → expanding haematoma → ↑ICP → herniation → brainstem compression → death.
Management
The overarching principle: ABCDE + C-spine control → GCS + risk-stratify → CT per NICE → treat bleeds/raised ICP → observe or discharge with safety-netting.
  • Immediate (ABCDE): airway with C-spine immobilisation (assume cervical injury until excluded — and know how it is excluded: CT the cervical spine if GCS is 12 or less, if the patient has been intubated, if there are focal neurological signs or limb paraesthesiae, if a definitive diagnosis is needed urgently, or if cervical injury is clinically suspected with either age 65 or over or a dangerous mechanism), breathing/oxygenation (avoid hypoxia), circulation (avoid hypotension — both worsen secondary brain injury). GCS ≤8 → intubate.
  • Tranexamic acid (TXA): for head injury with GCS ≤12 and no suspected active extracranial bleeding → consider IV TXA (2 g) ASAP, within 2 hours, before imaging.
  • Reverse anticoagulation if intracranial haemorrhage: warfarin → prothrombin complex concentrate + vitamin K; dabigatran → idarucizumab; apixaban/rivaroxaban → PCC, discussing urgently with haematology (there is no NICE-recommended specific antidote for factor Xa inhibitors in intracranial bleeding).
  • Discuss with a neurosurgeon immediately if there is a new surgically significant abnormality on imaging — or, whatever the scan shows: persisting coma (GCS 8 or less) after resuscitation; unexplained confusion lasting more than 4 hours; any deterioration in GCS after admission (especially a drop of 1 or more on the motor score); progressive focal neurological signs; a seizure without full recovery; definite or suspected penetrating injury; or a CSF leak.
  • Manage raised ICP: head-up positioning, avoid hypoxia, and keep the CO2 normal — avoid hypocapnia as well as hypercapnia, since over-ventilating constricts cerebral vessels and causes ischaemia.
  • The base-of-skull rule: with a suspected or confirmed basal skull fracture, never pass a nasogastric tube or a nasopharyngeal airway blindly — it can go through the cribriform plate into the cranial cavity. Use an orogastric tube instead.
  • Admission/observation (NICE): a new clinically important abnormality on imaging; GCS not back to 15 (or the pre-injury baseline) after imaging, whatever the scan shows; CT indicated but not obtainable in time; continuing worrying symptoms (persistent vomiting, severe headache, seizures); or other sources of concern — drug or alcohol intoxication, other injuries, shock, suspected non-accidental injury, meningism, a CSF leak.
    Note what is NOT on that list: being on an anticoagulant is not by itself a reason to admit. NICE looked at this specifically and found no clinically important excess of delayed bleeding — a patient on a DOAC with GCS 15, a normal CT and nothing else of concern can go home with head-injury advice.
  • Discharge + safety-netting: if low-risk/normal CT/GCS 15 — with written head injury advice (return if worsening headache, vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, weakness, visual changes, seizure) and a responsible adult.
Concussion & post-concussion
  • Concussion = a transient disturbance of brain function after head injury (brief confusion, headache, dizziness, amnesia). It is a clinical diagnosis — most concussed patients never meet the CT criteria and are never scanned, so a normal scan is neither required to make the diagnosis nor sufficient to exclude it.
  • Post-concussion syndrome: persistent headache, dizziness, poor concentration, mood and sleep disturbance for weeks to months → supportive management and a graded return to activity.
  • Return to sport (UK guidance): "if in doubt, sit them out" — anyone with a suspected concussion comes off immediately and does not return that day. Then relative rest for 24–48 hours, a graduated return to activity and to school or work, and sport last. A minimum of 21 days from the injury before returning to any match where contact is possible. Refer for assessment if symptoms persist beyond 28 days.
Exam pearls
GCS
/15 (Eyes /4, Verbal /5, Motor /6); ≤8 = coma → intubate; report as E_V_M_; motor most prognostic; mild 13–15 / moderate 9–12 / severe ≤8.
CT within 1 HOUR (NICE)
GCS <13 initially, GCS <15 at 2h, basal skull fracture signs (haemotympanum, panda eyes, CSF leak, Battle's sign), open/depressed fracture, seizure, focal deficit, >1 vomit.
CT within 8 HOURS
LOC/amnesia + (age ≥65, bleeding disorder, dangerous mechanism, >30 min retrograde amnesia); on anticoagulant/antiplatelet → CT within 8h even with no other indication.
Extradural
Lucid interval + biconvex CT (middle meningeal artery).
Subdural
Crescent-shaped, elderly/anticoagulated.
Deterioration
Falling GCS, Cushing's reflex (↑BP + bradycardia + irregular breathing), fixed dilated pupil (CN III / uncal herniation).
Management
ABCDE + C-spine, avoid hypoxia/hypotension (secondary injury); GCS ≤8 → intubate; TXA 2 g IV if GCS ≤12 and no extracranial bleeding, within 2h and before imaging; reverse anticoagulation for bleeds (warfarin → PCC + vit K; dabigatran → idarucizumab; apixaban/rivaroxaban → PCC); never a blind NG tube with a basal skull fracture; discuss with neurosurgery for GCS ≤8, any GCS drop, confusion beyond 4h or a CSF leak; safety-net on discharge — but being anticoagulated is NOT itself a reason to admit if the CT is normal and GCS is 15.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Guillain-Barré:
What & why
Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) = an acute, immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy — demyelinating in most UK cases (AIDP), but axonal in the AMAN variant, so "demyelinating" alone is too narrow causing rapidly progressive ascending flaccid paralysis, usually following an infection.
The core concept: a post-infectious autoimmune attack on peripheral nerve myelin (molecular mimicry) → an acute ascending, symmetrical, LMN (flaccid) paralysis with areflexia. The two things that make it an emergency are respiratory muscle failure (the leading cause of death → monitor FVC) and autonomic instability — so the priorities are recognising it early, monitoring respiratory/autonomic function, and treating with IVIG or plasma exchange.
  • The commonest cause of acute flaccid paralysis (since polio control); ~⅔ follow a preceding infection.
The decisive fork — GBS or another cause of acute weakness?
📷 Image placeholder — GBS (LMN — flaccid, areflexic, no sensory level) vs acute cord compression (UMN signs, a sensory level, bladder/bowel involvement) — the must-not-miss surgical emergency to exclude

The pattern (ascending, symmetrical, areflexic, LMN, post-infectious) is the key:

Points to GBSAlternative to consider
Ascending, symmetrical flaccid weakness + areflexiaspinal cord compression (UMN signs, sensory level, sphincter involvement)
Preceding infection (1–3 weeks before)transverse myelitis (sensory level, bladder)
LMN signs (↓tone, ↓/absent reflexes)myasthenia gravis (fatiguable, ocular)
CSF albuminocytological dissociationbotulism (descending, fixed dilated pupils), hypokalaemia, acute intermittent porphyria
Progression over days to ≤4 weeksorganophosphate poisoning
The rule: acute ascending symmetrical flaccid paralysis + areflexia + recent infection = GBS. The key contrast is spinal cord compression (UMN signs + a sensory level + bladder involvement — a surgical emergency to exclude). GBS attacks peripheral nerves → LMN signs (flaccid weakness, hyporeflexia/areflexia) — NOT the UMN signs of a cord lesion.
Pathophysiology & triggers
📷 Image placeholder — Molecular mimicry — post-infective anti-ganglioside antibodies (classically after Campylobacter) cross-react with peripheral-nerve myelin/axolemma, driving demyelinating (AIDP) vs axonal (AMAN) subtypes
  • Post-infectious autoimmune process: an infection triggers antibodies that cross-react with peripheral nerve myelin (molecular mimicry) → demyelination of peripheral nerves and roots.
  • The classic trigger: Campylobacter jejuni (gastroenteritis) — the commonest identified precedent, associated with more severe/axonal disease.
  • Other triggers: CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, HIV, influenza/other viral URTIs, (historically) vaccines — weakness begins ~1–3 weeks after the infection.
  • Subtypes: AIDP (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy — commonest in the West), AMAN (acute motor axonal — Campylobacter-associated), and the Miller Fisher variant.
Clinical features
FeatureDetail
Ascending weaknesssymmetrical, starts in the legs → ascends to arms/trunk; progressive over days (nadir usually ≤4 weeks)
Areflexia / hyporeflexiaabsent/reduced reflexes — a key sign (LMN). But reflexes can be normal in the first days, and are sometimes preserved in the axonal variant, so normal reflexes early do NOT exclude GBS
Sensory symptomsoften paraesthesia/pain (may precede weakness), but objective sensory loss is mild (predominantly motor)
Cranial nerve involvementbilateral facial weakness, bulbar (swallowing/speech)
Respiratory failurediaphragm/intercostal weakness → the leading cause of death → monitor FVC
Autonomic dysfunctionarrhythmias, labile BP, tachycardia/bradycardia, urinary retention, ileus
The two danger features: respiratory failure (weak diaphragm → ventilatory failure) and autonomic instability (arrhythmias, BP swings) — these drive mortality and the need for close monitoring/ICU.
Miller Fisher syndrome — the classic variant
A GBS variant with the triad: ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia (cranial-nerve onset, and without the typical limb weakness). Associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies (positive in ~90%). Usually follows infection; generally good prognosis.
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — FVC monitoring in GBS — serial FVC — below 20 mL/kg, or a rapidly falling trend, means critical-care review; below 15 mL/kg means intubation. Do not wait for hypoxia or a rising CO₂: those are late signs
  • First, exclude a compressive cord lesion. If there is a sensory level, bladder or bowel involvement, back pain, marked asymmetry, or brisk reflexes/extensor plantars, get an urgent MRI of the whole spine before or alongside anything else — doing a lumbar puncture on a compressive myelopathy loses hours.
  • Diagnosis is clinical (ascending flaccid paralysis + areflexia + preceding infection), supported by:
  • Lumbar puncture — CSF: ALBUMINOCYTOLOGIC DISSOCIATION = raised protein with a NORMAL white cell count (the classic finding) — reflects nerve-root inflammation; may be normal in the first week (so a normal early LP doesn't exclude it).
  • Nerve conduction studies: slowed conduction / conduction block (demyelination) — supports + subtypes; may be normal early.
  • Antibodies: anti-GQ1b (Miller Fisher), anti-ganglioside antibodies (not routine).
  • ECG + cardiac monitoring (autonomic instability); bloods to exclude mimics (U&E, potassium).
Respiratory monitoring (CRITICAL): serial spirometry / forced vital capacity (FVC) every few hours in progressing patients — a falling FVC → anaesthetic/ITU review for intubation (don't wait for hypoxia/blood gases to change — they're late).
Management — immunotherapy + supportive
The overarching principle: IVIG OR plasma exchange (not both) + intensive supportive care with respiratory/autonomic monitoring.

Immunotherapy (to hasten recovery):

  • Who to treat, and when: immunotherapy is for patients who are unable to walk 10 m unaided, or who have respiratory or bulbar involvement, or who are progressing rapidly — started within 2 weeks of the onset of weakness. A mildly affected patient who is still walking independently and not progressing is monitored, not automatically treated.
  • IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) — first-line (easier to give; usually preferred). 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 consecutive days (2 g/kg in total), as a single course. It is a pooled blood product: consent, record the batch, and be aware of anaphylaxis in IgA deficiency, and of thrombosis, aseptic meningitis and acute kidney injury.
  • OR plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) — equally effective.
  • Give ONE, not both: do NOT give plasma exchange after IVIG (it removes the immunoglobulin you just gave). Corticosteroids are NOT effective in GBS (an important negative).

Supportive care (the mainstay):

  • Respiratory: monitor FVC; ventilatory support / intubation if respiratory failure (ICU) — the key to survival.
  • Cardiac/autonomic: continuous cardiac monitoring for arrhythmias and labile blood pressure. The practical hazard: tracheal suctioning, laryngoscopy, turning and straining can provoke profound bradycardia or even asystole — pre-oxygenate, have atropine to hand, and treat hypertension only with short-acting agents, because these patients swing violently into hypotension.
  • VTE prophylaxis (immobile), catheter/bowel care (autonomic), neuropathic pain management — gabapentin or pregabalin work, but the MHRA warns of respiratory depression in exactly this group (compromised respiratory function, neurological disease, the elderly, renal impairment, other CNS depressants), so start low and monitor; the same applies to opioids, physiotherapy/OT, nutrition (bulbar involvement).
  • The two respiratory thresholds: FVC below 20 mL/kg (or a rapidly falling trend) → critical-care review and ITU-level monitoring; FVC below 15 mL/kg, or bulbar failure with an ineffective cough → intubate. NIV is generally avoided in neuromuscular respiratory failure with bulbar involvement — the airway is not protected. Remember the trap: the saturations and the blood gas stay normal until the patient is about to arrest.
  • ICU admission if: severe or rapidly progressing weakness, a falling FVC, bulbar involvement, or autonomic instability.
Prognosis
  • Most recover (over weeks–months), often fully or near-fully — GBS is typically monophasic, though it recurs in roughly 2–5%, and about 1 in 10 have a treatment-related fluctuation — a transient deterioration after initial improvement, which is treatable and does not mean the diagnosis was wrong.
  • But: about 20% are still unable to walk unaided at 6 months and mortality is around 3–7%; residual fatigue, pain and distal paraesthesiae are much commoner than that (respiratory/autonomic complications), and recovery can be slow.
  • A small proportion → CIDP (chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy — the chronic/relapsing counterpart, >8 weeks).
  • Poor prognostic factors: older age, rapid onset, axonal subtype, ventilator requirement, preceding Campylobacter/diarrhoeal illness.
Exam pearls
What it is
Acute, post-infectious, immune-mediated demyelinating polyneuropathy → ascending symmetrical flaccid paralysis + areflexia (LMN).
Trigger
Preceding infection 1–3 weeks before — classically Campylobacter jejuni; also CMV/EBV/Mycoplasma/HIV.
Features
Ascending weakness (legs→up), areflexia, mild sensory, bilateral facial/bulbar weakness; danger = respiratory failure + autonomic instability.
Distinguish from
Spinal cord compression (UMN + sensory level + bladder — surgical emergency) and myasthenia (fatiguable, ocular).
Miller Fisher variant
Ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia; anti-GQ1b antibodies.
Investigations
Exclude cord compression first if there are red flags (sensory level, sphincters, back pain) — urgent whole-spine MRI. CSF = albuminocytological dissociation (↑protein, normal WCC) — may be normal in week 1; NCS = demyelination; serial FVC — below 20 mL/kg means critical-care review, below 15 mL/kg means intubate.
Management
Treat if unable to walk unaided, or bulbar/respiratory involvement, within 2 weeks of onset: IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days OR plasma exchange (equally effective — give one, not both; never plasma exchange after IVIG); steroids don't work; intensive supportive care (respiratory + autonomic monitoring, VTE prophylaxis).
Prognosis
Usually monophasic (recurs in ~2–5%); most recover, but ~20% still cannot walk unaided at 6 months and mortality is ~3–7%; a small proportion → CIDP.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Febrile Convul:
What & why
A febrile convulsion = a seizure provoked by fever in an otherwise neurologically normal child, without CNS infection or another identifiable cause.
The core concept: a benign, self-limiting seizure triggered by a rapidly rising temperature in a young child — it is NOT epilepsy (it's a provoked seizure). Two priorities: (1) exclude a serious cause of the fever (especially meningitis/encephalitis — don't assume "just febrile") and (2) classify it as simple vs complex (complex carries higher risk). Above all — reassurance: the prognosis is excellent.
  • Common — affects ~3% of children; typically 6 months to 5 years; occurs early in a fever, usually from a viral infection.
The decisive fork — simple vs complex vs febrile status
📷 Image placeholder — Simple vs complex vs febrile status — the three-column split (duration, focality, recurrence, recovery) that drives risk and management

The single most important classification — it determines risk and management:

SimpleComplexFebrile status
Duration< 15 minutes> 15 minutes> 30 minutes (a prolonged complex seizure, not a separate category)
Typegeneralised (tonic-clonic)focal featuresprolonged
Recurrence in 24hnonemay recur within 24h—
Recoverycomplete recovery < 1 hourslower—
The rule: simple = <15 min + generalised + no recurrence in 24h + full recovery; complex = ≥1 of: lasting >15 min (no upper limit), focal, recurring within 24 hours or within the same febrile illness, or incomplete recovery within 1 hour. Febrile status epilepticus (>30 min) is a prolonged COMPLEX seizure — it is not a third, separate category, so it triggers every "complex" rule below. Complex febrile convulsions carry a higher risk of recurrence and a (slightly) higher risk of later epilepsy → warrant more caution.
Clinical features
  • Occur early in a febrile illness — often as the first sign the child is unwell, so the seizure may come before anyone has noticed the fever. A higher peak temperature makes one more likely.
  • Last < 5 minutes (typically).
  • Mostly tonic-clonic (generalised).
  • Age 6 months–5 years; the child is otherwise developmentally normal.
  • Often a family history of febrile convulsions.
The must-not-miss — exclude a serious cause of the fever
📷 Image placeholder — Red flags for meningitis/encephalitis in a child with fever + seizure — neck stiffness, non-blanching rash, bulging fontanelle, drowsiness/not recovering (never assume “just febrile”)

A febrile seizure is a diagnosis that requires excluding a CNS infection — the critical differential:

Must excludeRed flags
Meningitis / encephalitisneck stiffness, non-blanching rash, bulging fontanelle, drowsiness/altered consciousness, focal neurology, not recovering
Other serious infectionthe "red" features (pale/mottled, no response to social cues, grunting, tachypnoea)
Metabolichypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia
Epilepsyseizure without fever, or afebrile recurrences
The rule: any child with a seizure + fever must be assessed for meningitis/encephalitis — do NOT assume a febrile convulsion, especially if there are red flags, incomplete recovery, complex features, or the child is <18 months (meningitis signs are subtle in infants). If meningitis or meningococcal disease is suspected: transfer as an emergency and give empirical IV ceftriaxone immediately — do NOT delay antibiotics for a lumbar puncture (NICE), adding aciclovir if encephalitis is possible. In the community with a non-blanching rash, give IM benzylpenicillin before transfer if it will not delay it. Age caveat: febrile convulsions are unusual <6 months or >5 years → a seizure with fever outside this range needs closer scrutiny for another cause.
Assessment / investigations
  • Simple febrile convulsion with full recovery + clear infective source → often no investigations needed beyond finding the fever source (clinical assessment).
  • Find the fever source + exclude serious causes: examine thoroughly; urine dip/culture (UTI is a common occult source) and blood glucose in any child who has had a seizure; other bloods only if the child is unwell or the source is unclear.
  • Lumbar puncture — if meningitis/encephalitis suspected (complex features, not recovering, red flags). Signs of meningitis are unreliable under 18 months, so have a much lower threshold there. But stabilise first and defer the LP if there is shock, a non-blanching rash or any sign of raised intracranial pressure — and never let it delay antibiotics.
  • NOT routinely needed for a simple febrile convulsion: EEG, neuroimaging, routine bloods (over-investigation is a common error).
  • Complex FC / diagnostic doubt → lower threshold for admission + investigation.
Management
📷 Image placeholder — Parental safety-net — time the seizure, recovery position, call 999 if >5 minutes; antipyretics for comfort only (they do NOT prevent recurrence)
The overarching principle: acute seizure management + exclude serious infection + treat the fever source + reassure/safety-net the parents.
  • Admit to paediatrics if: the first febrile convulsion, OR features of a complex seizure, OR diagnostic uncertainty, OR the child is unwell or <18 months, OR there is no identified focus for the fever, OR the child is currently or recently on antibiotics (these can mask the signs of meningitis).

Acute seizure management:

  • Call 999 if the seizure lasts > 5 minutes.
  • Benzodiazepine rescue if recurrent/prolonged (specialist-initiated): buccal midazolam is the UK first choice (rectal diazepam if buccal midazolam is unsuitable or unavailable) — supplied for children with a history of prolonged febrile convulsions, and given if a seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes.
  • Supportive: protect from injury, recovery position, oxygen if needed.
  • Treat the underlying cause of the fever (the infection).
  • Antipyretics (paracetamol/ibuprofen) for comfort — but they do NOT prevent febrile convulsions → don't give them to prevent seizures.
  • No routine anticonvulsant prophylaxis — regular antiepileptics are not indicated for simple febrile convulsions.
Parental advice / safety-netting: ~1 in 3 chance of recurrence; very low risk of progression to epilepsy (reassure); how to manage a future seizure — time it, protect the head, do NOT restrain the child and do NOT put anything in their mouth, recovery position once the seizure has stopped, call 999 if it lasts >5 minutes. Seek urgent help if there is a non-blanching rash, drowsiness or difficulty waking, another seizure in the same illness, or the child does not recover as expected.
Prognosis — the reassurance
  • Recurrence: ~1 in 3 — higher if under 18 months at the first seizure, a family history of febrile convulsions, a lower peak temperature, or a short duration of fever before the seizure. (Complex features raise the risk of later epilepsy, not of recurrence.)
  • Risk of epilepsy: very low — only slightly above the general population for simple FC — about 1–2% absolute risk, against roughly 0.5–1% in the general population; higher with complex FC, neurodevelopmental abnormality, or a family history of epilepsy.
  • No effect on development/intelligence for simple febrile convulsions — reassure parents strongly.
Exam pearls
What it is
Fever-provoked seizure in a normal child, 6 months–5 years — a provoked seizure, NOT epilepsy.
Classification
Simple (<15 min, generalised, no recurrence in 24h, full recovery); complex = any of >15 min, focal, recurs within 24h/same illness, or incomplete recovery within 1 hour. Febrile status (>30 min) is a prolonged COMPLEX seizure, not a separate category.
Features
Occur early in a febrile illness — often before the fever is even noticed; usually tonic-clonic, <5 min.
Must-not-miss
Exclude meningitis/encephalitis (neck stiffness, non-blanching rash, bulging fontanelle, not recovering) — don't assume febrile convulsion, especially if <18 months, complex, or red flags.
Investigations
Simple FC → usually none (find fever source, urine dip); LP if meningitis suspected; no routine EEG/imaging.
Management
Admit if first seizure or complex; call 999 if >5 min; buccal midazolam (first choice; rectal diazepam if unsuitable) at 5 minutes if a rescue drug has been supplied; treat the infection; antipyretics don't prevent FCs.
Prognosis
~1 in 3 recurrence, very low epilepsy risk — reassure.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Epilepsy (clas:
What & why
📷 Image placeholder — characteristic patterns — generalised 3-Hz spike-and-wave complexes of childhood absence epilepsy, and focal/interictal epileptiform discharges localising to a lobe
Epilepsy = a tendency to recurrent, unprovoked seizures — defined as ≥2 unprovoked seizures >24 hours apart (or 1 unprovoked seizure with a high recurrence risk, e.g. a structural cause). A seizure = a transient episode of abnormal, excessive, synchronous electrical activity in the brain.
The core concept: three pillars — (1) classify the seizure (focal vs generalised — because it determines the drug), (2) treat the acute prolonged seizure (status epilepticus is an emergency), and (3) advise on the practical consequences (DVLA, safety, pregnancy). Classification drives everything, because the antiseizure medication depends on the seizure type.
  • Common (~1% lifetime); most present in childhood or older age.
The decisive fork — focal vs generalised

The ILAE classification first asks: where does the seizure start?

Focal (partial)Generalised
Onsetone part of one hemisphereboth hemispheres from the start
Awarenessfocal aware (conscious) or focal impaired awarenessconsciousness usually lost — but not always: awareness is typically preserved in myoclonic seizures
Examplestemporal lobe (aura, déjà vu, automatisms); can evolve to bilateral tonic-clonictonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic, tonic, atonic
Localisingfeatures localise to the lobe (cross-ref cortical syndromes)no focal onset
The rule: focal = starts in one area (may have an aura, automatisms, or evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic); generalised = both hemispheres from the start (loss of consciousness) — this split determines the drug choice.
The generalised seizure types
TypeFeatures
Tonic-clonictonic (stiffening) → clonic (jerking); LOC, tongue-biting, incontinence, post-ictal drowsiness/confusion
Absencebrief (typically 5–20 seconds) vacant staring/"blank", no post-ictal phase; children; 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG
Myoclonicsudden brief shock-like jerks (e.g. juvenile myoclonic epilepsy)
Tonicsudden stiffening → fall
Atonicsudden loss of tone → "drop attack"
The high-yield ones: tonic-clonic (the classic "grand mal"), absence (children, 3 Hz spike-wave, no post-ictal phase), myoclonic (JME).
Focal seizure features — localise to the lobe
LobeFocal seizure features
Temporalaura (déjà vu, rising epigastric sensation, fear), automatisms (lip-smacking, fidgeting), altered awareness
Frontalmotor features (Jacksonian march — spreading motor activity), posturing, Todd's paresis (post-ictal weakness)
Parietalsensory (tingling, numbness)
Occipitalvisual (flashes, patterns)
Todd's paresis: transient post-ictal focal weakness (can mimic a stroke). Jacksonian march: motor seizure activity "marching" along the body as it spreads across the motor cortex.
Assessment & investigations
Diagnosis is clinical — a detailed eyewitness account is the single most important thing (warning/aura, what happened, tongue-biting, incontinence, post-ictal confusion, duration).

Exclude provoked seizures / mimics first — a seizure isn't epilepsy if there's an acute provoking cause:

  • Provoking causes: hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal, drugs, infection (meningitis/encephalitis), eclampsia, head injury, hypoxia.
  • Mimics: syncope (vasovagal, cardiac — brief, quick recovery, situational), non-epileptic attack disorder (NEAD) (functional), TIA, migraine, panic.

Investigations:

  • EEG — supports classification (e.g. 3 Hz spike-wave = absence); a normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy (and an abnormal one doesn't confirm it).
  • MRI brain — to find a structural cause (esp. focal seizures, adults with new-onset — exclude tumour/AVM/malformation).
  • Bloods: glucose, U&E, calcium, magnesium, FBC (exclude provoked causes); ECG (exclude cardiac syncope/arrhythmia).
Antiseizure medications (NICE)
The overarching principle: treat by seizure type; usually start after a 2nd seizure (or 1st with structural cause/high risk); monotherapy first.

When to start: usually after a second seizure (or after a first if there's a structural lesion, an unequivocal epileptic EEG, or high judged risk).

First-line drugs (NICE):

Seizure typeFirst-line
Generalised tonic-clonicsodium valproate in boys and men, and women unable to have children; lamotrigine or levetiracetam in girls and women able to have children
Focallamotrigine or levetiracetam
Absenceethosuximide — first-line for everyone. Second-line is valproate (boys/men, women unable to have children) or lamotrigine/levetiracetam. Avoid carbamazepine (worsens absence)
Myoclonicsodium valproate in boys/men and women unable to have children; levetiracetam in girls and women able to have children (avoid carbamazepine; lamotrigine may worsen)
Tonic / atonicsodium valproate in boys/men and women unable to have children; lamotrigine in girls and women able to have children
Valproate restrictions (critical): The NICE table above gives the drug by seizure type; the MHRA rules below then gate whether valproate can actually be started. Valproate is teratogenic (neural tube defects, neurodevelopmental effects) → must NOT be used in women/girls of childbearing potential unless a pregnancy prevention programme is in place and no alternative. MHRA: do not start valproate in ANYONE under 55 — male or female — unless two specialists independently document that there is no other effective or tolerated treatment, or that there are compelling reasons the reproductive risks do not apply. In men: the man and his partner should use effective contraception during treatment and for 3 months after stopping, because of a possible small increase in neurodevelopmental disorders in children they father; review any man planning a family within the year.
Key drug points:
• Carbamazepine — enzyme inducer; can worsen absence + myoclonic seizures (avoid in generalised); SIADH/hyponatraemia.
• Lamotrigine — slow titration ( Stevens-Johnson syndrome risk). Lamotrigine and levetiracetam are the two with the most reassuring pregnancy data.
• Levetiracetam — neuropsychiatric side effects (irritability, low mood).
• Phenytoin — narrow therapeutic index (needs level monitoring), gum hyperplasia (used mainly in status now).
  • Withdrawal: consider after ≥2 years seizure-free, with specialist input; taper slowly.
Status epilepticus — the emergency
Definition: a seizure lasting >5 minutes, OR ≥2 seizures without recovery of consciousness in between (older definition was >30 min; ≥5 min now triggers treatment). A medical emergency — prolonged seizures cause neuronal injury, hypoxia, and death.

The stepwise protocol:

StepAction
1. ABCDE + immediatesecure airway, high-flow oxygen, check glucose (treat hypoglycaemia), IV access, thiamine (Pabrinex) if alcohol/malnourished
2. First-line — benzodiazepineIV lorazepam 4 mg (repeat once after 5–10 min if needed); community/no IV access → buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam. Two doses of benzodiazepine in total — and that count includes any dose already given before arrival by paramedics, family or carers. If it has already had two, move straight to second-line.
3. Second-lineif seizures continue → IV levetiracetam, phenytoin, or sodium valproate
4. Third-line (refractory)phenobarbital, or general anaesthesia with intubation in ICU
The rules: benzodiazepine first (lorazepam IV, or buccal midazolam if no access) → repeat once (two benzodiazepine doses in total, counting any given before arrival) → second-line IV antiseizure drug → phenobarbital or ICU/anaesthesia if refractory. Look for + treat the cause throughout (hypoglycaemia, infection, eclampsia, drug withdrawal).
DVLA & driving rules
The patient (not the doctor) must inform the DVLA — but the doctor must advise them to, and to stop driving; if you cannot persuade them to stop, or you find they are still driving against your advice, and that exposes others to a risk of death or serious harm, you should tell them you intend to disclose and then contact the DVLA promptly yourself (GMC) — writing to the patient afterwards and recording it. A patient who lacks the capacity to understand the advice is a separate situation in which you should also inform the DVLA.

Group 1 (car / motorcycle):

SituationRule
First unprovoked seizure6 months off driving (no structural/EEG abnormality; if there is → 12 months)
Established epilepsy / ≥2 seizuresmust be seizure-free for 12 months to drive
Seizures only ever in sleepif there has never been an awake seizure, an established ≥1 year pattern of sleep-only seizures; if there is a history of awake seizures, the pattern must be established over ≥3 years
Medication withdrawalstop driving during withdrawal and for 6 months after; if a seizure occurs → relicensing after 6 months on reinstated medication

Group 2 (HGV / bus — much stricter):

  • First seizure: 5 years seizure-free (off medication) before driving.
  • Epilepsy: 10 years seizure-free and off antiseizure medication.
The high-yield numbers: Group 1 — first seizure = 6 months; epilepsy = 12 months seizure-free; Group 2 — much stricter (5/10 years).
Special considerations
  • Pregnancy: valproate contraindicated; lamotrigine/levetiracetam preferred; high-dose folic acid (5 mg) pre-conception; specialist management.
  • SUDEP (Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy) — a rare but important risk (worse with uncontrolled seizures, non-adherence) → discuss + optimise control.
  • Safety advice: showers not baths, caution with heights/swimming/machinery.
  • Women & contraception: enzyme-inducing drugs (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone, topiramate) reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraception — the copper coil, the hormonal coil and the depot injection are unaffected. The interaction runs the other way for lamotrigine: the combined pill roughly halves lamotrigine levels (risk of losing seizure control), with a rebound rise in the pill-free week.
Exam pearls
Definition
≥2 unprovoked seizures >24h apart (or 1 + high recurrence risk); classify first: focal vs generalised (determines the drug).
Seizure types
Generalised: tonic-clonic, absence (children, 3 Hz spike-wave, no post-ictal), myoclonic (JME), tonic, atonic. Focal: localises to lobe (temporal = aura/automatisms; Todd's paresis = post-ictal weakness).
Exclude mimics
Provoked (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, alcohol withdrawal, infection) and mimics (syncope, NEAD) first; normal EEG doesn't exclude epilepsy.
First-line (NICE)
Generalised tonic-clonic, myoclonic, tonic/atonic → valproate for boys/men and women unable to have children, but lamotrigine or levetiracetam for girls and women able to have children; focal → lamotrigine/levetiracetam; absence → ethosuximide for everyone (carbamazepine worsens absence + myoclonic).
Valproate
Teratogenic → not in women of childbearing potential; don't start in ANY under-55 without 2 specialists (MHRA); men and their partners need contraception during treatment and for 3 months after.
Status epilepticus (>5 min)
ABCDE + glucose → IV lorazepam, repeat once (two benzodiazepine doses TOTAL, counting any given before arrival) → IV levetiracetam/phenytoin/valproate → phenobarbital or ICU/anaesthesia.
DVLA
Group 1: first seizure = 6 months off; epilepsy = 12 months seizure-free; withdrawal = 6 months off. Group 2 = 5/10 years. The patient informs the DVLA — but if they keep driving against advice and others are at risk, you tell the DVLA yourself.
Pregnancy
Lamotrigine/levetiracetam + 5 mg folic acid; SUDEP risk with poor control.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Diabetic Neuro:
What & why
Diabetic neuropathy = nerve damage caused by chronic hyperglycaemia — the commonest complication of diabetes and the commonest cause of peripheral neuropathy in the developed world.
The core concept: diabetic neuropathy is not one thing — it takes several forms (symmetrical sensory, autonomic, mononeuropathy, amyotrophy), but the classic and commonest is a distal symmetrical sensory "glove-and-stocking" polyneuropathy driven by length-dependent nerve damage (longest nerves — the feet — first). Clinical priorities: pain control, foot protection (to prevent ulcers/amputation), detecting autonomic involvement — and above all glycaemic control to prevent progression.
  • One of the microvascular complications of diabetes (alongside retinopathy + nephropathy); risk rises with duration + poor glycaemic control.
The decisive fork — which type of diabetic neuropathy?

Diabetic neuropathy has several distinct patterns — recognising which is present guides management:

TypePatternKey features
Distal symmetrical sensorimotor polyneuropathy (sensory > motor)the commonest — length-dependent"glove-and-stocking" sensory loss (feet first), numbness, burning/tingling pain, loss of proprioception/vibration
Autonomic neuropathyaffects the autonomic nervous systempostural hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, bladder dysfunction, silent MI, gustatory sweating
Mononeuropathy / mononeuritis multiplexsingle (or multiple discrete) nervese.g. CN III palsy (pupil-sparing), carpal tunnel, foot drop
Diabetic amyotrophy (proximal motor)lumbosacral plexuspainful, asymmetrical proximal (thigh) weakness + wasting
The rule: distal symmetrical sensory ("glove-and-stocking") is the classic/commonest; but know the others — autonomic (postural drop, gastroparesis, silent MI), mononeuropathy (CN III pupil-sparing), and amyotrophy (proximal painful wasting).
Pathophysiology
  • Chronic hyperglycaemia damages nerves through several mechanisms: microvascular damage to the vasa nervorum (ischaemia), the polyol/sorbitol pathway (osmotic + oxidative stress), advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), and oxidative stress → predominantly axonal damage (with some secondary demyelination).
  • Sensory > motor in the classic form (contrast with CMT, which is motor-predominant).
The length-dependent principle: the longest nerves are affected first → symptoms start in the feet ("stocking"), then the hands ("glove") as it progresses — this is why it's distal + symmetrical.
Distal symmetrical sensorimotor polyneuropathy — the classic form
📷 Image placeholder — Glove-and-stocking distribution — length-dependent sensory loss beginning in the feet (stocking) before the hands (glove)
  • "Glove-and-stocking" sensory loss — symmetrical, distal, feet before hands.
  • Positive symptoms: burning, tingling, "electric-shock", shooting pain, often worse at night (neuropathic pain).
  • Negative symptoms: numbness, loss of sensation (including loss of protective sensation → the key ulcer risk).
  • Loss of vibration + proprioception (large-fibre — dorsal column), reduced ankle reflexes.
The dangerous consequence: loss of protective sensation → unnoticed trauma → foot ulcers → infection → amputation — the diabetic foot is the major clinical concern. Charcot foot: neuropathy → repeated unnoticed trauma → progressive joint destruction/deformity. Recognise it ACUTELY, before the deformity: a hot, swollen, red foot with intact or bounding pulses and little or no pain, skin unbroken, afebrile, inflammatory markers near-normal — and the X-ray may be normal early. Suspect it even with no deformity, keep the patient non-weight-bearing, and refer to the multidisciplinary foot service within 1 working day (NICE); continuing to walk on it is what produces the irreversible "rocker-bottom" foot.
Autonomic neuropathy — often under-recognised
📷 Image placeholder — Autonomic features by system — postural hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, silent MI and hypoglycaemia unawareness
SystemManifestation
Cardiovascularpostural (orthostatic) hypotension, resting tachycardia, silent myocardial ischaemia (painless MI — a key danger)
GIgastroparesis (early satiety, bloating, vomiting, erratic glycaemic control), diarrhoea/constipation
Genitourinaryerectile dysfunction (often the earliest sign), neurogenic bladder (retention, incontinence)
Othergustatory sweating, hypoglycaemia unawareness (loss of adrenergic warning)
Silent MI: autonomic neuropathy blunts pain perception → diabetics can have "silent" (painless) myocardial infarctions → low threshold to investigate. Hypoglycaemia unawareness: loss of the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia → dangerous.
Assessment / investigations
📷 Image placeholder — The 10 g monofilament test at the standard sole sites — detecting loss of protective sensation at the annual diabetic foot check
  • Diagnosis is largely clinical — history + examination.
  • Diabetic foot check — at least annually if low risk, but every 3 to 6 months if moderate risk and every 1 to 2 months if high risk: 10g monofilament (protective sensation), 128 Hz tuning fork (vibration), ankle reflexes, pinprick, foot inspection (deformity, ulcers), pedal pulses (also check for peripheral arterial disease).
  • Lying + standing BP (postural drop — autonomic).
  • Nerve conduction studies — if diagnostic doubt or atypical.
  • Exclude other causes of neuropathy: don't assume all neuropathy in a diabetic is diabetic — check B12/folate, TFTs, U&E, alcohol history, drugs (a treatable cause may coexist).
  • Assess for the other microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy — they cluster).
Management — glycaemic control + pain + foot protection
The overarching principle: optimise glycaemic control (prevents progression) + neuropathic pain management + meticulous foot care + manage autonomic features.
  • Glycaemic control (the foundation): tight glucose control slows/prevents progression (especially in type 1) — the single most important disease-modifying step; also manage BP, lipids, smoking.

Neuropathic pain management (NICE):

  • First-line = one of: amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, or pregabalin (any of the four).
  • NICE does not rank the four — it is a free choice. In UK practice duloxetine is often chosen in diabetes because it is licensed for diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain (and helps if mood is low). Amitriptyline is used off-label (start 10 mg at night) and its antimuscarinic effects worsen postural hypotension and urinary retention — the very autonomic problems below.
  • Gabapentin and pregabalin are controlled drugs (Class C, Schedule 3) — CD prescribing rules apply, and the MHRA warns of misuse, dependence and severe respiratory depression, especially in the elderly, in respiratory disease, and combined with opioids (including the tramadol used for rescue). Both are renally cleared, so check eGFR and reduce the dose in CKD — diabetic nephropathy commonly coexists, and accumulation causes sedation, ataxia and myoclonus.
  • Carbamazepine is the exception, not a lower rung: it is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia specifically, and is not used for other neuropathic pain including diabetic neuropathy.
  • If the first is ineffective/not tolerated → switch to one of the other three (and can switch again).
  • Tramadol only for acute rescue — do not start long-term tramadol, morphine or other strong opioids for neuropathic pain outside a specialist pain service. Capsaicin cream for localised pain if oral treatments are unsuitable.
  • Foot care (critical — prevents amputation): diabetic foot protection — regular podiatry, patient education (daily foot checks, appropriate footwear), and — for any active foot problem (ulcer, spreading infection, critical ischaemia, gangrene, suspected Charcot) — referral to the MDT diabetic foot service within 1 working day (NICE).
  • Autonomic: postural hypotension → first review the drugs that worsen it (antihypertensives, diuretics, alpha-blockers, tricyclics), then conservative measures ± fludrocortisone/midodrine; gastroparesis → dietary measures plus a prokinetic — NICE suggests alternating erythromycin and metoclopramide (metoclopramide for a maximum of 5 days at a time, MHRA), with domperidone only exceptionally because of its cardiac risk; erectile dysfunction → PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil).
  • Multidisciplinary: diabetology, podiatry, pain team.
Key point: neuropathic pain responds to the agents above (amitriptyline/duloxetine/gabapentin/pregabalin), NOT to standard analgesics/NSAIDs.
Exam pearls
What it is
Commonest complication of diabetes; a microvascular complication (with retinopathy + nephropathy).
Types
Distal symmetrical sensory (commonest — "glove-and-stocking"), autonomic, mononeuropathy (CN III pupil-sparing, carpal tunnel), amyotrophy (proximal painful wasting).
Length-dependent
Feet first (stocking) then hands (glove); sensory > motor (contrast CMT = motor-predominant).
Key danger
Loss of protective sensation → foot ulcers → amputation (+ Charcot foot).
Autonomic
Postural hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, silent MI, hypoglycaemia unawareness.
Assessment
Annual foot check — 10g monofilament + 128 Hz tuning fork + reflexes + pulses; lying/standing BP; exclude other causes (B12, thyroid, alcohol).
Management
Glycaemic control (prevents progression) + neuropathic pain (amitriptyline/duloxetine/gabapentin/pregabalin — duloxetine favoured in diabetes) + foot care + autonomic management.
Pain agents
Neuropathic pain does NOT respond to standard analgesics/NSAIDs.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Creutzfeldt-Ja:
What & why
CJD = a rapidly progressive, fatal neurodegenerative disease caused by prions — misfolded proteins that induce further misfolding in the brain.
The core concept: CJD is the archetypal prion disease — an infectious/misfolding protein (not a virus or bacterium) triggers a chain reaction of protein misfolding → spongiform (vacuolated) brain degeneration → a rapidly progressive dementia + myoclonus, invariably fatal within ~1 year. The hallmark that flags it is rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus — far faster than Alzheimer's or the other dementias.
  • Rare; the prototype of the transmissible spongiform encephalopathies; no cure — management is palliative.
The prion mechanism
📷 Image placeholder — Templated misfolding — normal PrP^C converted to protease-resistant PrP^Sc β-pleated sheets that accumulate and cause spongiform change
  • Prions = abnormal, misfolded forms of a normal cellular protein (PrP): the misfolded prion protein induces normal PrP to misfold too → a self-propagating chain reaction.
  • The misfolded protein forms tightly-packed β-pleated sheets resistant to proteases → they accumulate, can't be broken down, and cause spongiform (vacuolated) neurodegeneration.
Key features of prions: not a conventional pathogen — no nucleic acid (DNA/RNA); a protein-only infectious agent. Resistant to standard sterilisation (protease-, heat-, radiation-resistant) → an infection-control concern (e.g. contaminated neurosurgical instruments). ALL forms — sporadic and genetic included — are potentially transmissible by inoculation of high-infectivity tissue (brain, spinal cord, posterior eye), so infection-control precautions apply to every type, not just vCJD. But CJD is NOT spread by casual contact, droplets or routine nursing care — no isolation is needed.
The decisive fork — which type of CJD?
📷 Image placeholder — Sporadic vs variant vs familial vs iatrogenic CJD — mechanism, typical age, onset (myoclonus vs psychiatric/pulvinar vs family history vs procedure)

CJD has several forms, distinguished by how the prion arose:

Type% / mechanismKey features
Sporadic CJD~85% (the commonest); spontaneous misfolding; ~1–2 per million per year in the UKolder adults — UK median onset 67; rapid dementia + myoclonus
Variant CJD (vCJD)acquired — eating BSE-infected beef ("mad cow disease")young adults (median onset ~26); psychiatric/behavioural onset + painful sensory symptoms; slower; pulvinar sign on MRI. UK: 178 cases in total, and none since 2016 — essentially historical, whereas sporadic CJD is what you will actually meet
Familial (inherited) CJD~10–15% — autosomal dominant PRNP mutationfamily history; younger onset
Iatrogenic CJDacquired — medical transmission (contaminated neurosurgical instruments, dura mater grafts, corneal grafts, cadaveric human growth hormone)history of relevant procedure
The high-yield distinctions: sporadic = commonest, elderly, rapid dementia + myoclonus; variant (vCJD) = younger, from BSE beef, psychiatric onset, pulvinar sign.
Clinical features
FeatureDetail
Rapidly progressive dementiathe hallmark — cognitive decline over weeks–months (far faster than other dementias)
Myoclonussudden involuntary jerks — the classic accompanying sign
Other neurologycerebellar signs (ataxia), visual disturbance, pyramidal/extrapyramidal signs, akinetic mutism (late)
vCJDearly psychiatric/behavioural changes + painful sensory symptoms
The rule: rapidly progressive dementia + myoclonus = CJD until proven otherwise — the speed (weeks–months) is the key clue distinguishing it from Alzheimer's/other dementias. Death usually within a year in sporadic CJD (median ~4 months); vCJD is slower, around 14 months.
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — DWI-MRI — cortical ribboning + basal-ganglia hyperintensity in sporadic CJD vs the bilateral posterior-thalamic pulvinar sign in vCJD
  • CSF (lumbar puncture): normal on routine analysis — but can send 14-3-3 protein + RT-QuIC (raised/positive support the diagnosis).
  • EEG: triphasic, high-amplitude sharp waves (periodic sharp-wave complexes) — classic in sporadic CJD.
  • MRI: in sporadic CJD, cortical ribboning (cortical DWI hyperintensity) and basal ganglia (caudate/putamen) hyperintensity; in vCJD, the "pulvinar sign" (bilateral posterior thalamic hyperintensity).
  • Definitive diagnosis = tissue biopsy: brain biopsy / post-mortem showing spongiform change + prion protein (rarely done ante-mortem due to risk + transmissibility).
  • Tonsil biopsy — prion protein in lymphoreticular tissue is highly sensitive and specific for vCJD (not sporadic CJD), and is the practical ante-mortem confirmatory test when vCJD is suspected. This matters because CSF RT-QuIC is usually NEGATIVE in vCJD, so a negative CSF panel does not exclude it.
  • Genetic testing (PRNP) for familial forms.
The differential — rapidly progressive dementia

CJD is the classic cause, but exclude treatable mimics of rapid cognitive decline:

CauseNote
CJD (prion)rapid dementia + myoclonus; EEG/MRI/CSF as above
Autoimmune / limbic encephalitistreatable — anti-NMDA, paraneoplastic; check autoantibodies
InfectionHIV, neurosyphilis, PML, viral encephalitis
Metabolic / toxicB12 deficiency, thyroid, Wernicke's
MalignancyCNS lymphoma, paraneoplastic
The point: rapidly progressive dementia warrants a workup for treatable causes (autoimmune encephalitis especially) before concluding CJD.
Management — palliative
The overarching principle: no cure → supportive/palliative care + infection control + notification.
  • No cure / no disease-modifying treatment — invariably fatal. Sporadic CJD has a median survival of about 4 months (most dead within a year); vCJD runs longer, around 14 months.
  • Palliative + supportive care: symptom control (myoclonus → clonazepam/levetiracetam, agitation, pain), MDT, family support, end-of-life care planning.
  • Infection control: prions are resistant to standard decontamination — they survive standard autoclaving and formalin fixation. Instruments used on high-infectivity tissue in a suspected case are quarantined pending the diagnosis and destroyed if it is confirmed, never simply reprocessed; use single-use LP needles; and involve the infection prevention and control team early.
  • Notification — two separate duties: CJD is a notifiable disease, so notify UKHSA / your local health protection team on suspicion; and separately refer and discuss every suspected case with the National CJD Research & Surveillance Unit in Edinburgh, which runs national surveillance and provides the specialist tests (CSF RT-QuIC, PRNP sequencing, neuropathology).
  • Blood, tissue and organs: vCJD has been transmitted by blood transfusion in the UK. Anyone with CJD, or identified as "at increased risk of CJD for public health purposes", must never donate blood, tissue or organs, and must tell surgical, dental and endoscopy teams before any invasive procedure. In the UK, anyone who has themselves been transfused since 1980 is deferred from blood donation.
  • Genetic counselling for familial CJD — note that a PRNP mutation makes at-risk relatives "at increased risk of CJD for public health purposes", with the donation and surgical-instrument implications above.
Exam pearls
What it is
Rapidly progressive, fatal prion disease → rapid dementia + myoclonus, death usually within ~1 year.
Prion mechanism
Misfolded PrP induces normal protein to misfold → protease-resistant β-pleated sheets → spongiform neurodegeneration; protein-only agent (no DNA/RNA), resistant to sterilisation.
Types
Sporadic (~85%, commonest, elderly); variant vCJD (BSE beef, younger, psychiatric onset, pulvinar sign); familial (PRNP mutation); iatrogenic (contaminated instruments/grafts/hGH).
The hallmark
Rapidly progressive dementia + myoclonus = CJD until proven otherwise (speed distinguishes from other dementias).
Investigations
CSF normal (± 14-3-3/RT-QuIC); EEG = periodic (triphasic) sharp-wave complexes at ~1–2 Hz; MRI = basal ganglia/thalamus hyperintensity (pulvinar sign in vCJD); definitive = tissue biopsy.
Exclude treatable mimics
Rapid dementia workup — especially autoimmune encephalitis.
Management
No cure → palliative; symptom control (myoclonus → clonazepam); prion infection-control precautions; notifiable disease.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Charcot-Marie-:
What & why
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT) = an inherited (hereditary) peripheral neuropathy affecting motor and sensory peripheral nerves — also called hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy (HMSN).
The core concept: CMT is a length-dependent, predominantly motor peripheral neuropathy — so it hits the longest nerves first (the feet/legs), producing the classic distal wasting + foot deformity + high-stepping gait picture. It's the commonest inherited neuropathy, is slowly progressive, and has no cure — management is supportive.
  • Usually presents in childhood/adolescence (CMT2 often presents later, in adulthood); mostly autosomal dominant; a lower motor neuron (LMN) pattern (it's a peripheral nerve disease).
The decisive fork — inherited or acquired neuropathy?

CMT must be distinguished from acquired peripheral neuropathies (far commoner and often treatable):

Points to CMT (inherited)Points to acquired neuropathy
Family history (autosomal dominant)no family history
Very slow onset (years), from childhoodsubacute/acute onset
Marked foot deformity (pes cavus, hammer toes) — implies long-standingless deformity
Symmetrical, distal, predominantly motorpattern varies (e.g. diabetic = sensory)
No identifiable acquired cause on screeningan identifiable cause (diabetes, B12, alcohol, drugs) — or CIDP, which is treatable
The rule: pes cavus + a positive family history + slow distal weakness = CMT; the foot deformity implies a long-standing (hence inherited) neuropathy. Always exclude acquired causes first (diabetes, B12 deficiency, alcohol, drugs, thyroid) — all of which are axonal. The one mimic that really matters is CIDP, because it is treatable and CMT is not: CIDP comes on over weeks to months, is often asymmetric with proximal as well as distal weakness, has no pes cavus and no family history, and shows patchy slowing with conduction block on nerve conduction studies (CMT1 slows uniformly, without block). CIDP responds to steroids, IVIg or plasma exchange — so an atypical or rapidly progressive "CMT" needs urgent neurology referral.
Pathophysiology
📷 Image placeholder — CMT1 (demyelinating) vs CMT2 (axonal) — CMT1A from a PMP22 duplication on chromosome 17 is the single commonest subtype
  • Caused by mutations affecting peripheral nerve myelin or axons → demyelinating (CMT1 — commonest, e.g. PMP22 duplication) or axonal (CMT2) subtypes.
  • Predominantly motor — motor > sensory involvement.
The length-dependent principle: the longest nerves are affected first → symptoms start in the feet/legs, then progress to the hands ("stocking then glove") → this explains the distal-first pattern.
Clinical features — the classic picture
📷 Image placeholder — Bilateral pes cavus, hammer toes and “inverted champagne-bottle” calves — distal wasting with preserved thighs, the classic CMT lower-limb picture

A peripheral neuropathy — predominantly motor weakness, with characteristic signs:

FeatureDetail
Pes cavushigh foot arches — the classic deformity
Hammer toes—
Foot dropweak dorsiflexion → high-stepping gait as compensation
"Inverted champagne bottle legs"distal muscle wasting + weakness — thin lower legs with preserved thighs
Areflexia (or marked hyporeflexia)LMN signs — reflexes are typically absent; tone is reduced or normal
Distal sensory lossmilder (stocking distribution)
The signature signs: pes cavus + "inverted champagne bottle" legs + high-stepping (foot drop) gait + areflexia = the classic CMT tetrad.
The LMN pattern (cross-ref motor pathways): because CMT is a peripheral nerve (LMN) disease, it produces LMN signs — wasting, hyporeflexia, hypotonia (not the ↑tone/hyperreflexia of a UMN lesion). Also: distal hand wasting/weakness (later), foot ulcers (sensory loss), palpably thickened nerves (demyelinating types).
Investigations
  • Diagnosis is clinical (characteristic picture + family history), supported by:
  • Nerve conduction studies (NCS) — slowed conduction (demyelinating CMT1) or reduced amplitudes (axonal CMT2); confirms a peripheral neuropathy and its type.
  • Genetic testing — confirms diagnosis + subtype (e.g. PMP22 duplication in CMT1A).
  • Nerve biopsy (rarely needed) — "onion bulb" formation in demyelinating types.
  • Exclude acquired causes: glucose/HbA1c (diabetes), B12/folate, TFTs, U&E, LFT.
Management — supportive, no cure
📷 Image placeholder — Ankle-foot orthosis (AFO) correcting foot drop — the first-line orthotic restoring a safe heel-strike gait
The overarching principle: no cure → multidisciplinary supportive care to maintain function and mobility.
  • Physiotherapy — maintain strength, range of movement, mobility.
  • Occupational therapy — aids and adaptations.
  • Orthotics — ankle-foot orthoses (AFOs) for foot drop, special footwear for pes cavus.
  • Podiatry — foot care (deformity, ulcer prevention from sensory loss).
  • Analgesia — for neuropathic pain, NICE offers a free choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin, switching to another if one fails. Note gabapentin and pregabalin are Schedule 3 controlled drugs with an MHRA warning about respiratory depression.
  • Orthopaedic surgery — for severe foot deformity/contractures.
  • Genetic counselling — most CMT is autosomal dominant (50% risk to offspring), but CMTX is the second commonest form: X-linked, males more severely affected, and an affected father transmits it to all his daughters and none of his sons. Recessive forms exist too, so the recurrence risk depends on the confirmed genotype.
  • Pregnancy: symptoms worsen in roughly a third of women, usually settling after delivery; there may be more operative deliveries, malpresentation and postpartum haemorrhage. Pregnancy is generally safe — offer pre-pregnancy genetic counselling and obstetric/anaesthetic review.
  • Driving: the patient must notify the DVLA if CMT affects safe vehicle control (foot drop, impaired pedal proprioception); many hold a time-limited licence or drive an automatic/adapted vehicle.
Safety point (the high-yield one): vincristine is CONTRAINDICATED in demyelinating CMT (BNF) — not merely cautioned. One or two doses can cause severe, sometimes irreversible deterioration, and it can unmask previously undiagnosed CMT, so ask about foot deformity and a family history of neuropathy before giving a vinca alkaloid. Paclitaxel/taxanes are the only other agent with good evidence of added risk. Use nitrofurantoin (a first-line UTI antibiotic, cautioned in pre-existing neuropathy), prolonged metronidazole, amiodarone and platinum agents with care and specialist advice.
Exam pearls
What it is
CMT (HMSN) = inherited, predominantly motor, length-dependent peripheral neuropathy; mostly autosomal dominant; commonest inherited neuropathy.
Classic picture
Pes cavus + hammer toes + foot drop (high-stepping gait) + "inverted champagne bottle" legs (distal wasting) + hyporeflexia/hypotonia.
LMN pattern
Peripheral nerve disease → wasting, ↓reflexes, ↓tone (NOT UMN signs).
Length-dependent
Feet/legs first (stocking), then hands (glove).
Inherited vs acquired
Family history + long-standing foot deformity = inherited (CMT); always exclude diabetes, B12, alcohol, thyroid.
Investigations
Nerve conduction studies (demyelinating CMT1 = slow conduction; axonal CMT2 = ↓amplitude) + genetic testing (PMP22).
Management
No cure → supportive — physiotherapy, orthotics (AFOs for foot drop), podiatry, analgesia, genetic counselling; vincristine is CONTRAINDICATED (and paclitaxel avoided); notify the DVLA if it affects safe driving.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cerebral Venou:
What & why
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) = a thrombus in the cerebral venous sinuses (or cerebral veins) obstructing venous drainage of the brain.
The core concept: unlike arterial stroke (which cuts off supply), CVST obstructs venous drainage → venous congestion → raised pressure → cerebral oedema, raised ICP, and venous (often haemorrhagic) infarction. This "backing-up" mechanism explains everything: the headache/raised ICP, the seizures, and — critically — why anticoagulation is given even when there's a haemorrhage (the bleed is caused by the venous congestion, so treating the clot relieves it).
  • Rare but important — a cause of stroke in young adults, women (hormonal), and pregnancy/puerperium; frequently missed/delayed because the presentation is variable.
The decisive fork — which sinus/vein is thrombosed?
📷 Image placeholder — The superior sagittal sinus is commonest (~50%) → headache, raised ICP, seizures, hemiplegia; transverse/sigmoid thrombosis can follow otitis/mastoiditis

The clinical syndrome depends on which venous structure is occluded:

SiteFrequency / features
Superior sagittal sinus~50% (the commonest); headache, raised ICP, seizures + hemiplegia, ↓consciousness
Cavernous sinusperiorbital erythema + oedema, ophthalmoplegia, eye pain (see below)
Transverse/sigmoid sinusheadache, ear/mastoid involvement (can follow otitis/mastoiditis)
Deep venous system (straight sinus)severe — thalamic/deep involvement, ↓consciousness
The rule: ~50% are isolated sagittal sinus thromboses (the commonest); cavernous sinus thrombosis has a distinctive eye-centred picture.
Clinical features

The presentation is variable — the common threads:

FeatureDetail
Headachethe commonest symptom — may be sudden onset (can mimic subarachnoid haemorrhage) or gradual/progressive; often a raised-ICP headache (worse lying down, worse on Valsalva)
Nausea + vomitingraised ICP
Reduced consciousness—
Seizuresmore common than in arterial stroke (a useful clue)
Focal deficitse.g. hemiplegia (sagittal sinus)
Papilloedema / visual symptomsraised ICP
Clues that point to CVST over arterial stroke: headache + seizures + focal signs that don't fit a single arterial territory + a young patient with thrombotic risk factors. Can mimic subarachnoid haemorrhage, IIH, meningoencephalitis, arterial stroke.
Cavernous sinus thrombosis — the distinctive eye syndrome
📷 Image placeholder — CN VI is affected first (runs centrally through the sinus) before CN III/IV (in the wall); often septic, spreading from the facial “danger triangle” → give antibiotics

A specific, exam-favourite subtype — because of what runs through the cavernous sinus:

FeatureMechanism
Periorbital erythema + oedemavenous congestion of orbital drainage
Ophthalmoplegia — CN VI (6th) affected before CN III/IVCN VI runs freely through the middle of the sinus (most vulnerable); III/IV run in the wall
Eye pain + facial hyperaesthesia (upper face)trigeminal (CN V₁/V₂) involvement
Proptosis, chemosisvenous congestion
The CN VI-first point: in cavernous sinus pathology the 6th nerve is affected before the 3rd/4th (it sits centrally, exposed) → early lateral rectus palsy (failure of abduction). Cavernous sinus thrombosis is often septic (spreading from facial/sinus/dental infection — the "danger triangle" of the face) → needs antibiotics too.
Risk factors — think "prothrombotic"

CVST is fundamentally a thrombotic disorder — look for a hypercoagulable state (Virchow's triad):

CategoryExamples
Hormonalcombined oral contraceptive pill, pregnancy + puerperium (postpartum — ~20% of cases), HRT
ThrombophiliaFactor V Leiden, antiphospholipid syndrome, protein C/S/antithrombin deficiency
Malignancyprothrombotic states
Infectionlocal (sinusitis, otitis/mastoiditis, dental, facial → cavernous/transverse sinus), meningitis
Dehydration, systemicdehydration, inflammatory disease (Behçet's, IBD, SLE), nephrotic syndrome
Otherhead injury, recent LP/neurosurgery; VITT (vaccine-induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia — a rare cause)
The high-yield associations: a young woman on the COCP or postpartum → classic CVST context.
Investigations
  • 1st-line / investigation of choice: MRI venography (MRV) — visualises the thrombosed sinus and any venous infarct/oedema; CT venography is an equally good alternative.
  • Non-contrast CT head can be normal in around 30% of cases — a key pitfall: a normal CT does NOT exclude CVST → if suspected, proceed to venography.
  • The "empty delta sign": on contrast CT/venography, a filling defect in the (superior sagittal) sinus — contrast outlines the sinus wall but not the clot → a triangular "empty" centre.
  • D-dimer: may support (often raised) but a normal D-dimer does NOT exclude CVST → don't rely on it.
  • Investigate the cause: pregnancy test, look for infection/malignancy, and test for antiphospholipid antibodies (these change the type and duration of anticoagulation). A heritable thrombophilia screen is NOT routinely indicated just because the clot is at an unusual site — it would not change management.
Management — the counterintuitive anticoagulation point
📷 Image placeholder — Anticoagulate even when there is a haemorrhagic venous infarct — the bleed is driven by venous congestion, so clearing the clot relieves it (the opposite of arterial haemorrhagic stroke)
The overarching principle: anticoagulate — even if there's a haemorrhage — plus treat the cause, seizures, and raised ICP.
  • Acute: anticoagulation with LMWH — low-molecular-weight heparin is first-line acute treatment. The one exception is VITT (thrombosis with thrombocytopenia after a COVID vaccine): here heparin must be AVOIDED — use a non-heparin anticoagulant plus IV immunoglobulin, under haematology.
  • Long-term: warfarin (or a DOAC) — but if the patient is pregnant, neither can be used: warfarin is teratogenic and DOACs are contraindicated, so continue LMWH throughout pregnancy and for at least 6 weeks postnatally. Typical total duration is 3–12 months (3–6 months if a transient/reversible factor e.g. pregnancy/COCP; 6–12 months if idiopathic; lifelong if recurrent/persistent thrombophilia/malignancy).
  • Treat the underlying cause: antibiotics if septic (esp. cavernous sinus thrombosis from facial/sinus infection); stop the COCP; treat malignancy/thrombophilia.
  • Supportive: antiepileptics for seizures; manage raised ICP; endovascular thrombectomy or decompressive surgery reserved for severe/deteriorating cases.
  • Pregnancy/future: avoid oestrogen-containing contraception afterwards; prophylactic LMWH in future pregnancies if prior CVST.
CRITICAL, counterintuitive: anticoagulate EVEN IN THE PRESENCE OF INTRACRANIAL HAEMORRHAGE — the venous (haemorrhagic) infarct is caused by the venous congestion, and anticoagulation (by clearing the clot) relieves the congestion and does not worsen the bleed. This is the opposite of arterial haemorrhagic stroke (where you would never anticoagulate).
Exam pearls
What it is
Thrombosis of the cerebral venous sinuses → obstructs venous drainage → congestion → raised ICP + cerebral oedema + (often haemorrhagic) venous infarction.
Commonest site
~50% = superior sagittal sinus → headache, seizures, hemiplegia.
Cavernous sinus thrombosis
Periorbital oedema/erythema, ophthalmoplegia (CN VI before III/IV), eye pain + upper-face hyperaesthesia (CN V); often septic (facial infection).
Features
Headache (commonest, may be sudden), N+V, seizures (more than arterial stroke), focal deficits, ↓consciousness, papilloedema.
Risk factors
COCP, pregnancy/puerperium (classic), thrombophilia, malignancy, local infection (sinusitis/otitis), dehydration, VITT.
Investigations
MRI/CT venography (1st-line); non-contrast CT is normal in ~30% (doesn't exclude it); empty delta sign; D-dimer doesn't exclude.
Management
LMWH acutely → warfarin long-term (3–12 months) — anticoagulate EVEN WITH intracranial haemorrhage (opposite of arterial stroke); treat cause (antibiotics if septic, stop COCP), antiepileptics, manage raised ICP.
Afterwards
Avoid oestrogen contraception; prophylactic LMWH in future pregnancy.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cerebral Palsy:
What & why
