Cerebral palsy (CP) = a disorder of movement and posture due to a non-progressive lesion of the developing brain's motor pathways (occurring antenatally, perinatally, or in early childhood — conventionally up to about 2 years).
The core concept: the two defining features are that the lesion is non-progressive (a fixed, one-off brain injury — it doesn't get worse), but the clinical picture evolves as the child develops (the motor signs become more apparent over time). CP is a clinical, umbrella diagnosis, classified by the type of motor disorder, which localises the injury (spastic → UMN/cortex; dyskinetic → basal ganglia; ataxic → cerebellum).
  • The commonest cause of physical disability in children; non-progressive is the key word (distinguishes it from neurodegenerative conditions).
The decisive fork — which type of motor disorder?

CP is classified by the predominant motor abnormality, which points to where the brain was injured:

Type%Motor abnormalityLesion site
Spastic~70–90% (the great majority)increased tone (spasticity) — UMN patternupper motor neurons (motor cortex/pyramidal tracts)
Dyskineticdystonia and/or choreoathetosis (slow writhing movements) + oro-motor problemsbasal ganglia + substantia nigra
Ataxiccerebellar signs (incoordination, ataxia)cerebellum
Mixedcombinationmultiple
The localisation logic (cross-ref motor pathways / basal ganglia / cerebellum):
• Spastic = UMN damage → ↑tone, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars (though extensor plantars are normal under about 1 year, so they carry little weight in infants).
• Dyskinetic = basal ganglia damage → athetoid/involuntary movements.
• Ataxic = cerebellar damage → the DANISH cerebellar signs.
The rule: the type of motor disorder tells you which part of the motor system was injured — a direct application of the "three motor flavours" (weakness/tone vs movement vs coordination).
Spastic CP subtypes
📷 Image placeholder — Why prematurity → spastic diplegia — periventricular leukomalacia damages the corticospinal fibres running nearest the lateral ventricles (which carry the leg signals), so legs are affected more than arms

Spastic CP (the commonest) is subdivided by which limbs are affected:

SubtypeDistribution
Hemiplegiaone side (arm + leg)
Diplegiaboth legs (arms mild/spared) — classically associated with prematurity
Quadriplegiaall four limbs (most severe; often with seizures, learning disability)
The spastic pattern: increased tone from damage to UMNs — so all spastic subtypes show the UMN signs (↑tone, brisk reflexes, clonus, upgoing plantars).
Causes — mostly antenatal
📷 Image placeholder — Prevention high-yield — antenatal magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection — offer between 24+0 and 29+6 weeks, consider between 30+0 and 33+6 weeks (NICE), and therapeutic hypothermia within 6h for moderate–severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy in term babies
TimingCauses
Antenatal (commonest)cerebral malformation, congenital infection (CMV, rubella, toxoplasmosis), placental insufficiency, genetic
Perinatalhypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (birth asphyxia — but this accounts for only about 10% of cases), prematurity, low birth weight, intraventricular haemorrhage of prematurity
Postnatalmeningitis/encephalitis, head injury (incl. non-accidental), kernicterus (severe neonatal jaundice)
High-yield links: CMV, rubella, and toxoplasmosis are TORCH infections that all cause CP (cross-ref congenital infections). Prematurity → periventricular leukomalacia / intraventricular haemorrhage → spastic diplegia classically.
Clinical features & presentation

CP typically presents in infancy/early childhood with:

  • Delayed motor milestones — not sitting by 8 months or not walking by 18 months (both corrected for gestation), or hand preference before 1 year. Any of these → refer to a child development service (NICE).
  • Abnormal tone (hypertonia/spasticity, or early hypotonia).
  • Abnormal posture/movements, asymmetry of movement (early hand preference <1 year is abnormal — suggests hemiplegia).
  • Persistent primitive reflexes, brisk reflexes (UMN signs).
  • Feeding difficulties (oro-motor).
Associated comorbidities (CP is rarely isolated): learning disability, epilepsy, visual/hearing impairment, speech/language difficulties, behavioural problems, GORD/feeding problems, constipation, hip subluxation, scoliosis → CP needs multidisciplinary care.
Non-progressive but evolving: the underlying lesion doesn't progress, but the manifestations change as the nervous system matures → worsening function over time should prompt reconsideration (a progressive picture is NOT CP).
Assessment / investigations
  • Diagnosis is clinical — history (risk factors, milestones) + examination (tone, posture, reflexes, movement pattern).
  • MRI brain — to identify the underlying lesion (e.g. periventricular leukomalacia, malformation) and support the diagnosis (not to make it) — a normal MRI does not exclude CP.
  • Exclude progressive/mimicking conditions (metabolic, neurodegenerative) — because CP is by definition non-progressive. Refer to paediatric neurology if there are no risk factors, a family history of a progressive neurological disorder, loss of skills already attained, new unexpected focal signs, or an MRI suggesting a progressive disorder or not matching the clinical picture (NICE).
  • Assess for the comorbidities (vision, hearing, cognition, epilepsy, feeding, orthopaedic).
  • GMFCS (Gross Motor Function Classification System) grades functional severity.
Management — MDT + symptom control
📷 Image placeholder — Spasticity ladder — focal (e.g. gastrocnemius equinus) → intramuscular botulinum toxin A; generalised → oral baclofen (or diazepam for short-term painful spasm) then intrathecal baclofen for severe generalised spasticity; ambulant spastic diplegia (GMFCS II–III) → selective dorsal rhizotomy; contractures → orthopaedic surgery
The overarching principle: no cure (the lesion is fixed) → multidisciplinary supportive care aimed at maximising function and managing spasticity + comorbidities.
  • Multidisciplinary team: physiotherapy (the cornerstone — maintain range of movement, function), occupational therapy, speech & language therapy (communication + feeding), dietitian, orthotics, social/educational support, paediatric neurology.

Managing spasticity:

  • Oral baclofen — for a sustained, long-term effect (the default oral agent).
  • Oral diazepam — for rapid, short-term relief of painful spasm; sedating, so usually short courses.
  • Intrathecal baclofen — for severe generalised spasticity.
  • Botulinum toxin type A (targeted intramuscular — for focal spasticity).
  • Orthopaedic surgery (for contractures, hip/spine).
  • Selective dorsal rhizotomy (neurosurgical) — for AMBULANT children with spastic diplegia (GMFCS II–III, aged 3–9, no dystonia), to improve gait. It is not for the most severely affected child — that is where intrathecal baclofen belongs.
  • Anticonvulsants for epilepsy; analgesia as required.
  • Eating, drinking and swallowing: ask about coughing, choking or colour change with feeds and recurrent chest infections — these mean an unsafe swallow. Refer to a dysphagia-trained SALT/MDT; aspiration is the commonest cause of death in CP.
  • Hip surveillance: every child with CP enters a surveillance programme from about age 2 (clinical examination + pelvic X-ray), with frequency set by GMFCS level — displacement risk rises from near zero at GMFCS I to around 90% at GMFCS V, and it is painless until advanced.
  • Pain is common and under-recognised. Unexplained irritability, distress or a change in behaviour is a physical cause until proven otherwise — hip subluxation/dislocation, dystonia or spasm, GORD, constipation, fracture, dental or urinary pain — not "just the CP".
  • Other comorbidities: GORD/feeding (may need gastrostomy), constipation, drooling, visual/hearing support, learning support.
  • The goal: not cure, but optimise function, comfort, and participation — lifelong support.
Exam pearls
What it is
Non-progressive lesion of the developing brain → disorder of movement & posture; the lesion is fixed but the clinical picture evolves with development.
Classification (localises the lesion)
Spastic (~70–90%, UMN damage — ↑tone), dyskinetic (basal ganglia — dystonia and/or athetoid movements), ataxic (cerebellum — cerebellar signs), mixed.
Spastic subtypes
Hemiplegia, diplegia (prematurity), quadriplegia (most severe). (NICE classifies these as unilateral vs bilateral spastic CP.)
Causes
Mostly antenatal — cerebral malformation, congenital infection (CMV, rubella, toxoplasmosis); also perinatal hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, prematurity, postnatal (meningitis, kernicterus, trauma).
Presentation
Delayed motor milestones (not sitting by 8 months, not walking by 18 months — corrected), abnormal tone/posture, early hand preference (<1yr), persistent primitive reflexes → refer to a child development service.
Comorbidities
Epilepsy, learning disability, visual/hearing/speech impairment, feeding problems and unsafe swallow (aspiration is the commonest cause of death), hip displacement (painless until late — everyone needs surveillance), and pain (common and under-recognised).
Non-progressive
A worsening course is NOT CP (reconsider the diagnosis).
Management (no cure — MDT)
Physiotherapy (cornerstone) + OT/SALT; spasticity → oral baclofen (diazepam for short-term painful spasm), botulinum toxin A for focal spasticity, intrathecal baclofen if severe and generalised, selective dorsal rhizotomy for AMBULANT spastic diplegia, orthopaedic surgery for contractures; anticonvulsants; manage comorbidities.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Brain Abscess:
What & why
A brain abscess = a focal collection of pus within the brain parenchyma, usually bacterial, surrounded by a capsule and oedema — a neurosurgical + infective emergency.
The core concept: a brain abscess presents as a combination of infection (fever) + a space-occupying lesion (raised ICP, focal deficit) + seizures — but the "classic triad" is often incomplete, so a high index of suspicion is needed, especially with a predisposing source. The diagnostic hallmark is a ring-enhancing lesion on imaging, and management combines prolonged antibiotics + neurosurgical drainage.
  • Can be fatal if untreated (raised ICP → herniation); higher risk in the immunocompromised.
The decisive fork — how did the infection reach the brain?
📷 Image placeholder — Routes of spread mapped to abscess site — otitis/mastoiditis → temporal lobe/cerebellum, sinusitis → frontal lobe, haematogenous (endocarditis, lung, cyanotic right-to-left shunt) → multiple grey–white junction lesions

The route of spread points to the likely organism and any co-existing focus to treat:

RouteSourceTypical organisms / location
Direct / contiguous spreadotitis media / mastoiditis → temporal lobe / cerebellum; sinusitis → frontal lobe; dental infectionstreptococci (especially the Streptococcus anginosus / "milleri" group — the commonest UK isolate), anaerobes (Bacteroides), oral flora
Haematogenous spreaddistant infection — endocarditis, lung abscess/bronchiectasis, skin, dental; cyanotic congenital heart disease (right-to-left shunt bypasses lung filter)often multiple abscesses, at grey-white junction; streptococci, Staph aureus
Penetrating trauma / neurosurgeryopen skull fracture, surgeryStaph aureus
ImmunocompromisedHIV, transplantToxoplasma (HIV), fungi (Aspergillus, Candida), Nocardia, TB
  • The high-yield source links: otitis/mastoiditis → temporal lobe/cerebellar abscess; sinusitis → frontal lobe; cyanotic congenital heart disease → haematogenous (the right-to-left shunt lets bacteria bypass the pulmonary filter).
In HIV: a ring-enhancing lesion is Toxoplasmosis until proven otherwise — the key immunocompromised differential. It is not treated like a bacterial abscess: give anti-toxoplasma therapy (pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid) and repeat imaging — a response within about 2 weeks confirms the diagnosis without needing to biopsy.
Clinical features — the triad (often incomplete)

The classic triad is present in <50% — so don't rely on all three:

FeatureFrom
Feverthe infection (may be absent — an important pitfall)
Headacheraised ICP / the mass (often the commonest symptom — dull, progressive, unremitting)
Focal neurological deficitdepends on abscess location (hemiparesis, aphasia, ataxia, visual field defect)
  • Also: seizures, nausea/vomiting, ↓consciousness/confusion, personality change, signs of raised ICP (papilloedema, worsening headache) — evolving over days to weeks.
The pitfall: fever is often absent and the presentation can be subacute → a brain abscess can masquerade as a tumour → the predisposing source (recent otitis/sinusitis/endocarditis) is a key clue.
Investigations — imaging is key
📷 Image placeholder — Contrast MRI — a ring-enhancing lesion with central necrosis and surrounding oedema, with the DWI panel showing central restricted diffusion (the key discriminator from a necrotic tumour)
  • Neuroimaging — the diagnostic hallmark: contrast MRI (preferred) or CT → RING-ENHANCING LESION with surrounding oedema and central necrosis.
  • MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is key: a brain abscess shows restricted diffusion centrally → distinguishes it from a necrotic tumour (which doesn't restrict) — the crucial radiological discriminator.
  • Blood cultures (before antibiotics — positive in ~25%), FBC/CRP (inflammatory markers, though can be normal), consider HIV test.
  • Identify the source: examine ears/sinuses/teeth; echocardiogram (endocarditis), CXR (lung source).
  • Definitive microbiology: from surgical aspiration of the abscess (send for culture — guides targeted therapy).
CRITICAL — do NOT do a lumbar puncture: LP is contraindicated in a space-occupying lesion with raised ICP → risk of coning (herniation) (cross-ref Raised Intracranial Pressure).
The ring-enhancing lesion differential

A ring-enhancing lesion isn't only abscess — the classic differential (mnemonic "MAGIC DR"):

CauseClue
Metastases / Malignancyoften multiple; no DWI restriction
AbscessDWI restriction; source of infection
Glioblastomairregular, older patient
Infarct (subacute)vascular territory
Contusiontrauma history
Demyelination (MS — incomplete ring)younger, other lesions
Radiation necrosis / Resolving haematomaprior treatment/bleed
Toxoplasmosis (in HIV)immunocompromised
The DWI point: abscess restricts on DWI; tumour does not — the key distinguisher.
Management — antibiotics + neurosurgery
📷 Image placeholder — Combined pathway — empirical IV ceftriaxone/cefotaxime + metronidazole (± vancomycin) for several weeks, stereotactic aspiration of larger abscesses, treat the source; NO lumbar puncture (coning risk)
The overarching principle: empirical IV antibiotics + neurosurgical aspiration/drainage + treat the source + manage raised ICP — a combined medical-surgical emergency.

Empirical IV antibiotics (start promptly, after blood cultures):

  • 3rd-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) + metronidazole (covers streptococci, anaerobes/Bacteroides, and Gram-negatives) — the standard empirical regimen.
  • ADD vancomycin if MRSA/Staph aureus is suspected (post-trauma, post-neurosurgery, endocarditis).
  • Then tailor to culture results from aspiration; prolonged course: IV for ~6–8 weeks (abscesses are hard to penetrate).

Neurosurgical drainage:

  • Stereotactic (CT-guided) aspiration or surgical excision — both diagnostic (get pus for culture) and therapeutic.
  • Generally abscesses >2 cm are aspirated/drained; small/multiple ones may be treated with antibiotics + monitoring.
  • Manage raised ICP: neurosurgical involvement; dexamethasone only if significant oedema/mass effect (used cautiously — can reduce antibiotic penetration), and it must never delay antibiotics or drainage.
  • Seizures: treat seizures that occur with an antiepileptic — routine prophylaxis is NOT recommended in patients who have not had a seizure.
  • Treat the source: e.g. ENT surgery for mastoiditis/sinusitis, treat endocarditis.
  • Monitor with serial imaging (repeat CT/MRI) to track resolution.
Exam pearls
What it is
Focal pus collection in the brain — an infective + neurosurgical emergency.
Triad (often incomplete)
Fever + headache + focal deficit — present in <50%; fever often ABSENT — don't be reassured.
Sources
Otitis/mastoiditis → temporal/cerebellar; sinusitis → frontal; haematogenous (endocarditis, lung, cyanotic congenital heart disease); trauma/surgery → Staph aureus; HIV → Toxoplasmosis.
Imaging
RING-ENHANCING LESION; MRI with DWI shows restricted diffusion → distinguishes abscess from necrotic tumour.
No LP
Contraindicated — raised ICP → coning (herniation) risk.
Ring-enhancing differential (MAGIC DR)
Metastases, Abscess, Glioblastoma, Infarct (subacute), Contusion, Demyelination, Radiation necrosis / Resolving haematoma — plus toxoplasmosis in HIV.
Management
Ceftriaxone/cefotaxime + metronidazole (± vancomycin for Staph) IV 6–8 weeks + neurosurgical aspiration (>2 cm) + treat source + antiepileptics; dexamethasone only for significant oedema.
In HIV
Ring-enhancing lesion = Toxoplasmosis until proven otherwise — treat with pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid and repeat imaging, NOT with antibacterials and aspiration.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Bell's Palsy:
What & why
Bell's palsy = an acute, idiopathic, unilateral lower motor neuron (LMN) facial nerve (CN VII) palsy — a diagnosis of exclusion.
The core concept: the single most important clinical task is distinguishing this LMN facial palsy (forehead involved) from an upper motor neuron (UMN) facial palsy (forehead spared → stroke). Because CN VII also carries fibres for taste, tears, saliva, and the stapedius, an LMN lesion produces a characteristic cluster beyond just facial droop. It's a stroke mimic, so getting the UMN/LMN distinction right is what prevents a missed stroke.
  • Commonest cause of facial nerve palsy; ~3× more common in pregnancy (especially the third trimester and just after delivery), and also associated with diabetes (which predicts slower, less complete recovery); thought to involve viral reactivation (HSV) causing nerve inflammation/oedema in the facial canal.
The decisive fork — UMN vs LMN facial weakness (forehead sparing)
📷 Image placeholder — Face diagram — LMN (Bell's) palsy weakens the WHOLE half of the face including the forehead, whereas an UMN (stroke) lesion spares the forehead (bilateral cortical innervation of frontalis)

This is the exam and clinical point — it determines whether you're looking at Bell's palsy or a stroke:

LMN facial palsy (Bell's palsy)UMN facial palsy (stroke/tumour)
ForeheadINVOLVED (can't wrinkle forehead / raise eyebrow / close eye)SPARED (can still wrinkle forehead)
Weaknesswhole half of the face (forehead + lower face)lower face only (spares forehead)
Lesionfacial nerve nucleus or nerve (pons → periphery)above the nucleus (cortex / internal capsule)
Other signsisolated CN VII (± its branches)often limb weakness, other deficits
The mechanism (cross-ref motor pathways): the forehead (frontalis) has bilateral cortical innervation (input from both hemispheres). So:
• a UMN lesion (one side) → the forehead is still driven by the other hemisphere → forehead spared.
• an LMN lesion (the final common pathway) → no input reaches the forehead → whole side including forehead is paralysed.
The rule: forehead SPARED → UMN → think stroke; forehead INVOLVED → LMN → Bell's palsy (or other LMN cause). If unsure, treat as a suspected stroke and put the patient on the hyperacute stroke pathway — do not give prednisolone instead.
Clinical features — the LMN CN VII cluster
📷 Image placeholder — CN VII lesion map linking each branch to its sign — stapedius (hyperacusis), chorda tympani (loss of taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue), motor (facial droop + Bell's phenomenon on attempted eye closure)
  • Rapid onset (<72 hours) of unilateral facial weakness — the whole half of the face: drooping mouth, inability to smile on that side, inability to close the eye or wrinkle the forehead, drooling.

Because CN VII carries more than motor fibres, associated features can include:

  • Bell's phenomenon: the eye rolls up and out on attempted closure (visible because the lid won't close).
  • Hyperacusis (sounds seem loud — loss of stapedius muscle dampening).
  • Loss of taste on the anterior ⅔ of the tongue (chorda tympani).
  • Reduced/altered tear + saliva production, post-auricular pain.

Onset is acute, typically progressing over ~24–72 hours; usually reaches maximal weakness within days.

Is it really Bell's, or a secondary cause? — exclude these

Bell's palsy is idiopathic and a diagnosis of exclusion — features that suggest an alternative cause (and warrant further investigation):

Red flag / alternativeCause to consider
Vesicular rash (ear/palate) + severe painRamsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster of the geniculate ganglion)
Forehead sparing / limb weakness / other deficitsstroke / UMN lesion
Gradual onset or progressivetumour (e.g. parotid, acoustic neuroma)
Bilateral facial palsyLyme disease, sarcoidosis, Guillain-Barré, leukaemia — never "Bell's"; arrange same-day hospital assessment, and if Guillain-Barré is possible (ascending weakness, areflexia) monitor the FVC
Recurrentconsider underlying pathology
Associated ear/parotid signsotitis media, cholesteatoma, parotid tumour (CN VII runs through the parotid)
Systemic / other cranial nervesbrainstem lesion, MS
Ramsay Hunt syndrome: herpes zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion → LMN facial palsy + painful vesicular rash in the ear/auditory canal/palate + often vertigo/hearing loss → treat with oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days (the zoster dose — much higher than the herpes simplex dose) plus prednisolone, started as soon as possible; get urgent ENT advice and assess hearing and balance. Worse prognosis than Bell's.
Investigations — largely clinical
  • Diagnosis is clinical — an acute isolated LMN facial palsy with no other neurology and no alternative cause; routine bloods/imaging are NOT needed in typical cases.
  • Investigate only if atypical: red flags above → consider MRI (mass lesion, if not recovering by ~3 months), Lyme serology (exposure/geography), blood glucose (diabetes), examine the ear + parotid.
  • Grade severity: House-Brackmann grading (I–VI) is used to document facial nerve function.
Management (NICE) — steroids + eye care
📷 Image placeholder — Management — oral prednisolone started within 72h (age ≥16) plus eye protection (daytime lubricant drops, night-time ointment + taping); an antiviral is added to the steroid only on specialist advice; Ramsay Hunt is a separate diagnosis and always gets an antiviral
The overarching principle: prednisolone within 72 hours + meticulous eye protection; most recover well.
  • Prednisolone (the key drug): give oral prednisolone to those aged 16 and over presenting within 72 hours of onset — either 50 mg daily for 10 days, or 60 mg daily for 5 days then reducing by 10 mg a day to complete 10 days (NICE). Benefit is proven only within 72 hours, so treat that as the target window; beyond it the benefit is unproven rather than disproven, so take advice rather than automatically withholding. Pregnancy is not a contraindication — still offer it. Warn about steroid effects, and in diabetes expect blood glucose to rise sharply → advise more frequent monitoring.
  • Under 16: steroids are not routinely recommended (the paediatric trial was negative) — but do not simply do nothing: discuss with or refer to paediatrics/paediatric ENT, examine the ears and check the blood pressure, and start eye care whatever the age.
  • Antivirals: antiviral alone is NOT recommended; adding an antiviral (e.g. aciclovir/valaciclovir) to prednisolone may be considered in severe cases (evidence modest/mixed).
  • Eye care (CRITICAL): because the eye won't close, there's a risk of exposure keratopathy / corneal damage → lubricating eye drops (daytime) + ointment + taping the eye shut at night (check the lid is fully closed before taping — tape over a partly open eye scratches the cornea). Same-day ophthalmology if there are corneal symptoms (pain, redness, visual change) or if the cornea stays exposed when they try to close the eye, even without symptoms.
  • Supportive: reassurance (good prognosis but recovery may take weeks–months); soft diet/straw if eating affected; facial physiotherapy/retraining for persistent weakness or synkinesis.
  • Follow-up: refer urgently to ENT/neurology if there is NO improvement after ~3 weeks of treatment — this is a referral trigger, not a watch-and-wait point. If recovery is still incomplete at ~3 months, refer for MRI to exclude a structural cause.
Prognosis
  • Most patients recover fully (majority within weeks): about 70% recover completely without treatment, rising to ~85% with prednisolone started within 72 hours.
  • Worse prognosis: complete (vs partial) palsy, older age, Ramsay Hunt (worse than Bell's), no recovery by 3 weeks.
  • Complications: incomplete recovery, synkinesis (aberrant reinnervation → involuntary co-movements, e.g. eye closes when smiling), crocodile tears (tearing while eating), exposure keratopathy.
Exam pearls
Definition
Acute idiopathic UNILATERAL LMN facial (CN VII) palsy — a diagnosis of exclusion.
Forehead sparing (THE key)
LMN (Bell's) = whole side, forehead INVOLVED; UMN (stroke) = forehead SPARED (bilateral cortical innervation of frontalis). If unsure, treat as stroke.
Features
Rapid onset (<72h) unilateral weakness + can't close eye/wrinkle forehead, Bell's phenomenon, hyperacusis (stapedius), loss of taste anterior ⅔ tongue (chorda tympani).
Red flags (not Bell's)
Vesicular rash → Ramsay Hunt; forehead sparing/limb weakness → stroke; gradual/progressive → tumour; bilateral → Lyme/sarcoid/GBS.
Ramsay Hunt
Zoster of geniculate ganglion (facial palsy + ear vesicles + vertigo) → aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days + prednisolone, as early as possible.
Management
Prednisolone within 72 hours (aged 16+; 50 mg for 10 days, or 60 mg for 5 days then taper); under 16 → refer, do not just observe; antiviral never alone and only on specialist advice; meticulous EYE CARE (lubricants + tape at night; same-day ophthalmology for corneal symptoms or an exposed cornea). No improvement at 3 weeks → refer urgently.
Prognosis
Most recover fully (weeks–months); complications = synkinesis, crocodile tears.
Associations
Pregnancy (3×; still give prednisolone), diabetes (worse recovery; steroids raise glucose).
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Arteriovenous:
What & why
A cerebral AVM = an abnormal tangle of blood vessels connecting arteries directly to veins, bypassing the normal capillary bed — a high-flow, high-pressure lesion.
The core concept: the abnormal direct artery-to-vein shunt (no capillary bed to buffer the pressure) means the draining veins are exposed to arterial pressure → they become fragile and prone to rupture. The whole clinical concern is the risk of haemorrhage — which is what management aims to prevent.
  • Usually considered congenital (though sporadic AVMs are now attributed to post-zygotic somatic mutations); a minority are found incidentally. The commonest symptomatic presentation is haemorrhage, frequently in young adults.
  • Natural history — the number that drives every decision: an unruptured AVM bleeds at roughly 2–3% per year. After a first bleed the rebleed risk is much higher — around 6–15% in the first year — before falling back toward baseline. Deep location, exclusively deep venous drainage and an associated aneurysm all raise the risk.
The abnormal shunt — why AVMs are dangerous
📷 Image placeholder — Schematic — a normal artery → capillary bed (drops pressure) → vein, vs an AVM artery → nidus → vein with NO capillary bed, so draining veins take full arterial pressure, dilate and rupture
Normal: artery → capillary bed (high resistance, drops the pressure) → vein.
AVM: artery → direct connection (the "nidus" — a tangle of vessels) → vein, with no capillary bed.
  • The draining veins receive blood at arterial pressure → become dilated, tortuous, and fragile → rupture → haemorrhage (the main risk).
  • The surrounding brain suffers from a combination of arteriovenous shunting ("steal"), venous hypertension, and gliosis with haemosiderin deposition from occult microbleeds → seizures and focal deficits (the gliosis/haemosiderin is now thought to be the main reason they seize).
The rule: an AVM's danger = rupture → intracranial haemorrhage (typically intracerebral ± subarachnoid).
Risk factors / associations
  • Usually sporadic/congenital; the main heritable association is:
    • Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT / Osler-Weber-Rendu) — the classic heritable AVM association
    • Capillary malformation–AVM syndrome (RASA1)
  • Cross-ref the phakomatoses (Neurocutaneous Syndromes / genetics notes).
Clinical features
A minority of brain AVMs (roughly 10–15%) are found incidentally on imaging done for another reason; most come to attention symptomatically:
PresentationFrequency
Haemorrhage (intracerebral ± subarachnoid)~50% — the commonest and most serious
Seizures~25–40%
Persistent headaches~10–15%
Focal neurological deficit~5–10% (mass effect, venous hypertension or vascular steal)
  • Haemorrhage: presents like any intracranial bleed — sudden severe headache, focal deficit, ↓consciousness, seizures; a leading cause of haemorrhagic stroke in young adults (cross-ref Stroke / TIA).
  • Pulsatile bruit may occasionally be heard over the skull (high-flow shunt).
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Digital subtraction angiography of an AVM — the feeding artery, the nidus tangle and an early-filling draining vein (the gold standard for defining anatomy)
Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) = gold standard — defines the location, size, feeding arteries, and draining veins (essential for planning treatment). The differential for a haemorrhagic stroke in a young adult: ruptured saccular aneurysm, cavernoma, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, sympathomimetic/cocaine use, and coagulopathy. A dural arteriovenous fistula is the lesion that classically causes pulsatile tinnitus or a bruit.
  • CT/MRI — first-line to detect the AVM and any haemorrhage; CT angiography (CTA) / MR angiography (MRA) for non-invasive vascular imaging.
  • Follow-up after treatment: MRI/MRA, with catheter DSA to confirm obliteration (e.g. after radiosurgery).
  • Crucial caveat: a cavernoma is angiographically OCCULT — low-flow, no arteriovenous shunt, and invisible on DSA. A normal DSA does not exclude a vascular malformation: MRI (T2*/SWI, showing "popcorn" mixed-age blood with a haemosiderin rim) is the test for cavernoma.
  • In acute haemorrhage: urgent non-contrast CT head first (detect the bleed), then angiography to find the source.
The Spetzler-Martin grading system
📷 Image placeholder — Spetzler-Martin grading — size (<3 cm=1, 3–6 cm=2, >6 cm=3) + eloquent location (0/1) + deep venous drainage (0/1) = grade I–V (higher = higher surgical risk)
Grades the AVM to guide management + predict surgical risk, based on three features:
ComponentGraded as
Sizesmall / medium / large
Eloquence of adjacent brainwhether it sits in a functionally critical area — non-eloquent / eloquent
Venous drainagesuperficial / deep
  • Higher grade = higher surgical risk (larger, in eloquent cortex, with deep venous drainage = harder/riskier to treat).
  • The three-tier Spetzler-Ponce classification condenses the Spetzler-Martin grades (which run I–V, from the summed points): Class A = grade I–II (surgery); Class B = grade III (multimodality); Class C = grade IV–V (usually observation). Size scores 1 point if under 3 cm, 2 for 3–6 cm, 3 if over 6 cm; eloquence and deep venous drainage score 1 each.
Management — prevent haemorrhage
📷 Image placeholder — unruptured brain AVMs: medical/conservative management alone outperformed intervention for death/stroke, supporting observation of selected low-risk unruptured lesions
The overarching principle: the goal is to prevent haemorrhage/rupture; treatment choice is guided by the grade and, above all, by whether the AVM has bled. The ARUBA trial randomised patients with UNRUPTURED brain AVMs to medical management alone versus intervention, and medical management alone was clearly superior for death or symptomatic stroke (about 10% versus 31%). So in the UK an unruptured AVM is usually managed conservatively, with intervention reserved for selected cases after neurovascular MDT discussion. ARUBA does NOT apply to ruptured AVMs, where the high rebleed risk favours treatment.
  • Surgical resection (microsurgery) — definitive removal; best for low-grade, accessible, non-eloquent AVMs (Class A).
  • Endovascular embolisation — catheter-delivered occlusion of feeding vessels; often used to reduce the AVM before surgery/radiosurgery.
  • Stereotactic radiosurgery (e.g. Gamma Knife) — for small, deep, or eloquent AVMs unsuitable for surgery (works gradually over months–years).
  • Multimodality (combinations of the above) — Class B.
  • Observation / conservative — for high-grade, high-risk AVMs where treatment risk outweighs benefit (Class C), and for most UNRUPTURED AVMs of any grade, on the ARUBA evidence.
Acute haemorrhage: manage as for intracranial haemorrhage (cross-ref haemorrhagic stroke) — urgent blood-pressure lowering: if presenting within 6 hours with a systolic of 150–220 mmHg, target a systolic of 130–139 mmHg within 1 hour, sustained for at least 7 days. Reverse anticoagulation urgently — warfarin: prothrombin complex concentrate + IV vitamin K; DOAC: the drug-specific reversal agent. Do NOT try to reverse an antiplatelet: platelet transfusion for antiplatelet-associated intracerebral haemorrhage caused more death and dependence in the randomised trial. Control seizures; neurosurgical evacuation in selected cases; definitive AVM treatment once stabilised. Symptomatic: anti-seizure medication to treat seizures that occur (prophylaxis is not indicated); analgesia for headache. After a first seizure the patient must notify the DVLA and stop driving (6 months after a first unprovoked seizure; 12 months for epilepsy, Group 1).
Exam pearls
What it is
Abnormal tangle (nidus) connecting arteries directly to veins, NO capillary bed → high-pressure shunt → fragile draining veins → rupture.
Main risk
Haemorrhage (intracerebral ± subarachnoid) — a leading cause of haemorrhagic stroke in young adults.
Presentations
~50% haemorrhage, ~25% seizures, ~10–15% headaches, ~5–10% focal deficit; only ~10–15% are incidental.
Associations
Classic heritable association: HHT (Osler-Weber-Rendu); most cerebral AVMs are sporadic.
Gold-standard Ix
DSA (digital subtraction angiography); CT/MRI + angiography for detection/bleed.
Spetzler-Martin grading
Size (1 if <3 cm, 2 if 3–6 cm, 3 if >6 cm) + eloquence + deep venous drainage, summed → grade I–V. The Spetzler-PONCE classes condense these: A = I–II (surgery), B = III (multimodality), C = IV–V (observation).
Management goal
Prevent haemorrhage: surgery, embolisation, stereotactic radiosurgery, or observation (by grade AND rupture status — ARUBA favours conservative management for UNRUPTURED AVMs); anti-seizure medication for seizures that occur. Acute bleed: urgent BP lowering, reverse anticoagulation (but NOT antiplatelet — platelet transfusion causes harm).
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Aphasia & Cort:
What & why
Aphasia (dysphasia) = an acquired disorder of language (production and/or comprehension) due to damage to the language areas of the dominant hemisphere (usually left). Cortical syndromes = the characteristic deficits produced by damage to each lobe — patterns that localise the lesion.
The core concept: higher cortical function is anatomically localised, so the pattern of deficit tells you where the lesion is. The whole clinical skill is mapping the deficit to the cortical area — which makes aphasia one of the most powerful localising signs in neurology (and a stroke red flag).
  • Aphasia ≠ dysarthria: aphasia is a language disorder (the words/meaning are wrong); dysarthria is a motor speech disorder (articulation slurred but language intact) — high-yield distinction.
The dominant hemisphere & the language pathway
📷 Image placeholder — Lateral view of the dominant hemisphere — Wernicke’s area (superior temporal gyrus) → arcuate fasciculus → Broca’s area (inferior frontal gyrus), with superior vs inferior MCA divisions
  • Language sits in the dominant hemisphere — left in ~95% of right-handers and most left-handers.
The language circuit: spoken word heard at the ear → Wernicke's area (superior temporal gyrus) → comprehension → signal passes via the arcuate fasciculus → Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus) → generates the motor plan → fluent speech.
  • Wernicke's area (superior temporal gyrus) = comprehension — supplied by the inferior division of the left MCA.
  • Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus) = speech production — supplied by the superior division of the left MCA.
  • Arcuate fasciculus = the tract connecting Wernicke's → Broca's (allows repetition).
The vascular link (high-yield): the language areas are MCA territory → aphasia is a classic sign of an MCA stroke (cross-ref Stroke / TIA).
The decisive fork — fluency, comprehension, repetition
📷 Image placeholder — Decision tree — fluent? → comprehension? → repetition? → landing on Broca’s, Wernicke’s, conduction, global, transcortical or anomic aphasia
Every aphasia is classified by three questions: Is speech fluent? Is comprehension intact? Is repetition intact?
AphasiaFluent?Comprehension?Repetition?Lesion
Broca's (expressive)NO (effortful, "BRoken")intactimpairedinferior frontal gyrus
Wernicke's (receptive)YES ("Waffly", neologisms)impairedimpairedsuperior temporal gyrus
ConductionYES (fluent)intactPOOR (the hallmark)arcuate fasciculus

The high-yield trio
  • Broca's = BRoken speech — non-fluent, effortful, but understands (frustrated because they know what they want to say) — frontal.
  • Wernicke's = Waffly speech — fluent but nonsensical (word salad, neologisms), doesn't understand (unaware of the error) — temporal.
  • Conduction = fluent + comprehends but CAN'T REPEAT — arcuate fasciculus.
The repetition rule: repetition distinguishes conduction (impaired) from the transcortical aphasias (intact) — if comprehension + fluency seem fine but repetition is out → conduction aphasia.
Broca's vs Wernicke's — the bedside contrast
Broca's (expressive / non-fluent)Wernicke's (receptive / fluent)
Speechhalting, effortful, telegraphic, few wordsfluent, normal rhythm, but meaningless (neologisms, paraphasias)
Comprehensionpreservedimpaired
Insightaware + frustratedoften unaware of the deficit
Associatedoften right hemiparesis (adjacent motor cortex)often no hemiparesis; ± visual field defect
Locationfrontal (Broca's)temporal (Wernicke's)
The frustration clue: Broca's patients know what they want to say and are frustrated (comprehension intact); Wernicke's patients talk fluently but nonsensically and are often unaware — a useful bedside discriminator. Beware: because Wernicke's is inferior-division MCA it usually comes with no limb weakness, so a fluent, incoherent, agitated patient with no insight is routinely mislabelled delirium or acute psychosis — and misses the thrombolysis window. Sudden onset means stroke, not confusion.
Aphasia vs dysarthria vs dysphonia
ProblemFeature
Aphasialanguage (cortical)wrong words/meaning; comprehension and/or production affected
Dysarthriamotor articulation (speech muscles — UMN, cerebellar, extrapyramidal as in Parkinson's, or LMN/neuromuscular junction as in bulbar MND and myasthenia, which also carry an aspiration risk)slurred but language intact (right words, badly pronounced)
Dysphoniavoice production (larynx / vocal cords)hoarse / quiet voice
The rule: aphasia = language; dysarthria = articulation; dysphonia = voice — don't conflate them.
The cortical lobe syndromes — localising by lobe
📷 Image placeholder — Four-lobe map — frontal (behaviour/Broca’s/motor), temporal (Wernicke’s/superior quadrantanopia), parietal (neglect/Gerstmann’s/inferior quadrantanopia), occipital (cortical blindness)
LobeKey deficits
Frontalpersonality/behaviour change (disinhibition/apathy), expressive (Broca's) aphasia (dominant), primitive reflexes, contralateral motor weakness, perseveration, anosmia, urinary incontinence
Temporalreceptive (Wernicke's) aphasia (dominant), memory impairment, superior quadrantanopia (Meyer's loop), auditory/complex hallucinations, temporal lobe epilepsy
Parietalcortical sensory loss, apraxia, agnosia, neglect (non-dominant), inferior quadrantanopia, Gerstmann's syndrome (dominant)
Occipitalvisual field defects; cortical blindness — which requires BILATERAL occipital damage (PCA territory), with normal pupil reactions and normal fundi; visual agnosia (occipitotemporal), including prosopagnosia for faces (fusiform, usually right-sided or bilateral) (cross-ref Visual Field Defects)
Dominant vs non-dominant parietal:
• Dominant (left) parietal → Gerstmann's syndrome: acalculia (can't calculate), agraphia (can't write), finger agnosia, left-right disorientation.
• Non-dominant (right) parietal → neglect (of the left side/space), dressing/constructional apraxia, anosognosia.
The quadrantanopia rule — PITS: Parietal Inferior, Temporal Superior → parietal lesion = inferior quadrantanopia; temporal lesion (Meyer's loop) = superior quadrantanopia (cross-ref Visual Field Defects).
The key cortical deficits (the "A" signs)
SignMeaning
Aphasia / dysphasialanguage disorder
Apraxiainability to perform learned skilled movements despite intact motor and sensory function and intact comprehension of the task (you cannot call it apraxia if they did not understand the command)
Agnosiainability to recognise/interpret (objects, faces = prosopagnosia) despite intact senses
Acalculiainability to calculate (Gerstmann's)
Agraphiainability to write
Neglectfailure to attend to one side of space (non-dominant parietal)
Assessment — the bedside language exam
  • Test the components systematically: fluency (listen to spontaneous speech), comprehension (follow commands), repetition ("no ifs, ands, or buts"), naming (name objects), reading + writing.
  • This localises the aphasia: fluency → Broca's vs Wernicke's; comprehension → receptive involvement; repetition → conduction vs transcortical; naming → anomic.
  • Then examine for associated signs (hemiparesis, visual fields, neglect) to localise the lobe.
  • Context: sudden-onset aphasia = stroke until proven otherwise → stroke pathway (cross-ref Stroke / TIA); check the capillary glucose immediately — hypoglycaemia is the one instantly reversible stroke mimic (NICE). Then consider tumour, abscess, MS, migraine, post-ictal (Todd's) for other tempos, and HSV encephalitis (fever + dysphasia + confusion — start aciclovir empirically), which is classically temporal.
  • Imaging: in sudden-onset aphasia the first scan is not a localisation exercise — get an immediate non-enhanced CT head to exclude haemorrhage and assess thrombolysis/thrombectomy eligibility (NICE). MRI comes later, for diagnostic uncertainty or non-vascular causes.
  • SWALLOW FIRST: any acute stroke patient is nil by mouth until a validated swallow screen by a trained professional within 4 hours of arrival — before any drink, food or oral medication. A failed screen goes to speech and language therapy for swallow assessment. Aphasia and dysphagia very often coexist after a left MCA stroke.
  • Refer early to speech and language therapy (SLT): SLT diagnoses the communication disorder, delivers therapy for as long as meaningful gains continue, and advises the team and family on how to communicate.
  • Before labelling anyone aphasic: check their first language and arrange an interpreter, and check hearing aids and glasses are in.
Exam pearls
Aphasia ≠ dysarthria ≠ dysphonia
Aphasia = language (dominant/left hemisphere); dysarthria = articulation; dysphonia = voice.
Aphasia is not stupidity
It impairs language, not intellect or capacity. Do not assume incapacity: use short sentences, closed questions, writing, pictures and gesture, allow time, and involve SLT before any capacity assessment.
Before anything else
Nil by mouth until a validated swallow screen within 4 hours; check the glucose; immediate CT if sudden onset; refer early to SLT.
Classify by 3 questions
Is speech fluent? Is comprehension intact? Is repetition intact? — these three answers localise every aphasia.
Broca's = BRoken
Non-fluent, effortful, but comprehends (frustrated) → frontal (inferior frontal gyrus).
Wernicke's = Waffly
Fluent but nonsensical (neologisms), poor comprehension, unaware → temporal (superior temporal gyrus).
Conduction
Fluent + comprehends but CAN'T REPEAT → arcuate fasciculus. Global = all impaired (large MCA stroke).
Repetition rule
Repetition is preserved ONLY in the transcortical aphasias and in anomic aphasia. It is impaired in Broca's, Wernicke's, global AND conduction — so "repetition impaired = conduction" is wrong on its own. Among fluent aphasias with intact comprehension: repetition impaired → conduction; repetition intact → anomic.
Vascular link
Language areas = MCA territory → aphasia is a classic MCA stroke sign.
Lobe syndromes
Frontal (personality, Broca's, motor); temporal (Wernicke's, memory, superior quadrantanopia); parietal (sensory, neglect, apraxia, Gerstmann's if dominant, inferior quadrantanopia); occipital (visual).
Gerstmann's (dominant parietal)
Acalculia + agraphia + finger agnosia + left-right disorientation.
Quadrantanopia PITS
Parietal = Inferior, Temporal = Superior.
Sudden aphasia
Stroke until proven otherwise.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Neuromuscular:
Overview — neuromuscular junction disorders
Disorders of transmission across the neuromuscular junction (NMJ), causing fatigable weakness. The two to know — myasthenia gravis and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome — are classically contrasted by which side of the junction fails and how the weakness behaves with use.
The organising principle: MG = postsynaptic (antibodies block ACh receptors) → weakness worsens with use (fatigability); LEMS = presynaptic (antibodies block voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → less ACh release) → weakness improves briefly with use. Both are antibody-mediated and both have an important association (thymoma / small-cell lung cancer).
MG vs LEMS (high-yield comparison)
Myasthenia gravis Lambert-Eaton (LEMS)
Defectpostsynaptic — anti-AChR (± anti-MuSK) antibodiespresynaptic — anti-voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channel (VGCC), ↓ACh release
Weakness with useworsens (fatigability) — worse through the dayimproves transiently (post-exercise facilitation)
Patternocular first (ptosis, diplopia), bulbar, proximal limbproximal legs first, gait; ocular/bulbar less prominent
Reflexes / autonomicreflexes normal; no autonomic featureshyporeflexia (may return after exercise); autonomic (dry mouth)
Associationthymoma / thymic hyperplasiasmall-cell lung cancer (paraneoplastic)
Key treatmentpyridostigmine; immunosuppression; thymectomytreat underlying cancer; 3,4-diaminopyridine
The one-liner: MG = fatigues with use, postsynaptic (AChR), thymoma; LEMS = improves with use, presynaptic (VGCC), small-cell lung cancer + hyporeflexia + autonomic.
What & why
Myasthenia gravis (MG) = an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) — antibodies against the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor (AChR) → impaired neuromuscular transmission → fatigable muscle weakness.
The core concept: the defining feature is fatigability — weakness that worsens with use and improves with rest. Each nerve impulse releases less effective ACh signalling (receptors are blocked/destroyed), so with repeated activity the muscle progressively fails, then recovers after rest. The clinical priorities are recognising the fatigable, ocular/bulbar-predominant pattern, checking for a thymoma, and being alert to myasthenic crisis (respiratory failure).
  • Postsynaptic disorder (contrast Lambert-Eaton = presynaptic — see LEMS tab); associated with thymic abnormalities and other autoimmune disease; bimodal (young women, older men).
The decisive fork: MG vs LEMS vs the mimics
The rule (high-yield): MG = postsynaptic, anti-AChR, thymoma, weakness WORSENS with use, prominent eye involvement; LEMS = presynaptic, anti-VGCC, small cell lung cancer, weakness IMPROVES with use, reduced reflexes + autonomic features. (Full side-by-side table on the Overview tab.)

Other mimics to exclude:

  • MND — no fatigability, has UMN signs + fasciculations, and spares the eyes.
  • Botulism — a presynaptic toxin causing symmetrical descending paralysis that starts with the cranial nerves (diplopia, ptosis, dysarthria, dysphagia) and moves down to the limbs and respiratory muscles. The bedside discriminator from myasthenia is the pupil: botulism gives fixed dilated pupils and other anticholinergic autonomic features, whereas myasthenia spares the pupil. Sensation and consciousness are normal. Sources include food, wound botulism in people who inject drugs, and cosmetic botulinum toxin. It is a notifiable disease — tell UKHSA immediately on clinical suspicion, without waiting for confirmation; antitoxin comes through UKHSA and must be given early, because it only neutralises toxin still circulating and cannot reverse paralysis that has already happened. Otherwise the mainstay is supportive care with ventilation.
  • Thyroid eye disease — ophthalmoplegia/lid signs without fatigable limb weakness.
  • Muscular dystrophy — inherited, non-fatigable, ↑CK.
Pathophysiology
📷 Image placeholder — Annotated neuromuscular junction — myasthenia gravis (postsynaptic anti-AChR antibody blockade/destruction) vs Lambert-Eaton (presynaptic anti-P/Q voltage-gated calcium-channel antibodies)
  • Autoantibodies against the postsynaptic AChR (present in ~85% of generalised MG): they block + cross-link + destroy AChRs (complement-mediated) → fewer functional receptors → each impulse produces a smaller endplate potential → transmission fails, especially with repeated use → fatigable weakness.
  • Anti-MuSK antibodies (muscle-specific kinase) — in some AChR-negative patients (more bulbar/respiratory, respond less to pyridostigmine).
The thymus link (high-yield): the thymus is abnormal in most MG — thymic hyperplasia (around 70% of early-onset, AChR-positive disease; nearer half across all MG) or thymoma (~10–15%) → the thymus drives the autoimmunity → all MG patients need a CT chest to look for a thymoma.
Clinical features — the fatigable pattern
📷 Image placeholder — Fatigable bilateral ptosis worsening on sustained upgaze with complex diplopia — the ocular-first presentation of myasthenia gravis

The hallmark: fatigable weakness — worse with repeated use / towards the end of the day, better with rest.

RegionFeatures
Ocular (often first)ptosis (worse on sustained upgaze), diplopia (extraocular muscle weakness) — eye involvement is characteristic
Bulbardysarthria, dysphagia, "fatigable" chewing, facial weakness (myasthenic "snarl")
Limbproximal weakness (worsens with repetition)
Respiratoryrespiratory muscle weakness → myasthenic crisis (§6)
Eye involvement (high-yield): MG characteristically affects the eyes (ptosis + diplopia), often as the presenting feature — a key contrast with MND (which spares the eyes). Fatigability signs: ptosis worsens on sustained upgaze; weakness worsens on repeated testing and recovers with rest. ~15% remain purely ocular (ocular MG); the rest generalise.
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Repetitive nerve stimulation — a decremental response in myasthenia gravis vs a low-baseline incremental (post-exercise facilitation) response in LEMS
  • Antibodies: anti-AChR — positive in ~85% of generalised MG (the key test); anti-MuSK — if AChR-negative.
  • Repetitive nerve stimulation / single-fibre EMG: decremental response on repetitive stimulation (single-fibre EMG most sensitive).
  • CT/MRI chest (high-yield): look for a thymoma / thymic hyperplasia — essential in all MG.
  • Bedside: ice-pack test — ice held on a ptotic lid for about 2 minutes improves the ptosis by more than 2 mm, because cooling slows acetylcholinesterase so ACh lingers in the cleft, fatigability testing; the edrophonium/Tensilon test is largely historical.
  • Screen for associated autoimmune disease (esp. thyroid — check TFTs).
Myasthenic crisis (the emergency)
Myasthenic crisis = severe weakness involving the respiratory muscles → respiratory failure — life-threatening.
  • Triggers: infection, surgery, stress, pregnancy, tapering or stopping immunosuppression, starting or rapidly escalating corticosteroids (see below), and certain drugs.
  • Drugs that worsen myasthenia — the ones to know: antibiotics — aminoglycosides (gentamicin), macrolides (clarithromycin) and fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin); beta-blockers; quinine; intravenous magnesium (a real trap — magnesium sulfate is the treatment for eclampsia, in exactly the young women who get myasthenia); penicillamine, which can actually cause myasthenia; also phenytoin, procainamide and lithium.
  • Monitoring — the single most important thing to get right. Measure serial FVC (not peak flow), and watch the trend rather than any one value. FVC below about 20 mL/kg (roughly 1–1.5 L in an adult) → ITU; below about 15 mL/kg (~1 L) → intubate. At the bedside, a single-breath count under 20 is worrying.
  • The trap that kills: in neuromuscular respiratory failure the oxygen saturation and the blood gas stay normal until the patient is about to arrest. Hypoxaemia and a rising CO2 are terminal signs, not triggers to act. A myasthenic with a falling FVC and saturations of 98% on air is in danger.
  • Treatment: IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) or plasma exchange (PLEX) as rapid rescue, ventilatory support, and treat the trigger.
  • Distinguish it from cholinergic crisis — too much anticholinesterase, which also causes weakness but adds muscarinic excess: miosis, salivation and bronchorrhoea, sweating, abdominal cramps, bradycardia and fasciculations, usually after a recent pyridostigmine increase. The managements are opposite: in cholinergic crisis you STOP the pyridostigmine, support ventilation and give atropine for the secretions — IVIG and plasma exchange are for myasthenic crisis. If a myasthenic is deteriorating, the answer is not simply to give more pyridostigmine.
Management of MG
The overarching principle: symptomatic pyridostigmine + immunosuppression + thymectomy where indicated; IVIG/plasma exchange for crisis.
  • Symptomatic — 1st-line: pyridostigmine (an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor → ↑ACh at the NMJ → improves transmission), typically 30–60 mg four to six times a day, titrated to response. Its muscarinic side effects are dose-limiting — abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, salivation, sweating, lacrimation, bradycardia — and pushing the dose past them is what produces cholinergic crisis.
  • Corticosteroids (prednisolone) for more than mild disease, usually with a steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine, or mycophenolate) — check TPMT activity before starting azathioprine, then monitor FBC and LFTs.
  • The steroid rule (safety-critical): starting steroids in myasthenia causes a transient but severe worsening in the first week or two, which can tip a patient into myasthenic crisis. So start low and go slow — a few milligrams daily, increased every few days — and start in hospital, or under very close supervision, if there is any bulbar or respiratory involvement.
  • Thymectomy: indicated if a thymoma is present (any MG); also beneficial in AChR-positive generalised MG up to ~65 (improves outcomes, reduces medication) — even without thymoma.
  • Rescue / crisis / refractory: IVIG or plasma exchange (PLEX) — for myasthenic crisis, severe exacerbation, or pre-operative stabilisation; rituximab (especially MuSK MG), with newer biologic therapies available for refractory disease under specialist care.
  • Avoid drugs that worsen MG: aminoglycosides, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, beta-blockers, quinine, IV magnesium and penicillamine. Also flag myasthenia before any operation — these patients are markedly sensitive to non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers.
Exam pearls
What it is
Autoimmune, POSTsynaptic NMJ disorder; anti-AChR antibodies → fatigable weakness (worse with use, better with rest).
Characteristic pattern
Ocular (ptosis + diplopia, often first) + bulbar (dysphagia, dysarthria) + proximal limb + respiratory weakness.
Thymus
Thymic hyperplasia (~70%) or thymoma (~10–15%) → CT chest in all MG.
Investigations
Anti-AChR (±anti-MuSK), repetitive nerve stimulation (decrement) / single-fibre EMG, CT chest (thymoma), ice-pack test.
MG vs LEMS
MG = postsynaptic, anti-AChR, thymoma, WORSENS with use, eye involvement; LEMS = presynaptic, anti-VGCC, SCLC, IMPROVES with use, ↓reflexes + autonomic.
MG vs MND
MG = fatigable + eye involvement, no UMN signs; MND = mixed UMN/LMN, spares eyes.
Myasthenic crisis
Respiratory muscle failure → serial FVC (ITU below ~20 mL/kg) — and remember saturations and the blood gas stay NORMAL until the patient is about to arrest. IVIG/plasma exchange. Beware aminoglycosides, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, beta-blockers, quinine, IV magnesium and penicillamine. Cholinergic crisis is the opposite: STOP the pyridostigmine.
Management
Pyridostigmine (symptomatic; muscarinic side effects are dose-limiting) + prednisolone — started LOW and increased slowly, because steroids transiently worsen myasthenia — with azathioprine (check TPMT first); thymectomy for thymoma, or AChR+ generalised MG under ~65; IVIG/PLEX for crisis.
What & why
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) = an autoimmune disorder of the PREsynaptic neuromuscular junction — antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC) → reduced acetylcholine (ACh) release → muscle weakness.
The core concept: LEMS is the presynaptic mirror-image of myasthenia gravis. Where MG blocks the postsynaptic receptor, LEMS blocks the presynaptic calcium channel that triggers ACh release — this single difference explains its two signatures: weakness that IMPROVES with use (repeated firing lets calcium accumulate → more ACh released) and its strong link to small cell lung cancer (SCLC) as a paraneoplastic syndrome. The clinical priority: recognise the pattern, and hunt for an underlying SCLC.
  • Much rarer than MG; often paraneoplastic (SCLC), sometimes primary autoimmune.
The decisive fork: paraneoplastic (SCLC) or primary autoimmune?

The first question in LEMS is whether there's an underlying cancer — because about 50–60% are paraneoplastic:

Paraneoplastic LEMSPrimary autoimmune LEMS
Causesmall cell lung cancer (SCLC)autoimmune, no cancer
Frequency~50–60%the rest
Clueolder, smoker, weight loss, coughyounger, other autoimmune disease
PriorityFIND + treat the SCLCimmunosuppression
The rule (high-yield): LEMS is in most cases a paraneoplastic syndrome occurring with SCLC, but can also be a primary autoimmune condition → every LEMS patient needs a hunt for SCLC (CT chest ± PET, and ongoing surveillance, as LEMS can precede the cancer by months–years).
The decisive fork: LEMS vs MG (the mirror image)
The single best discriminator (high-yield): LEMS IMPROVES with repeated use (post-exercise facilitation); MG WORSENS with use (fatigability) — opposite behaviours, both explained by the pre- vs postsynaptic mechanism. The other LEMS-specific clues: reduced/absent reflexes + autonomic dysfunction (both typically absent in MG). (Full side-by-side table on the Overview tab.)
Pathophysiology
  • Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC): VGCCs are needed for ACh release — when the impulse arrives, Ca²⁺ influx through the VGCC triggers ACh vesicle release into the synapse.
  • Antibody-mediated destruction of the Ca²⁺ channels → less Ca²⁺ influx → less ACh released → reduced muscle contraction.
The facilitation mechanism (why it improves with use): with repeated/sustained stimulation, calcium accumulates in the presynaptic terminal → progressively more ACh released → weakness (and reflexes) temporarily improve after brief exercise — the physiological signature of a presynaptic disorder.
  • The paraneoplastic mechanism: SCLC cells express VGCCs → the anti-tumour immune response cross-reacts with the NMJ calcium channels (molecular mimicry) → explains the SCLC link.
Clinical features
  • Proximal muscle weakness — difficulty climbing stairs, standing from a seat, raising arms overhead (a proximal, legs > arms pattern); improves transiently with exercise (facilitation), then fatigues with sustained effort.
  • Autonomic dysfunction: dry mouth (commonest), blurred vision, impotence/erectile dysfunction, constipation, postural hypotension.
  • Reduced/absent tendon reflexes — which may return/increase after brief exercise (post-exercise facilitation of reflexes).
  • Eye/bulbar involvement is usually mild (contrast MG — where it's prominent).
The triad (high-yield): proximal weakness + autonomic dysfunction + hyporeflexia = LEMS.
Investigations
  • Anti-VGCC antibodies (anti-voltage-gated calcium channel) — the specific test.
  • Repetitive nerve stimulation / EMG (high-yield): low baseline amplitude that INCREMENTS (increases) with high-frequency repetitive stimulation or after exercise — the electrophysiological hallmark of facilitation (opposite to MG's decremental response).
  • Hunt for SCLC (essential): CT chest ± PET-CT; if negative, ongoing surveillance (LEMS can precede the cancer).
  • Screen for associated autoimmune disease.
Management
The overarching principle: treat the underlying SCLC + enhance ACh release + immunosuppression.
  • Treat the underlying cancer (high-yield): if SCLC is found, treating it often improves the LEMS — the priority in paraneoplastic cases.
  • Symptomatic — enhance ACh release: 3,4-diaminopyridine (amifampridine) — blocks presynaptic potassium channels → prolongs depolarisation → more Ca²⁺ influx → more ACh release (the first-line symptomatic drug).
  • Pyridostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) — may be added (less effective than in MG).
  • Immunosuppression: corticosteroids + steroid-sparing agents (azathioprine); IVIG or plasma exchange for severe cases.
  • Surveillance: continued screening for SCLC if not initially found.
Exam pearls
What it is
Autoimmune PRESYNAPTIC NMJ disorder; anti-voltage-gated calcium channel (VGCC) antibodies → ↓ACh release.
SCLC link
50–60% paraneoplastic → small cell lung cancer → always hunt for SCLC (CT chest ± PET; can precede the cancer).
Triad
Proximal weakness (legs > arms) + autonomic dysfunction (dry mouth, impotence) + reduced/absent reflexes.
The signature
Weakness + reflexes IMPROVE with exercise (facilitation) — the opposite of MG's fatigability.
LEMS vs MG
LEMS = presynaptic, anti-VGCC, SCLC, improves with use, ↓reflexes + autonomic, mild eye involvement; MG = postsynaptic, anti-AChR, thymoma, worsens with use, prominent eye involvement.
Investigations
Anti-VGCC antibodies; EMG = INCREMENTAL response to high-frequency stimulation (vs MG's decrement); CT chest for SCLC.
Management
Treat the SCLC; 3,4-diaminopyridine (↑ACh release); pyridostigmine; immunosuppression/IVIG/PLEX.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Brain Tumours:
Overview — brain & CNS tumours
Intracranial tumours are primary (arising from CNS tissue — glioma, meningioma, pituitary, schwannoma) or secondary/metastatic. In adults, metastases are the commonest intracranial tumour overall; of the primaries, gliomas and meningiomas dominate, and they are mostly supratentorial. In children the picture inverts: brain tumours are the commonest solid tumour of childhood, they are mostly infratentorial (posterior fossa), metastases are rare, and the two to know are pilocytic astrocytoma (the commonest overall, low grade, good prognosis after resection) and medulloblastoma (the commonest malignant one, midline cerebellar, obstructing the fourth ventricle → hydrocephalus).
The organising principle: tumours present through three mechanisms — raised ICP (morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema), focal deficit (by location), and seizures (new-onset seizure in an adult → image the brain). The cell of origin + location define the specific tumour.

The UK referral pathway (NICE): in an adult with progressive, sub-acute loss of central neurological function, consider an urgent direct-access MRI of the brain within 2 weeks (CT if MRI is contraindicated). In a child or young person with newly abnormal cerebellar or other central neurological function, make a very urgent referral, to be seen within 48 hours. A normal scan does not end the matter — keep the patient under review.

Driving: a diagnosed brain tumour must be notified to the DVLA by the patient, and they stop driving meanwhile; the licence restriction depends on the tumour type and grade. If there has been a seizure, the epilepsy rules apply on top, and a structural lesion means a longer period off the road than the usual six months. The exception is a small incidental meningioma needing no treatment and causing no seizures, where the licence is unaffected.

What & why
Gliomas = tumours arising from the glial (neuroepithelial support) cells of the brain/spinal cord — astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependymal cells.
The core concept: gliomas are the commonest primary malignant brain tumour, behaving along a spectrum from low-grade (slow, well-differentiated) to high-grade (aggressive, poorly-differentiated) — with glioblastoma the most aggressive. They present like any space-occupying lesion (seizures, focal deficit, raised ICP), and the modern classification integrates molecular markers alongside histology.
  • Glial cells surround and support neurones; gliomas are graded WHO 1–4 by aggressiveness.
The decisive fork — which glial cell type, and what grade?

Gliomas are classified by cell of origin and grade (1–4) — the three types most → least malignant:

TypeOriginNotes
Astrocytomaastrocytesthe commonest; most aggressive form = glioblastoma (grade 4)
Oligodendrogliomaoligodendrocytesoften frontal; calcification; better prognosis if 1p/19q co-deleted
Ependymomaependymal cells (line ventricles)can cause hydrocephalus; commoner in children
WHO grading: Grade 1 = slow-growing, well-differentiated (most benign) → Grade 4 = fast-growing, aggressive, poorly-differentiated (most malignant). Note the terminology changed with the current WHO classification: "anaplastic astrocytoma" no longer exists — IDH-mutant tumours are now simply astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, grade 2, 3 or 4 — and glioblastoma is by definition IDH-wildtype, so the old idea of a "secondary glioblastoma" evolving from a low-grade astrocytoma has gone.
Glioblastoma — the most aggressive
📷 Image placeholder — Axial contrast MRI of a “butterfly” glioblastoma crossing the corpus callosum — irregular ring enhancement, central necrosis and surrounding vasogenic oedema
  • Glioblastoma (GBM) = grade 4 astrocytoma — the commonest malignant primary brain tumour in adults; peak age 50–60; very poor prognosis (median survival ~12–15 months).
  • The classic imaging sign: a frontal mass that crosses the corpus callosum — the "butterfly glioma" appearance; typically ring enhancement + central necrosis + surrounding oedema.
  • Histology: necrosis + microvascular proliferation.
The current WHO molecular reclassification
📷 Image placeholder — Summary of the key molecular markers — IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion and MGMT-promoter methylation — and their diagnostic, treatment and prognostic significance (WHO CNS5 2021)
A major change: gliomas are now classified by molecular markers integrated with histology (current WHO classification), not histology alone.
MarkerSignificance
IDH mutationIDH-mutant = better prognosis (usually lower-grade/secondary); IDH-wildtype = worse. Glioblastoma is now defined as IDH-wildtype grade 4 astrocytoma
1p/19q co-deletiondefines oligodendroglioma (+ IDH mutation); predicts better response to chemo (PCV) + radiotherapy
